en: Now, the invocation: May Sarasvatī, who is entirely pure, the female swan sporting in the forest of the lotus-faces of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), delight eternally in my mind. (1)

Having bowed deeply to the ancient and venerable Puruṣa born from the lotus, the son of Umā, and to the auspicious Sarasvatī, the *Vikramārka-carita* is composed by me. (24) Now follows the introduction.
Seated upon the peak of the glorious Kailāsa mountain, the Supreme Lord was addressed by the Mother of the World: "The time of the wise passes in the diversion of poetry and the sciences;
that of fools, however, passes in vice, sleep, or quarrel. (3)

Therefore, in order to pass the time, some story that delights the minds of all people must be told. Then the Supreme Lord said to Pārvatī: "O Mistress of my life! Listen, a story that captivates the hearts of all is being told by me.
[Thus the introduction.
Now follows the story of Bhartṛhari’s renunciation. There is a city named Ujjayinī, where the gods are amazed by every object and which surpasses even Indra’s abode in its virtues.
In that region there was a king named Bhartṛhari, whose pair of lotus-feet were reddened by the vermilion of his queens' parting lines;
he was proficient in all arts and learned in all the scriptures. His younger brother was named Vikramāditya, who surpassed the prowess of his enemies through his own valor.
That brother Bhartṛhari’s wife was named Anaṅgasenā, who had utterly conquered the celestial damsels with her qualities of beauty and charm.

In that city lived a certain brahmin who was proficient in all the śāstras, particularly an expert in the science of mantras; yet, being extremely poor, he propitiated Bhuvaneśvarī through the performance of mantras.
Satisfied, she said to the brahmin, "O brahmin! I am pleased with your mantra-performance and your devotion; choose a boon.
The brahmin replied, "If you are pleased with me, then make me free from old age and death."
Then the goddess gave him a single divine fruit and said, "O son! Eat this fruit, and you shall become free from old age and death.
Thereupon, the brahmin took that fruit, returned home, performed the worship of the deities and other rites, and as he was about to eat the fruit, this thought arose in his mind:

"Why should I, being so poor, benefit anyone even after becoming immortal? For even one who lives for a very long time must merely wander for alms. Therefore, this result belongs to the person who benefits others for the sake of their own welfare. For it is said: 'The life of that man alone is fruitful who, endowed with qualities such as wisdom, power, and valor, lives even for a moment. Thus it has been stated:
"That renowned man who lives even for a moment, possessed of the qualities of wisdom, heroism, power, and the like, [is truly alive]."
The virtuous declare that alone to be true life in this world; even a crow lives for a long time and eats offerings.
That life which is lived in conjunction with fame and righteousness is indeed true living;
the crow lives for a long time, though it suffers while devouring offerings.
Moreover:
He alone truly lives, in whose living many others live.
Do not even birds fill their own bellies with their beaks? (6)
Furthermore:
There are thousands of petty men whose bellies are filled with the business of maintaining themselves;
that man alone is the leader of the virtuous for whom the welfare of others is his own self-interest.
The submarine fire drinks the lord of rivers merely to fill its own insatiable belly, whereas the cloud drinks them to dispel the world's torment accumulated during the summer heat.

Having reflected thus, and having considered, "If this fruit is given to the king, that king will become free from old age and death and will become a benefactor to all," he took that fruit, approached the presence of the king, and said: "Wearing a garland of snakes and clad in yellow garments, may Hara and Hari bring you prosperity, O King! (8)

Having thus spoken with words of blessing and placed the fruit in the king’s hand, he said: "O King! Eat this unprecedented fruit, obtained through the grace of a divine boon; you shall become free from old age and death."

The king, having taken that fruit and bestowed many agrahāras upon him, dismissed him and reflected: "Aha! By eating this fruit, I shall attain immortality. Yet I have such intense affection for Anaṅgasenā; she will die while I am still alive, and then I shall not be able to endure the sorrow of separation from her. Therefore, I shall give this fruit to my beloved Anaṅgasenā. Having summoned Anaṅgasenā, he gave it to her.

A certain Mathuran merchant was the most beloved servant of that Anaṅgasenā; she, having reflected, gave the fruit to him. That Mathuran merchant had a certain maidservant who was his most beloved; he gave it to her. She, too, felt affection for a certain cowherd, and she gave it to him. He, moreover, felt affection for a certain dung-collector woman, and he gave it to her as well.

Then that cow-dung carrier, having taken cow dung from outside the village and placed the vessel for it upon her head, set that fruit on top of it and proceeded along the royal highway. Just as she arrived there, King Bhartṛhari had gone out with his princes for recreation. Seeing him, even though unasked, she joyfully offered that fruit to him herself; the king also took it and returned home in haste.

Then, having summoned the Brahmin, he said, "O Brahmin! Is it true that no other fruit like the one you have given can be obtained? The Brahmin replied, "O King! That fruit is divine, obtainable only through the grace of a deity's boon; there is nothing else like it. The king, however, is the manifest Lord (Īśvara); one must not speak untruth before him; he is to be regarded as a deity. As it has been said:
"A king is proclaimed by the seers (*ṛṣi*) to be composed of all the gods.
Therefore, regarding him as a god, a wise man should not speak falsehood. (Verse 9)

Then the king said, "Someone shows such a fruit; how is that possible? The Brahmin asked, "Was that fruit eaten or not? The king replied, "It was not eaten by me; it was given to Anaṅgasenā, who is as dear to me as my own life. The Brahmin said, "Ask her what was done with that fruit."

Then the king summoned her, made her swear an oath as to what had been done with that fruit, and questioned her. She replied, "It was given to the seller of wine. Then he summoned him and questioned him; he said, "It was given to the female slave. The female slave [said it was given] to the cowherd, and the cowherd [said it was given] to the dung-collector. Thereupon the king, lamenting and falling into extreme despondency, recited these two verses:
"She for whom I constantly think is indifferent toward me; she desires another man, and that man is attached to someone else."
Yet another woman is pleased even for my sake; fie upon her, and upon him, and upon Madana, and upon her, and upon me! 10.
In forms that captivate the mind and in the bloom of youth, the increase of pride in men is utterly in vain;
for the Mind-born Lord acts exactly as He wills within the hearts of those with arched brows. 11.
Oh! The mind of a woman cannot be grasped by anyone. As it has been said:
"The leaping of a horse, the thundering of Indra, the conduct of women, and the fortune of a man;
likewise, drought and excessive rain—the god does not know these, so how could a human? (1-2)
Hunters capture a bird in the forest that has paused in its flight;
a river carries away a boat, but no one can seize the fickle movement of women.

Furthermore, by divine favor, the glory of sovereignty might belong to the son of a barren woman, and the beauty of flowers to the sky; but not even the slightest purity of mind can arise in women. 14.
Moreover: Even those yogins who always live having conquered pleasure and pain surely become deluded; they do not understand the behavior of women. (15)
Furthermore, all women, by their very nature, desire another man upon reaching the abandonment of their husbands; thus speak those of pure intention. (16)
Likewise,
without this mantra, tantra, and discipline,
women can deceive a man in an instant, even one whose wealth is wisdom. (17)
I consider a man who has fallen from his family and caste, who is base and of wicked conduct, and who is otherwise untouchable, to be dear to women once he has attained the status of a lover.
Even when established in dignity, virtues, and the assembly of the virtuous, women themselves cast off their steadfastness once they have fallen into the mire of faults. 19.
These women laugh and weep for the sake of wealth;
they inspire confidence in men, yet they do not themselves trust.
Therefore, a man of noble character should always [be on guard].
Women are to be avoided like flowers from a cemetery. || 20 ||
There is no fortune greater than dispassion, no friend superior to awakening, no protector other than Hari, and no enemy more formidable than saṃsāra. (21)

Having recited these verses, he attained supreme detachment; having consecrated Vikramārka upon the throne, he himself departed for the forest. Thus ends the story of Bhartṛhari’s renunciation. Now follows the story of how Vikramāditya obtained the throne.

Thereupon, King Vikramāditya, fulfilling the desires of gods, Brahmins, the helpless, the poor, the afflicted, the hunchbacked, the lame, and others, protected his subjects properly. He delighted his attendants and the like by providing them with satisfaction, and he won over his ministers, vassals, and others by honoring their words. Thus, through the complete gratification of all, the king governed his kingdom.
Then, on one occasion, a certain naked ascetic (Digambara) approached the king and, like Hara, sportively held snakes coiled into circles.
May the divine Varāha bestow upon you even greater prosperity.

Having spoken thus with words of blessing, the king placed a fruit in his hand and said, "O King! On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, I shall perform a fire-sacrifice (*havana*) in the great cremation ground using the Aghora mantra; you must serve as my assistant (*uttarasādhaka*) there. The king consented. Through that association, a *vetāla* became favorable toward him, and he attained the eight great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*). No one on earth could equal Vikrama, and his fame flowed unimpeded through the three worlds like the Ganges.

In the meantime, Indra, the lord of the gods, apprehensive of Viśvāmitra’s ascetic power, summoned Rambhā and Urvaśī and said: "Between you two, whichever is more proficient in dance and song must go to that penance grove to break Viśvāmitra’s austerity; to her who destroys Viśvāmitra’s penance, I shall grant a reward.
Having heard these words, Rambhā replied, "I am proficient in dance. Urvaśī replied, "O Lord, I know the dance exactly as it is prescribed in the scriptures."

When a dispute arose between the two of them, an assembly of the gods was summoned for the sake of a decision. On the first day, there was a dance by Rambhā; on the second day, there was a dance by Urvaśī. Then, the entire host of gods, having witnessed the dances of both, attained satisfaction. Yet, no one reached a conclusion, saying, "This one is more skilled in dancing."

At that moment, Nārada said, "O King of the Gods! On the surface of the earth there is Vikramāditya; he is proficient in all arts, and is especially expert in the sciences of music and dance. He alone shall provide a decision on this dispute."

Then Mahendra dispatched Mātali toward Ujjayinī to summon Vikrama. Summoned by him, Vikrama arrived; having paid his respects, he was seated with due honor. Immediately thereafter, the occasion for dancing was once again adorned. First, Rambhā took her place on the stage and performed a dance. On the second day, Urvaśī ascended the stage and performed a dance according to the scriptures. Thereupon, Vikramāditya praised Urvaśī and bestowed victory upon her.
Indra asked, "How was victory granted to her? Vikrama replied, "O Lord, in dance, the primary requirement at the outset is the elegance of the limbs. As it is stated in the treatise on dance:
'The movement of the limbs should be neither too high nor too low, and the feet should be agile.'"
The symmetry of the hips, elbows, head, eyes, and ears [is auspicious]. || 23 ||
For those who know the art of dance, there is the beauty of well-known repose, the fullness of the chest, feet that are not deficient through practice, and physical grace. (24)
Furthermore, a dancer must manifest the specific postures appropriate for the stage. And that specific posture has been described in the treatises on dance:
"With feet together and square, and hands in the *latākara* position—this is said to be the general rule at the commencement of all dances."
For her body shall become such that it cannot be seen by others at all. || 25 ||
Her face has long eyes and the luster of the autumnal moon; her arms reach down to her shoulders;
her chest is compact with firm, elevated breasts; her sides appear as if smoothed away;
her waist is measured by a single span; her hips are broad; and her feet have gracefully curved toes.
Just as rhythm is closely bound to the mind of the dancer, so too is one's own body. || 26 ||
A specific posture for dancing should be remembered:
placing the left hand on the hip with the bracelets motionless at the joint, and making the second [right] arm hang down loosely like the branch of a *śyāmā* creeper.
Her beautiful left foot, possessing great luster, completely veiled her pair of feet as they were cast down upon the mosaic floor strewn with flowers crushed by her big toes during her dance.
What need is there for much speaking?
The true meaning has been indicated by the limbs through their internal expressions;
the placement of the feet follows the rhythmic tempo (laya), and there is absorption in the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).

The soft gesture (abhinaya) has its source in the branches [of the arts]; as it follows their various modifications, one emotion (bhāva) pushes another emotion away from its object, and that very thing is the bond of passion (rāgabandha). 28.
Thus, the dancer Mayūrvaśī was praised for being endowed with the characteristics described in the treatises on dance (*nṛtyaśāstra*).
Thereupon, the great Indra, being well-pleased, honored Vikramārka with garments and other gifts, and bestowed upon him a highly precious throne inlaid with choice jewels.
Upon that throne were thirty-two statuettes inlaid.
Having placed his foot upon their heads, he sat upon that throne.
Taking possession of that exceedingly beautiful throne and the command of Indra, Vikramārka returned to his own city.
Thereafter, at an auspicious moment and under a favorable planetary alignment, he ascended the throne and ruled the kingdom.
Thus ends the story of the attainment of the lion-throne. Now begins the great departure of Vikramāditya.
Thereafter, after many years had passed, Śālivāhana was born from the lord of serpents, Śeṣanāga, in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna during the second year and a half of the Kanyā [lunar mansion] period.

In Ujjayinī, portents such as earthquakes, comets, and atmospheric fires were observed by both the king and the people. Thereupon, Vikramāditya summoned the astrologers and said, "O astrologers! Why do these portents occur daily, being seen by both the king and the people? What is their fruit? Of whom do they foretell misfortune?
They replied, "O King! This earthquake occurred at the time of twilight; therefore, it indicates misfortune for the king. And so it is stated in the Nāradīya:
An earthquake occurring at either of the two junctions [of day and night] brings misfortune to kings;
it is declared to be a comet that portends the destruction of monarchs.
If a fire in the quarters is yellow in color, it bestows fear upon the rulers of the earth. (29)

Having heard these words of the astrologer, the king spoke again: "O astrologer! Lord Śiva, being propitiated by my ascetic penance, said to me: 'O King, I am pleased; ask for immortality in exchange.
Then I replied: 'O God, if a son shall be born to a maiden of two and a half years, let my death come from that alone, and not from any other cause. Lord Śiva then said, 'So be it.
How then will she give birth to such a one?"
The astrologers said, "O King! The divine creation is inconceivable; such a person will be born in some place or other, and you shall see it for yourself.

Thereupon, the king summoned the Vetāla, informed him of all this, and said, "O Yakṣa! As you wander throughout the entire earth, ascertain and identify the specific country and city in which such a person was born, and return here immediately."

Then the Vetāla, saying "Great favor indeed," took the betel-roll, surveyed the islands beginning with Kuśadvīpa, returned to Jambūdvīpa, and entered the city of Pratiṣṭhāna. There, in the house of a potter, he saw a certain young boy playing with a certain girl and asked, "Aha! Do you two have power over one another? Then the girl said, "This is my son. The Vetāla asked, "Who is your father? Thereupon, a certain Brāhmaṇa was pointed out.
Then the Vetāla asked the Brāhmaṇa, "Who is she?"
The Brahmin said, "This is my daughter, and this is her son.
Hearing this, the Vetāla was filled with wonder and spoke again to the Brahmin: "O Brahmin, how can this be?
The Brahmin replied, "The conduct of the gods is beyond human comprehension. The Lord of the Śeṣa Nāgas united with her, and from that union this son, Śālivāhana, was born."

Having heard that, the Vetāla quickly returned to Ujjayinī and related the entire account to King Vikramāditya. The king gave him a reward as a prize for his service, took up his sword, and went to the city of Pratiṣṭhāna. Just as he was about to strike Śālivāhana with the sword, he was struck by a staff and fell from the city of Pratiṣṭhāna back into Ujjayinī. Unable to endure the pain, he cast off his body.
Thus ends "The Great Expedition of Vikramāditya. Now follows "The Casting Down of the Throne."
Then all the wives of that king set about entering the fire. Thereupon, the ministers deliberated: "This king is sonless; what should be done?
Bhaṭṭin said, "Let it be considered: perhaps among these women there might be one who is pregnant."

Then, upon investigation, it was determined that one woman was pregnant for seven months. Thereupon, all the ministers assembled and performed the consecration of the fetus; however, the ministers themselves proceeded to govern the kingdom. Thus, the throne given by Indra remained empty as before. Once, in the midst of the assembly, an incorporeal voice spoke: "O ministers! There is no such king worthy to sit upon this throne and personally govern the kingdom; therefore, let this throne be placed in a fertile field."
Having heard that, all the ministers deposited that throne in an exceedingly sacred place. After its deposit, many hundreds of years passed.
Thus ends the account of the deposition of the throne.
Now begins the story of King Bhoja’s recovery of the throne.

Then, in due course, King Bhoja obtained the kingdom. While he was ruling the realm, once a certain Brāhmaṇa plowed a field where the throne had been placed and sowed barley and other grains. A great harvest grew in that field. Thinking that the place where the throne had been set was a high ground, the Brāhmaṇa constructed a platform over it and, sitting upon it, would drive away the birds.

Then, once upon a time, as King Bhoja was proceeding toward that field accompanied by all the princes in order to enjoy a diversion, a Brahmin seated upon a platform said: "O King! This field has yielded a bountiful harvest; please come with your army and enjoy it as you wish. Let chickpeas be given to the horses. Today my birth has become fruitful, for you have become my guest; when does such an opportunity arise?"

Hearing that, the king entered the middle of the field along with his army. Then the Brahmin, having descended from his litter, spoke to the king standing in the middle of the field: "O King! Why is this unrighteousness being committed? Is this Brahmin’s field being destroyed by you? If an injustice is committed by others, it is reported to you for the sake of redress; yet you yourself have set out to commit an injustice! Now who indeed will restrain you? And it is said:
"When an elephant is itching, when a king is being carried away [by passion], or again when a deer is being taken..."
And among those who are wise yet commit evil deeds, what being here is there to restrain them? || 30 ||

"You are an expert in the treatises on dharma; why then do you destroy the property of a Brāhmaṇa? This is the property of a Brāhmaṇa, which is like poison. For it is said: 'They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brāhmaṇa is called poison. Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brāhmaṇa destroys sons and grandsons. (31)

Having heard what he said, as soon as the king, together with his retinue, was about to go outside the field, the brahmin raised the birds up again, mounted the couch once more, and said: "O King, why are you leaving? The field has borne a fine harvest; let the horses and other animals eat the stalks of the barley, and let them enjoy the cucumbers and fruits that are there."

Having again heard the words of the brahmin, as the king, together with his retinue, was entering the middle of the field, [the brahmin] descended from the platform to raise the bird and spoke once more in that same manner. Then the king reflected within his mind: "Aha! What a marvel! When this brahmin ascends the platform, the thought arises in his mind, 'I must give,' 'I must eat'; but when he descends, he becomes one whose mind is dejected. Therefore, I shall ascend the platform and observe. Having said this, he ascended the platform.

Then, such a latent disposition arose in the mind of King Bhoja: "The suffering of the world must be removed; the poverty of all people must be thoroughly dispelled; the wicked must be punished; the virtuous must be protected; and the subjects must be governed according to righteousness. What need is there for more? At this time, if anyone should request even my own body, that too must be given. Filled with joy, he reflected further: "Aha! This field itself produces such an intellect in me! And it is said:
Oil in water, a secret in a rogue, even a slight gift in a worthy recipient,
and a scripture in a wise person— each spreads by its own inherent power.
Reflecting on how this greatness of the field might be known, he summoned a Brahmin and said, "O Brahmin, what profit do you derive from this field? I wish to purchase it."

The Brahmin said: "O King! There is nothing unknown to you who possess every virtue; do whatever you deem fit. A king is indeed a direct incarnation of Viṣṇu; upon whomsoever his gaze falls, that person’s misery, famine, and other afflictions perish. For a king is truly a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa); you have come within the range of my sight today, and thus the end of my wretchedness, poverty, and so forth has arrived. How much land [do you require]?"

Then the king, having gratified the Brahmin with wealth, grain, and other gifts, took possession of that field and began to have it excavated beneath the couch. When a pit the height of a man had been made, a single, most beautiful stone slab was observed. Beneath that, he beheld a single divine lion-throne, fashioned from moonstone, inlaid with various jewels, adorned with thirty-two statues, and exceedingly lovely.

Upon seeing that lion-throne, King Bhoja’s heart became filled with waves of supreme bliss; yet, as soon as he attempted to lift the throne to carry it toward his village, it became increasingly heavy and would not move. Thereupon, he said to his minister, "O Minister, why does this lion-throne not move? The minister replied, "O King, this lion-throne is divine and unprecedented; without offerings, fire-oblations, worship, and the like, it will not move, nor will it come under your control."
Having heard his words, the king summoned the Brahmins and had them perform every ritual procedure. Thereupon, that lion-throne became light and rose up of its own accord.
Thus ends the story of King Bhoja’s restoration of the lion-throne. Now follows the introduction to the story of Bhānumatī.

Seeing that, the king said to his minister, "O Minister! This throne was previously unattainable for me; however, now, through the power of your intellect, it has come into my hands. Oh! Association with the wise leads to profit and happiness. Then the minister replied, "O King, listen: he who is not himself intelligent and does not even listen to the wisdom of others will surely meet with ruin in every way."
"You are not such a person; for even though you are intelligent, you listen to the words of trustworthy authorities, and therefore there is no obstacle to any of your undertakings.
The king said, "He alone is a minister who prevents what is harmful and accomplishes future objectives. And so it has been said:
'For the sake of bringing about the success of an established undertaking...'"
He who considers it necessary for the sake of the possibility of future gain,
and for the sake of warding off misfortune and harmful actions—
he indeed is the supreme counselor. (33)
The minister said: "O King! A minister must perform what is beneficial for his master. As it has been said:
'Those whose counsel follows the task and whose task follows the welfare of their master—they alone are the ministers of kings, and not those who are merely like elephants. (34)
Just as a kingdom without a minister, a house without grain and the like, or good fortune without youth, so too is dispassion without knowledge. (35)

The peace of the wicked, the intellect of heretics, the affection of courtesans, the friendship of the base, the stability of one dependent on others, the anger of the poor, the wrath of a servant, the love of a master, the home of a miser, the devotion to a man of an unchaste woman, the strategy of thieves, and the consensus of fools—all this should be known as fruitless action.

Furthermore, O King, a king must serve the great, hearken to the words of the trustworthy, protect the gods and the Brahmins, and conduct himself according to the path of justice. O King! All the qualities described as the marks of royalty are found in you; you are the most excellent among all kings of kings.

A minister, too, must be preeminent in such qualities; he should be knowledgeable in family traditions and rituals, and proficient in all the sciences and arts, including the works of Kāmandaka, Cāṇakya, and the *Pañcatantra*. His virtues consist of exerting himself for the sake of his master’s affairs, fear of sin, protecting the subjects from harm, the proper employment of attendants, following the king’s disposition of mind, and discerning what is appropriate for the occasion. Furthermore, the king must be dissuaded from harmful actions. One endowed with such qualities is fit for the office of minister.
Just as King Nanda’s minister, who was deeply learned, averted the king’s sin of killing a Brahmin.
King Bhoja asked, "How was that? The minister replied, "O King! Listen, I shall tell you."
Thus ends the introduction to the story of Bhānumatī. Now begins the story of Bhānumatī.

In the city of Viśālā, there was a king named Nanda, endowed with great valor. By the strength of his own arms, he reduced all rival monarchs to subservience at his lotus-feet and ruled the kingdom under a single umbrella.

That king had a son named Jayapāla, a minister named Bahuśruta who was skilled in the sixfold application of punishment and weaponry, and he had a wife named Bhānumatī. She was exceedingly dear to the king; the monarch remained constantly devoted to her, experiencing the pleasures of love with her. Whenever he sat upon the throne, he would have Bhānumatī sit on his left side, and he could not endure being separated from her for even a moment.

Once, the minister reflected in his mind: "This king, having become shameless, places a woman upon the throne in the midst of the assembly, and everyone beholds her; this is highly improper. He who is driven by passion does not distinguish between what is proper and what is improper. For instance: 'Are there no celestial nymphs with eyes like blue lotuses? Why did the Lord of the Thirty-Three (Indra) consort with Ahalyā, the wife of a sage?'"
When the thatched hut of the heart is being consumed by the fire of passion, who—even a wise man—can discern what is appropriate or inappropriate? || 36 ||

As long as one is not pierced by the arrows of women’s sidelong glances, so long does one maintain one's standing and fortitude. Thus it has been said: "One maintains one's standing for only so long, calms the fickleness of the mind for only so long, and the thread of the ultimate truth—the sole lamp for the entire world—shines in the heart for only so long."

As long as my heart is not struck by the side-long glances of this proud woman—glances that play upon the shore of the ocean of milk and possess long, tremulous, and wide eyes—[I shall remain thus]. (37)
Oh! Behold the majesty of Madana; he renders even one who knows the proper time powerless. And it is said:
"In a mere moment, the god whose banner is the sea-monster (Makaradhvaja) discomfits the skilled in the arts, mocks the pure, purifies the fallen, and truly agitates even the steadfast. (38)
And so it is said: "Learning, truth, austerity, virtue, wisdom, and the supreme reality—the fool turns these into fuel by entering the fire of a woman. (39)
People driven by desire do not perceive the events that have transpired, the end of their strength, the blemish upon their own family, or that death is standing near at hand. (40)
Having reflected thus, he seized an opportunity one day and said to the king: "O King, there is something I wish to report.
The king asked, "What is it? Speak.

The minister replied, "That this Bhānumatī sits upon half the throne in the midst of the assembly is highly improper; for the authors of the scriptures state that 'the wives of kings are not to be seen by the sun' (i.e., they must remain veiled), yet here various kinds of people have gathered and behold her."
The king said, "I know everything; what can I do? I have great affection for her; I am unable to remain for even a moment without her.
The minister said, "In that case, let it be done thus.
The king asked, "What should be arranged?"
He said, "Having summoned a painter, have Bhānumatī’s form painted upon a cloth; then, by superimposing it upon a wall situated in front, her true appearance may be observed.
These words took root in the king's mind.

Thereupon, the king summoned the painter and said, "O painter! Bhānumatī’s form must be depicted in a painting. The painter replied, "O King! I shall first observe her form every day, and afterwards I will paint it according to each of its features."

Having heard that, the king summoned Bhānumatī and showed her to him. Upon seeing her, he recognized, "This woman is a *padminī*," and he recorded her as being endowed with the characteristics of a *padminī*. The characteristics of a *padminī* are as follows: "She who is as soft as a lotus bud, whose body possesses the fragrance of a full-blown lotus and a divine scent during the waters of sexual union..."
Her eyes, resembling startled deer and reddish at the corners, and her pair of breasts, priceless and mocking the beauty of the *śrīphala* fruit; 41.
Always possessing a nose like a sesame flower and being ever devoted to the worship of the twice-born and the preceptor of the gods,
there is a certain woman, dark as the petal of a blue water-lily yet fair as a campaka flower.
With her blooming lotus-bud breasts and lovely leaf-like eyelashes, the slender woman, whose waist is most charming with its three folds, moves slowly and gracefully like a royal swan;
she possesses a beautiful smile and is elegantly attired. || 42 ||
She eats soft, light, and pure food, is firm in her conduct, has beautiful hair, and is fond of white flowers; such a woman is a Padminī. || 43 ||

Having painted her form endowed with the characteristics thus described, he presented it into the king’s hand. The king, too, seeing her depicted there in the painting, was exceedingly pleased and gave the painter his due reward.

Thereafter, when Śāradānanda, the royal preceptor, saw Bhānumatī as she had been drawn upon the canvas, he said to the painter: "O painter! You have depicted every characteristic of Bhānumatī, yet one thing has been forgotten by you.
He replied: "O Master! Tell me, what has been forgotten?"
Śāradānanda said, "There is a fish-shaped *tilaka* on her left hip; you have not drawn it."

The king, having heard Śāradānanda’s words, in order to verify them, looked at her left hip at the time of sexual union; there he saw a mole in the shape of a fish. Seeing it, the king thought to himself: "How did I see this mole situated in such a private part of hers? There must certainly have been some contact between him and her! Otherwise, how could he have known this? One must indeed entertain suspicions of wickedness regarding women.
And so it is said:
They converse with one man, look at another with amorous gestures, and think of yet another in their hearts; for women, delight is never found in a single object.
Fire is not satiated by a flood of wood, nor the great ocean by rivers;
Death is not satiated by all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman by men. 45.
"There is no privacy, there is no opportunity, and there is no man who makes advances;
in this way, O Nārada, the devotion to their husbands arises among women. (46)
That fool who, out of delusion, thinks, "This loving woman shall sport with me," will fall under her control like a bird engaged in dance and play. (47)
He who, though virtuous, makes light of their words—even if they are few, true, and very weighty—certainly incurs insignificance in this world. (48)
Just as a man, having been squeezed, is made red by lac-dye,
so too is he who is forcibly colored by women cast down at his own feet.

Having reflected thus, he summoned his minister and related the previous events. The minister, at that time, spoke in a manner suited to the king's disposition: "O King, who can know what kind of mind anyone possesses? This account must certainly be true."

The king said, "O Minister! If you are dear to me, then kill this Śāradānanda. The minister, having replied, "So be it," held Śāradānanda before the people and bound him. At that moment, Śāradānanda said, "Aha! The popular proverb that 'no one is truly dear to kings' has proven true. For instance: Who, having acquired wealth, does not become arrogant? And for which sensualist have calamities ever ceased?"
Whose mind on earth has not been shattered by women? Who indeed is beloved by kings?
And who has not come within the range of Time?
Who among those seeking wealth has attained honor? Or what man, having fallen into the snares of the wicked, has emerged in safety? || 50 ||
Purity in a crow, truthfulness in a gambler, heroism in a eunuch, reflection on reality in a drunkard,
patience in a serpent, and the cessation of desire in women— [these are as rare as a lotus in the sky].
By whom has a king been seen or heard as a friend? || 51 ||
Whomever the king is angry with, that person becomes impure even if he is pure. Thus it has been said:
"Through the wrath of the lord of men, a man—whether pure or impure, clever or clumsy, brave or cowardly, long-lived or short-lived, or of noble birth—becomes base-born. (52)
Then, as he was being led by the minister toward the place of execution, he recited this supreme verse:
"In the forest, in battle, amidst enemies, water, or fire, in the great ocean, or upon the peaks of mountains..."
Meritorious deeds performed in the past protect one who is asleep, heedless, or in a precarious situation.

The minister reflected within his own mind: "Aha! Whether this be true or false, why is the killing of a Brāhmaṇa being committed? This is highly improper. Thinking thus, he led Śāradānanda away from the others into the inner apartments without their knowledge, cast him into a subterranean pit, and returned to the king. The minister said, "O King, your command has been executed. The king remarked, "Well done! Thus ends the story of Bhāmunatī. Now follows the story of Prince Bhallūka.

Immediately thereafter, on one occasion, the prince went out to the forest for the purpose of hunting. At the time of his departure, ill omens occurred; namely, unseasonable rain, the birth of a corpse, a thunderclap, and likewise the falling of meteors.
Such unfavorable portents arose, as did the words of friends intended to dissuade him. (54)

On that occasion, the minister’s son, Buddhisāgara, said: "O Jayapāla, do not go hunting today; a great ill omen is seen. Then Jayapāla replied: "There is no certainty regarding an ill omen. He [Buddhisāgara] said: "O Prince, an undesirable ill omen must be regarded as a sign by a wise man. And it is said:
In this matter, the omen reveals to those traveling the ripening of the auspicious or inauspicious karma performed by men in previous births. (55)
One should not revile the assembly of yogins, nor should one harbor hatred toward Brahman;
a wise person should not consume poison, nor should he play with serpents.
Although thus dissuaded by him, the prince disregarded his words and departed.
At the time of his departure, he said, "O Jayapāla! The time of your destruction has arrived; otherwise, such a thought would not have occurred to you. And so it is said:
"A golden deer has never been led away by anyone, nor has it ever been seen before, nor even heard of."
Nevertheless, at the time of his destruction, the craving of the descendant of Raghu became perverted in its perception. ||57||
How could there be the destruction of accumulated karmas without their being experienced? As it has been said:
"There is no true affection among courtesans, no stability in riches, no discernment in fools, and no destruction of karmas. (58)

Then the prince, having gone to the forest, killed many beasts of prey; seeing a black antelope, he followed it and entered a vast wilderness. As soon as he looked, his entire retinue was caught on the path back to the city. The black antelope also became invisible there. He himself, alone and mounted on his horse, saw a lake ahead in the forest.

Having dismounted from his horse there, he tied the horse to a tree branch, drank water, and sat down on the ground beneath the tree; at that moment, a certain terrifying tiger approached. Seeing it suddenly, the horse broke its tether and fled toward the city road.
The prince, trembling with fear, climbed the tree by grasping a branch; seeing a bear already perched there, he was seized once again by extreme terror.
Then that bear said, "O Prince! Do not fear; today you have come to me for refuge, and therefore I shall do nothing harmful to you. Having placed your trust in me, you need not fear even the tiger.

The prince replied, "O King of Bears! It is indeed true that I have come to you for refuge, especially as I am terrified by fear; therefore, I must certainly be protected. For great merit arises from protecting one who has sought refuge, [a merit] equal to all sacrifices accompanied by thousands of boons."
On one hand, it is the protection of the lives of living beings who are terrified by fear. || 59 ||

Then the prince was comforted by the bear. The tiger also came down from the tree, and subsequently the sun set. When sleep came upon the prince who was exceedingly exhausted by the night’s journey, the bear said, "As you fall asleep beneath this tree, come and rest in my lap. Having spoken thus, the prince fell asleep in the bear's lap.

Then the tiger said, "O bear! This is a village-dweller; he will surely kill us again with his hunting. He is an enemy; why have you taken him onto your lap? Since he is a human being, even though he has been helped by you, he will only do you harm. Therefore, throw him down! I shall eat him and depart in peace, and you too may go to your own hermitage."
The bear said, "Regardless of what he may be, he has come to me for refuge; I shall not strike him down. To kill one who has sought refuge is a great sin. As it is said:
'Those who betray trust and those who kill one who has sought refuge dwell in a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings. (60)
Immediately thereafter, the prince became free from sleep. The bear said, "O Prince! I shall sleep for a moment; you must remain vigilant.
He replied, "So be it. Then the bear fell asleep beside the prince. At that time, the tiger said, "O Prince! Do not place your trust in him, for he is one whose weapons are his claws. And it is said:
*Of clawed beasts, of rivers, of horned animals, and of those with weapons in hand,*
One should never place trust in women or in royal families.
Moreover, this person is seen to have a fickle mind; therefore, even his favor is truly terrifying. As it has been said:
"Pleased one moment and angry the next, angry one moment and pleased the next—among those whose minds are unstable, even their favor is terrifying. (62)
"This one wishes to eat you himself after having saved you from me; therefore, throw that bear down below. I shall depart after devouring him, and you too may go to your own city.
Upon hearing this, as soon as the prince threw it down, the bear caught hold of another branch midway while falling from the tree. Seeing this again, the prince was seized with fear.

The bear also said, "O most wicked one! Why do you fear? Whatever karma was previously earned by you must be experienced by you. Therefore, become possessed by a *piśāca* while saying 'sa se mi rā'! He thus uttered a curse.

Then morning arrived. The tiger departed from that place. The bear, having cursed the prince, went to his own abode. The prince, too, becoming possessed by a *piśāca* while uttering "sa se mi rā," wandered through the forest.

The prince’s horse returned to the city empty of the prince. Seeing the horse alone, the people reported to the king that only the horse had arrived. Thereupon, the king summoned his minister and said, "O Minister! When the prince went out to the forest for the sake of hunting, there was a great ill omen; he departed despite it, and its significance has now become known."
"Therefore, the horse has returned from the forest empty-handed; hence, we shall go toward the forest to search for it. He replied, "Your Majesty, let it be done so."

Then the king, together with his ministers and retinue, went by that very path along which he had gone to the forest. Seeing the prince wandering in the midst of the forest, possessed by a *piśāca* and crying out "Se mi rā," he was submerged in an ocean of great sorrow; taking him up, he returned to his own city. Having summoned those who were experts in gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, the prince was treated by them, yet he did not recover his health.

At that moment, the king said to his minister: "O Minister! Had Śāradānanda been present at this time, he would have cured him in a mere instant; yet he was killed by me. Whatever action is undertaken by a man must be done only after due deliberation, otherwise supreme calamities arise. As it is said: 'One should not perform an act impulsively; lack of discernment is the seat of supreme calamities.
For riches, longing for virtue, seek out of their own accord the man who acts with reflection. (63)
At that moment, there was no one to prevent it. The minister said, "That very same situation persisted; whatever was destined to happen, such an intellect also arose. And it is said:
"Hope gives rise to an idea, which becomes an intention, and then a conviction;
one should know that one's helpers are exactly like what is destined to be. (64)

"For that which is not destined to be does not come to pass; yet that which is destined to be occurs even without effort. Indeed, even what is held in the palm of one's hand perishes for one whose destiny is unfavorable.
The king then said, "It happened according to his karma. Now, a great effort must be made regarding this matter.
The minister asked, "How so?"
The king said, "A proclamation must be issued: 'To whoever shall provide a cure for this son, half of the kingdom shall be given to him.
The minister, having caused this to be done, returned to his own residence and related everything that was being proclaimed before Śāradānanda.
Having heard all of that, Śāradānanda said, "O Minister! Present this before the king: 'I have a certain daughter; her appearance must be arranged, for she will devise some remedy.'"
Having heard that, the minister related the matter exactly as it was before the king.
Thereupon, the king, accompanied by his entire assembly, went to the minister’s palace and sat down.
At that time, the prince also sat down, saying, "Sasemirā."
Hearing that, Śāradānanda, standing behind the curtain, spoke these verses:
"What skill is there in deceiving those who have placed their trust in one? What indeed is the manliness of a killer who strikes those sleeping in his lap? (66)
Having heard that verse, the prince omitted one syllable from among the four syllables. Then he recited a second verse:
"At Setubandha on the ocean, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the sea, the slayer of a Brahmin is released from sin, but the betrayer of a friend is not released. (67)
Having heard that verse, the prince omitted two syllables. Then he recited the third verse:
"The betrayer of a friend, the ungrateful person, and the violator of trust—these three go to hell until the dissolution of all beings. (68)
Then the prince recited a single syllable;
immediately thereafter, he recited the fourth verse:
"You are a king, you are a prince, if you desire prosperity."
Give gifts to the twice-born and perform the propitiation of the deities.
When Śāradānanda had spoken thus, the prince became composed and attentive. Then he related the previous account of the bear before his father. Having heard that, the king said:
“O maiden, you live in a village; you never go into the forest. How do you know the speech of bears, tigers, and humans? (70)
Then, from behind the curtain, Śāradānanda said:
"By the grace of the gods and the twice-born, Sarasvatī dwells at the tip of my tongue;
therefore, I understand [the nature of] Bhānumatī as clearly as a sesame seed. (71)

Having heard those words, the king was filled with wonder; as soon as he drew aside the curtain, he beheld Śāradānanda. Then Śāradānanda was saluted by the king and all the others. Thereupon, the minister related the previous events. The king said to his highly learned minister: "O Minister, through your association I have attained fame and my misfortune has departed; therefore, a person should cultivate the company of the virtuous, for by that both purposes are achieved. And so it is said:
For service to the virtuous wards off present calamity and indeed future misfortune;
just as the water of the Ganges, once drunk, destroys the thirst that leads to an evil rebirth.
"Even my son has been saved from a great web of calamity through the skill of your intellect. A king should gather such virtuous men of noble lineage. And it is said:
'He who effects the gathering of one of noble family, even as one does with a serpent, that minister alone is praised, just like a skilled physician of the Garuḍa-mantras. (73)
Having thus honored the minister with various kinds of clusters of pleasing words and gratified him with garments and other gifts, he ruled the kingdom.
Having told this story to King Bhoja, the minister spoke again: "O King! That king who listens to the words of his minister becomes long-lived and happy.
[Thus ends the Story of the Prince and the Bear.]

Now begins the first narrative, titled "The Description of the Power of Generosity. Then King Bhoja, having praised his minister and honored him with garments and other gifts, had that throne brought into the city. There, he had a pavilion constructed with a thousand pillars. At an auspicious moment, seated there amidst his ministers, honored by the blessings of Brahmins, and extolled by panegyrists, he gratified the four castes with gifts and honors. Having bestowed alms upon the poor, the deaf, the lame, the humpbacked, and others, he was marked by the royal umbrella and fly-whisks as far as the head of the statue.

As soon as he placed his lotus-feet [upon the throne], the statuette spoke to the king in a human voice: "O King! If you possess a likeness to Vikrama in terms of heroism, generosity, courage, and other such qualities, then sit upon this throne.
The king said: "O statuette! I possess all the generosity and other virtues you have mentioned; what is lacking? I too have given to all supplicants that which was appropriate for the occasion."

Having heard that, Pittalikā said: "O King! This itself is improper for you, that you proclaim yourself by your own mouth! He who proclaims his own virtues is merely a wicked person; a virtuous man does not speak in this way. And it is said:
'In this world, a wicked person is able to speak of his own virtues or the faults of others, but a virtuous man truly cannot speak of the faults of others or his own virtues. (74)
Furthermore:
"Longevity, wealth, domestic secrets, counsel, the administration of medicine, sexual union, giving, honor, and dishonor—these nine should always be kept concealed. (75)

"For this very reason, one's own virtues should not be praised by oneself, nor should others be censured. Hearing these words spoken by the statuette, King Bhoja, filled with wonder, spoke again to the statuette: "What you have said is true; he who proclaims his own virtues is indeed a fool. My own virtues were proclaimed by me—this was truly improper. Tell me of the magnanimity of him to whom this throne belongs."

The statuette said, "O King! This throne belongs to Vikramārka. When he is pleased, he bestows ten million gold pieces upon those who seek his favor. For instance: 'Upon being looked upon, he gives a thousand;
when addressed, a hundred thousand;
to the great, the king gives a lakh; but when fully satisfied, he always grants ten million. (76)

"If such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this lion-throne. The king remained silent. [Thus ends the first narrative, titled "The Description of the Power of Generosity," in the account of the Apsaras and King Bhoja within the Legend of the Lion-Throne from the *Vikramārka-caritra*. || 1 ||
Now begins the second narrative, titled "The Fulfillment of the Brahmin’s Desire.

Again, just as the king was about to place his lotus-feet upon the head of another puppet, that puppet spoke to the king in human voice: "O King, if there exists any resemblance to Vikrama’s heroism, generosity, courage, and other such qualities, then sit upon this throne.
King Bhoja said, "O puppet, tell me the account of that Vikrama’s heroism, generosity, and so forth."
She said, "O King! Listen:

once, while Vikramāditya was ruling his kingdom, he summoned his spies and said, 'O messengers! While you are traveling throughout the earth, wherever you behold anything remarkable or a special sacred site (tīrtha), report it to me; I shall go there myself.'"

As time passed in this manner, once while wandering through another region, a certain messenger informed the king: "O King! In the midst of a penance grove near Mount Citrakūṭa, there is an exceedingly beautiful temple. There, from a high place on the mountain, a pure stream of water falls. If one performs a bath there, then all great sins are destroyed; moreover, from the body of whoever commits a great sin, extremely black water flows out. He who bathes there is a meritorious person."

Furthermore: there, a certain Brahmin was performing oblations in a great sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*), and it could not be known how many years had passed for him. The ashes deposited outside the pit every day had become like a mountain. That Brahmin did not converse with anyone. Thus, a most extraordinary place was seen.

Having heard that, the king went to that place alone with him and, attaining supreme joy, said: "Aha! This place is exceedingly pure; the Mother of the World herself dwells here in person. Upon seeing this place, my mind has become stainless. Having spoken thus, he performed a bath in the water of the sky there, paid obeisance to the deity, and having gone to where the Brahmin was performing the oblation, he said to the Brahmin:
"O Brahmin, how many years have passed since you began these oblations?"

The Brāhmaṇa said, "When the constellation of the Seven Sages was situated in the first quarter of the Revatī asterism, I began the fire-oblation; now, however, it resides in the Aśvinī asterism. Although a hundred years have passed while I performed the *homa*, the deity has not become propitious. Having heard this, the king himself called the deity to mind and cast an oblation into the sacrificial pit. Even then, the Goddess did not become propitious.

Immediately thereafter, with the thought, "I shall offer the lotus of my own head as an oblation," just as the king was placing the sword against his throat, a deity intervened, seized the sword, and said: "O King! I am pleased; choose a boon."

The king said, "O Queen! Is there any gift of a boon more illuminating than this supreme bliss—that you, by whose constant remembrance yogis, their sins shaken off, reach the conclusion of the farce of the afflictions of worldly existence, have come within the range of vision for one such as me and address me with affection? Therefore, you ask something merely out of curiosity: that this Brahmin performs sacrifices for a long time, yet he offends no one, nor..."
"Even though he has deviated from his vow, why are you not pleased with him? Or what kind of worthy offering have I made that you should become pleased so quickly?

She replied, "O King! He performs this sacrifice by overstepping the path of recitation (*japa*); moreover, there is no true devotion in his heart, and for that reason I am not pleased. As it is said:
'That which is recited upon the tip of a finger, and that which is recited while overstepping the *meru* [of the fingers]...'"
That which is muttered during the junctions of the lunar phases becomes threefold and partless. ||77||
In a mantra, a sacred ford, a twice-born, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, and a teacher—
whatever one's conception is, such is the success that occurs.
The Goddess does not exist in wood, nor in stone, nor in clay.
"For the deity resides in existence; therefore, existence is indeed the cause.
(79) Thus [it was said]. The king said, "If you have become pleased with me, then fulfill the desires of this brahmin.
She replied, "O King, are you like a great tree that benefits others, enduring hardship for your own body to destroy the toil of another? And it is said:"
They provide shade for others while they themselves stand in the heat;
indeed, these great trees bear fruit for the sake of others—truly, they are great trees.
Rivers flow for the benefit of others; cows yield milk for the benefit of others;
trees bear fruit for the benefit of others; and this body exists for the benefit of others.
Having thus praised the king, he fulfilled the Brahmin’s desire. The king also returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja: "O King, if such fortitude exists in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the second episode, titled "The Fulfillment of the Brahmin’s Wish," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the throne. || 2 ||

Now begins the third narrative, titled "The Description of the Sacrifice in Which One's Entire Possessions are Given as the Fee. Again, as the king was proceeding to sit upon the throne, another statuette spoke: "O King, this throne must be occupied by one alone who possesses generosity equal to that of Vikrama. Bhoja said, "O statuette, tell me the account of his generous conduct."

She said, "Listen, O King! There is no king on the face of the earth equal to Vikramārka. In whose mind there is no such dualistic thought as 'this one is another' or 'this one is mine,' that noble-minded one protects the entire universe. And so it has been said:
'The distinction between "this is my own" and "that is another" belongs to those of deluded minds; for those of noble hearts, the whole earth is but a single family. (82)
In daring, exertion, and fortitude, there was no one equal to him; therefore, Indra and the other gods rendered him assistance. And it is said:
"Exertion, daring, fortitude, power, intellect, and valor—if these six abide in a man, even a god fears him. (83)
O King! The Lord fulfills the desire of him who fulfills the wish of those in need. As it has been said:
"When men have made a firm resolve, Viṣṇu fulfills their desire, provided there is perfection of steadfastness; this is truly, truly so, O man! (84)
Moreover:
one who is endowed with energy, not dilatory, knowledgeable in the methods of action, and unattached to vices;
Fortune herself desires to dwell with one who is heroic, grateful, and firm in resolve. (85)

Thus King Vikrama, the abode of all virtues, replete with every prosperity, once reflected within his mind: "Alas! This worldly existence is essence-less; it is not known when, for whom, or what shall come to pass. Furthermore, even the wealth that has been acquired does not bear fruit without being used for charity or enjoyment.
Therefore, the sole fruit of wealth is its gift to a worthy recipient; otherwise, it meets only with destruction. And it is said:
'Giving, enjoyment, and ruin—these are the three destinies of wealth.'"
He who neither gives nor enjoys [the merit] has a third destiny. || 86 ||
And so it has been said:
"The very relinquishing of accumulated wealth is its true preservation, just as the overflow of waters contained within the belly of a reservoir. (87)
The third narrative, titled "Description of the Sacrifice with All One's Possessions as the Fee.
Furthermore:
"In regard to wealth, one should give and enjoy it; no accumulation should be made."
Behold here how others carry off the wealth accumulated by the honey-bees.
Having reflected thus, he began to perform a sacrifice in which his entire possession was given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvasvadakṣiṇa*).
Then, a most enchanting pavilion was constructed by artisans; all the materials for the sacrifice were gathered, and the gods, sages, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *siddhas*, and others were invited.

At that moment, a certain Brāhmaṇa was sent to the seashore to invoke the ocean. Having gone to the shore and performed the sixteen-fold ritual service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he said: "O Ocean! King Vikramārka is performing a sacrifice; I have been sent by him and have come to invite you. Having thus offered a handful of flowers into the midst of the water, he stood there for a moment. Yet, no one gave him any reply.

Then, as he was returning toward Ujjayinī, the Ocean, his body blazing with light, approached him in the form of a Brāhmaṇa and said: "O Brāhmaṇa! You have been sent by Vikrama to summon us; therefore, the honor which he intended for us has indeed been attained. This alone is the mark of a friend: that gifts, respect, and the like are bestowed at the proper time. And it is said:
'He gives and receives, he reveals secrets and asks them, he eats and shares [meals]—these are the sixfold marks of affection. (89)
It should not be said that affection perishes for those who are far away and increases for those who are nearby; in this matter, love alone is the measure. Thus it has been said:
"He who dwells in the mind is near, even if he is far away;
he who is distant in heart is far away, even if he is nearby. (90)
And it is said:
"The peacock is on the mountain, the cloud is in the sky,
the sun is a hundred thousand leagues away, and the lotus is in the water."
The moon is the friend of the night-lotus at a distance of two hundred thousand leagues;
for indeed, that which is a friend's is not far away.

Therefore, I must go by all means, yet I have a certain purpose here: I shall give these four jewels to that king for his expenses. As for their greatness: one jewel gives whatever object is remembered;
by the second jewel, food and other things arise like nectar;
from the third jewel, a fourfold army is produced.
From the fourth jewel, divine ornaments are produced.
Therefore, take these jewels and place them in the king’s hand.

Then, having taken those jewels, the brahmin arrived at Ujjayinī; by the time he reached there, the completion of the sacrifice had occurred. Having performed the ritual ablution (*avabhṛthasnāna*), the king fulfilled the desires of all supplicants.
Upon seeing the king and presenting the jewels, the Brahmin described the specific virtues of each one.

Then the king said, "O Brahmin! You have arrived after the time for the sacrificial fee (*yajñadakṣiṇā*) has passed; I have already gratified the entire assembly of Brahmins with the fee. Therefore, from among these four, take whichever you please.
The Brahmin replied, "I shall go home and consult my wife, son, and daughter-in-law, and then I will take whatever pleases everyone."
The king said, "Do so.
The brahmin also returned to his own home and related the entire account before them.
Upon hearing this, the son said, "We shall accept that jewel which provides a fourfold army; for thus we shall be able to govern the kingdom with ease."
The father said, "A wise man should not aspire for sovereignty. And it has been said:
the departure of Rāma, the subjugation of Bali, the forest exile of the sons of Pāṇḍu, the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, and the fall of King Nala from his kingdom.

Having reflected upon Saudāsa in that state, the slaughter of Arjuna, and the Lord of Laṅkā who was reduced to such mockery for the sake of a kingdom, the wise man should not desire that [kingdom]. ||92||
Again the father said: "Take whatever wealth can be obtained; for by means of wealth, everything is obtainable. And it is said: 'There is nothing in this world that cannot be obtained through wealth.
Therefore, a wise person, having reached a firm decision, should strive solely for wealth. (93)
The wife said: "Let that jewel which produces the six flavors be taken; for by food alone is the sustenance of life maintained for all living beings. And it is said:
'Food was ordained by the Creator as the sustainer of life for mortals;
therefore, one should never pray for anything superior to food. (94)
The daughter-in-law said: "Whatever jewel, such as a jeweled ornament, she produces, that should be accepted. And it is said:
"One should respectfully adorn her with beautiful ornaments according to one's means, for the sake of increasing purity and good fortune, and for the increase of longevity and prosperity. (95)

Dwelling constantly among friends is always a source of auspiciousness and is itself an ornament; likewise, the propitiation of the deities with jewels is an adornment even for one who wears ornaments.
Thus, a mutual dispute arose among the four.
Then the Brahmin approached the king and related the account of their quarrel. Having heard this, the king gave all four jewels to that Brahmin.
Having told this story, the statuette said to the king: "O King! That which is called magnanimity (*audārya*) is an innate quality, not one produced by external conditions. And it is said:
Just as fragrance is in *campaka* flowers, luster in pearls, and sweetness in the stalk of sugarcane, so too is magnanimity innate. (97)
"If such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this throne.
Having heard that, the king remained silent.
Thus ends the third episode, titled "The Sacrifice with All One's Possessions as the Fee," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.

Now begins the fourth narrative, titled "The Examination of Gratitude. Again, having restrained the king as he desired to ascend the throne and being questioned by him, another statuette spoke: "O King, listen! While Vikramāditya was ruling the kingdom, there was once a certain Brāhmaṇa who was proficient in all branches of learning and adorned with every excellence, yet he remained childless. One day his wife said to him: 'O Lord of my life, those who know the Smṛtis declare that for a householder there is no path [to higher realms] without a son. For instance:"
For one who has no son, there is no destination, neither heaven nor anything else;
therefore, having seen the face of a son, one subsequently becomes an ascetic. (98)
The moon is the lamp of the night; at dawn, the sun is the lamp;
Dharma is the lamp of the three worlds; and a virtuous son is the lamp of the family. (99)
An elephant shines with rut, a pond with lotuses, a night with the full moon,
a woman with virtuous conduct, a horse with speed, and a mansion with constant festivities;
speech with grammar, rivers with pairs of swans, and an assembly with scholars.
A family [is elevated] by a virtuous son, the earth by a king, and the three worlds by Viṣṇu.

The Brāhmaṇa said: "O dear one! You have spoken the truth; however, wealth can be obtained through exertion toward others, and even knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, while fame and progeny are not accomplished without the propitiation of the Supreme Lord. And it is said:
'If there exists within the heart an uninterrupted longing for happiness, one should worship the Beloved of Bhavānī, making one's resolve most firm. (101)
The wife said, "You are omniscient; therefore, some vow or other should be performed for the sake of obtaining the grace of the Supreme Lord.
He replied, "I have already accepted her words.
Why?"
A statement that is consistent with reason should be accepted even from a child; likewise, a wise person should always accept the words of an elder, provided they are not ill-spoken. 102.

Having spoken thus, the Brāhmaṇa performed the ritual worship of Rudra for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord. Then, one night, the Lord of Bhavānī—the creator of all beings, who bears a crown of matted hair and has the bull as his vehicle—manifested himself before that Brāhmaṇa in a dream and said: "O Brāhmaṇa! Perform the Pradoṣa vow; by the performance of that vow, a son shall be born to you. Thereupon, at dawn, the Brāhmaṇa related the account of his dream in the presence of the elders.
They said, "O Brahmin! This dream is indeed true. And it is stated in the *Svapnādhyāya*:
'Gods, twice-born ones, gurus, cows, ancestors, ascetics, and kings—whatever word they speak in a dream, one should declare that to be exactly so. (101)
"When this vow has been performed, a son shall be born to you.

Having heard their words, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Saturday, the Brāhmaṇa performed the Pradoṣa vow according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpas. By the performance of that vow, the Supreme Lord became pleased and granted him a son.

Thereafter, when a son was born, the Brahmin performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) for that son; on the twelfth day, having performed the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) and given him the name Devadatta, he carried out at the appropriate times all the rites from the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) up to the initiation (*upanayana*).

Then, having instructed him in the Vedas, scriptures, and other subjects, and having arranged his marriage in the sixteenth year after the *godāna* ceremony, he—desiring to undertake a pilgrimage himself—imparts this wisdom to his son: "O son! Even when you have fallen into a most miserable state, do not abandon the practice of your own dharma; do not engage in disputes with others; show compassion toward all living beings; cultivate devotion to the Supreme Lord; do not even look upon the wife of another; and do not enter into opposition with those who are powerful."

"One should act with deference toward those who know the vital points; one should speak in accordance with the occasion; one should spend according to one's own means; the virtuous should be served; the wicked should be avoided; forgiveness should be shown toward offenders; and the secrets of women must not be disclosed. Having thus given manifold beneficial advice to his son, he recited this verse:
"Enjoyments were not enjoyed, but we ourselves were consumed; austerity was not practiced, but we ourselves were scorched."
Time has not passed; we ourselves have passed away.
Thirst has not grown old; we ourselves have grown old. (104)

"Therefore, in my advanced years, what is there to contemplate that brings happiness in the final stage of life, other than one's chosen deity? Furthermore, that [contemplation] is most fitting only at a sacred pilgrimage site purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā; thus, I now desire to go to such a site. Having said this, he departed for Vārāṇasī.

Devadatta, too, remaining in that very city while following his father’s instructions, once entered the great forest to gather sacrificial wood for a fire oblation. While he was cutting the wood, King Vikramārka, having gone to the forest for the hunt, entered the great forest while pursuing a boar. Not knowing the way forward, he saw Devadatta and asked him for the path to the city. Thus questioned, Devadatta led the king to the city himself, walking ahead of him.
Then the king, having honored Devadatta in many ways, appointed him to a certain office. After that, a long time passed.
One day the king said, "How shall I ever repay the favor done for me by Devadatta, since he brought me from the midst of a great forest to this village?
Hearing these words of the king, Devadatta reflected in his mind: "Aha! This is a virtuous man who does not forget a favor once rendered. As it is said:
Remembering how little water they drank in their youth,
those who bear the weight of coconuts upon their heads would offer that nectar-like water until the end of their lives.
For the virtuous do not forget a favor that has been done for them. || 105 ||

Thinking, "Let it be; whatever the king says must be examined for its truth or falsehood," he concealed the prince in his own residence without anyone knowing, gave the prince's ornaments to a servant, and sent him into the middle of the city for the purpose of selling them.

At that moment, a great commotion arose in the royal palace because the prince had been abducted by some thief. The king also dispatched all his officials to search for his son. Then, while they were searching through the marketplace, they saw Devadatta’s servant with the ornaments in his hand. Recognizing those ornaments as belonging to the prince, they bound him and brought him before the king.

Afterwards, the servants said, "O you of wicked conduct! How did this ornament come into your hand? He replied, "It was given into my hand by the brahmin Devadatta; I am his servant," and he added, "Bring me wealth by selling this ornament in the marketplace. Thereupon, the king summoned Devadatta and said to him, "O Devadatta! By whom was this ornament given into your hand?"

Devadatta said, "No one gave it to me; being greedy for wealth myself, I killed your son, took all his ornaments, and from among them, gave this one ornament into his hand to sell. Now, do whatever you please. It was only through the power of my own karma that such a thought arose in me," and having spoken thus, he hung his head. Hearing those words, the king remained silent.

Then, in the midst of the assembly, some said, "Aha! Even though he is a knower of the sacred laws and scriptures (*dharma-śāstra*), how could he have set his mind upon such an evil deed? Another said, "What is surprising about this? Such an intellect arises only for one impelled by his own past actions (*karma*). And it is said:
"What can a man do when he is driven by his own prior karma?
For the intellect of human beings generally follows the lead of their actions. (106)

Thereupon, the courtiers said, "O King! This man is a child-killer and furthermore a thief of gold; therefore, he ought to be executed with a stake of *khadira* wood. Then, other ministers said, "Having cut him into a hundred pieces, an offering of his flesh should be given to the vultures.

Hearing their words, the king said, "O courtiers! This man is my dependent and was previously a benefactor by showing me the way. Therefore, a virtuous person should not concern himself with the merits or faults of those who have sought refuge. As it is said:"
The moon wanes, its natural form is crooked, it is cold-natured, and it becomes the source of faults at the time of the misfortune of its friend;
yet even so, it is borne upon the head by the Supreme Lord.
For the great, there is no consideration of virtues or faults in those who have taken refuge in them.
Moreover:
What merit is there in being kind toward those who do one a favor?
He who is kind toward those who do him harm is called truly virtuous by the wise. (108)

Having said this, he spoke to Devadatta: "O Devadatta! Do not harbor any fear in your heart. My son was slain by powerful, ordinary karma; what could you possibly have done? For no one is able to transcend ordinary karma. As it has been said: 'Mother is Lakṣmī, father is Viṣṇu, and he himself is the wielder of the terrible weapon (Śiva); yet even he was consumed by Śambhu. Who can transcend ordinary karma? (109)"

Furthermore, having consoled him by saying, "I cannot repay even a thousandfold your great kindness for bringing me back to the city after I had fallen in the great forest," he honored Devadatta with garments, ornaments, and other gifts, and then dismissed him.
Thereupon, Devadatta brought that prince and presented him to the king. Then the king, filled with wonder, asked, "What is this?"

Devadatta said, "The illustrious one previously stated that he would not emerge from his debt even after having performed a service. I did this solely to test your character. You have now seen proof of it. The King said, "He who forgets a service rendered is indeed the lowest of men.
Devadatta replied, "O King! You have benefited the entire world even without any cause; therefore, you alone are a virtuous man in this world. And so it has been said:"
Those beings who live with the desire for the welfare of others are indeed virtuous, wealthy, skillful, and likewise happy. (110)
Having told this story, the statuette said to the king, "If such acts of altruism and magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne. King Bhoja remained silent.
Thus ends the fourth episode, titled "The Test of Gratitude," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.

Now begins the fifth tale, titled "The Conversation with the Jewel-Maker. Then again, having restrained the King of Mālava—who likewise desired to ascend the throne—the other statuette spoke: "O King, listen! Once, while Vikramārka was ruling the kingdom, a certain merchant of jewels arrived and presented a priceless gem into the King's hand."

The king, too, seeing that brilliantly shining jewel, summoned experts and said, "O experts! What kind of jewel is this? Is it genuine or not? Determine its value. Having examined the jewel, they replied, "O King! This jewel is priceless. If we were to act without knowing its value, a great transgression would fall upon us.
Hearing their words, the king gave them abundant wealth and said, "O merchant! Does another such jewel exist?"
The merchant said, "O King, there are no jewels like these brought here; however, in the village there are ten such jewels. If you have need of them, let their price be fixed and they may be taken."

Then the appraisers set the value of each jewel at sixty million gold pieces. The king gave that much gold to the merchant and sent him along with a trusted servant and a jeweler. He said, "O jeweler, if you return with the jewels within eight days, I shall give you what is appropriate. He replied, "Your Majesty, I shall see Your Majesty's feet again within those very eight days;
otherwise, let me be punished."

Having spoken thus, the jeweler went with that merchant to his native city. There, the merchant gave him ten jewels. While he was returning along the road carrying them, a heavy rain fell. By that rain, the river flowed with both its banks completely filled. Then, unable to reach the opposite shore, he spoke to the boatman standing on the bank: "O helmsman! Take me across the river."
He said, "O traveler! This river has overflowed its banks; how can it be crossed? A wise person should avoid crossing a powerful river. As it is said:
'One should avoid from afar crossing a great river, subduing a great man, and opposing a great multitude. (111)
When the conduct of women is complete, like the water of a river, O King,
one should never place trust in the affection of merchants anywhere at all.
The jeweler said, "O helmsman! What you have said is indeed true; nevertheless, I have an important matter at hand. An exceptional task is more powerful than an ordinary one. And it is said:
'An exceptional case is surely more powerful than an ordinary one;
generally, in this world, the latter is seen to be set aside by the former. (113)
"Therefore, my crossing of the river is a minor matter, whereas the king's business is more important.
The boatman said, "The king's business is great; what is it?
The jeweler replied, "If I do not take ten jewels today and bring them before the king, the king will punish me for disobeying his command."
The boatman said, "If you will give me five jewels from among those jewels, then I shall ferry you across the river.
Thereupon, the jeweler gave five jewels to that boatman, crossed the river, and having arrived in the presence of the king, placed the five jewels in his hand.
The king said, "O jeweler! Why have only five jewels been brought? What has become of the remaining five?"

The jeweler said, "O King, please listen to my petition: having departed from this city and gone to that city with that merchant, I took the ten jewels given by him; then, as I was returning after departing from there, on the way, due to a heavy rain, the river overflowed both its banks and flowed with powerful waters."

Reflecting that the feet of the Master must be seen within eight days and that the river was difficult to cross, he gave five jewels to the boatman for the purpose of crossing the river and brought the five [jewels] into the presence of the Lord. He thought, "If I do not arrive within eight days, then due to the violation of his command, sorrow will arise in the heart of the Master. And it is said:
"The violation of the commands of kings, the disparagement of the honor of Brahmins, and a separate bed for women—these are called death without a weapon. (114)
Having reflected thus, he gave them away.

The king, too, hearing those words, was satisfied and gave the remaining five jewels to that jeweler. Having told this story, the statuette spoke again to Bhoja: "Vikramāditya was preeminent in the quality of supreme magnanimity. If such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.
Thus ends the fifth episode, titled "The Conversation with the Jeweler," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, the Legend of the Throne. ||5||
