Now begins the sixth narrative, titled "The Gift of the Kingdom to the Religious Student.

Then, having restrained King Bhoja—who, despite being a knower of the virtues of Vikrama, would not listen to a prohibition out of curiosity—another statuette spoke: "Listen, O King! While Vikramārka was ruling his kingdom, once during the spring festival in the month of Caitra, he went to the Śṛṅgāra forest for sport, accompanied by all the women of his harem."

In that Śṛṅgāra Forest, adorned with various kinds of trees, its courtyards fashioned from beautiful moonstones set against walls inlaid with sapphires, and perfumed by various incenses, the king sported for a long time together with the four classes of women—those who had taken up their roles in the pleasure-house, such as the lotus-bearers—who were arrayed in garments, betel, flowers, and ornaments.

Near that forest there was a temple of Caṇḍikā. A certain celibate student (brahmacārī) residing there, seeing the king arrive at that place, reflected in his mind: "Alas! While performing penance, I am spending my life in vain. Even in my dreams, I do not experience the pleasure born of contact with sense objects. And it is said:
"Whatever pleasure is born of contact with sense objects, that too is created for the sake of suffering"—this is merely the deliberation of fools.
Who indeed would completely reject it? Would a man strive to hear about grains mixed with husks when there are white rice grains [to be heard] instead? || 115 ||
Therefore, even after undergoing great hardship, one must experience the pleasure of women within saṃsāra. And it has been said:
"In this truly essence-less saṃsāra, the deer-eyed woman is indeed the essence;
for her sake they desire wealth, and if she is abandoned, what is the use of that wealth? (116)
"Within this essence-less cycle of existence, the woman with shapely hips is the very essence.
Having reflected thus, Śambhu indeed took Pārvatī upon his left half. (117)

"King Vikramārka has arrived here by chance. Therefore, having requested a certain agrahāra from him and married a maiden, I shall enjoy the pleasures of worldly life"—having thus reflected, he approached the king and said:

"May your side-glance protect me—a glance that bears the grace of a bee hovering and swaying over the ear-ornament as it moves, desiring to simultaneously seize the essence of the nectar from the five faces of Śiva while they revel in their passion for the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain. (118)
Thus he gave his blessing.
Then the king, having seated him upon a throne, said: "O Brahmin, from where have you come?"

He said, "I remain right here performing service to Jagadambikā. Fifty years have passed for me while constantly serving her, and during all that time I have remained a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). Today, at the end of the night, the Goddess approached me and said, 'O Brāhmaṇa! You are weary from such long service to me; I have become pleased with you, so now you should enter the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*). "
Therefore, having first produced a son, you should afterwards fix your mind on liberation; otherwise, there is no path for you. For:
"He who, having bypassed the three stages of life (*āśrama*), would enter into liberation—practicing such a course through delusion—he falls downward. (119)

"First one should be a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), then, having become a householder, one should renounce the world (*pravrajita*). "Therefore, inform King Vikramārka of your entire life story; he will fulfill your heart's desire. Thus was it spoken by the Goddess in a dream. For this reason, I have come into your presence. Having said this, he addressed the king with these deceitful words.

Having heard that, the king, having thoroughly understood the operation of that deceitful speech, thought to himself: "He speaks falsehoods without hesitation; be that as it may, he is still a petitioner, and his desire must be fulfilled by all means. For it is said:
'By giving a gift to one in distress, by worshipping a vacant linga, and by constantly protecting a dependent, a king obtains the fruit of the Ashvamedha sacrifice. (120)

Having reflected thus, he caused a city to be built there, consecrated him, and established him in that city, providing him with a hundred courtesans. Having given fifty elephants, five hundred horses, and four thousand warriors to that Brāhmaṇa, he gave the city the name Caṇḍikāpura. Then, his desires fulfilled, the Brāhmaṇa requested blessings from the king, and the king likewise returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to the king: "O King! If such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this lion-throne. The king remained silent.
[Thus ends the sixth episode, titled "The Granting of the Kingdom to the Brahmachārī," within the narrative of Vikramārka, concerning the Lion-Throne, in the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja.]

Now begins the seventh tale, titled "Restoring the Dead to Life. Then, on the following day, as Bhoja—who was overcome by his waking desires and was gazing affectionately at the throne with a longing to ascend it—was being restrained by another statuette with chains of words, she spoke: "O Great King Bhojadeva! While Vikramārka ruled the kingdom, every person lived in happiness; there was no thorn of a wicked man in the world, and all people were possessed of virtuous conduct."

The Brāhmaṇas became devoted to the study of the Vedas and Śāstras, intent upon their own duties and conduct, and dedicated to the six traditional occupations (*ṣaṭkarman*). They possessed a keen interest in the success and reputation of every caste, a disposition toward performing service for others, a lack of affection for untruth, an absence of greed and hatred, a disregard for slandering others, a passion for compassion toward living beings, devotion to the Supreme Lord, detachment from the body, inquiry into the nature of eternal and non-eternal things, an orientation of the intellect toward the world beyond, truthfulness in speech, and firmness in maintaining what has been promised.

In his heart resided the quality of magnanimity. Thus, the entire world, relying upon virtuous impressions (*sadvāsanā*) and having their inner selves purified by the king’s grace, lived in happiness.

In that city, there was a certain merchant named Dhanada. There was no limit to his wealth; whatever object anyone thought of could be obtained from his house. As this merchant, the repository of all prosperity, developed the realization of impermanence regarding all things—thinking, "This worldly existence is essence-less; every category of object, however difficult it may be to obtain, is impermanent"—for it is said: [The verse follows: *anityāni śarīrāṇi vibhavo naiva śāśvataḥ | nityaṃ saṃnihito mṛtyuḥ kartavyo dharmasaṅgrahaḥ ||* (Bodies are impermanent, wealth is not eternal, death is ever-present; therefore, one should accumulate merit.)
The meeting with beloved ones is like a city in the sky;
youth, wealth, one's own kin, children, the body, and so forth, are like a mass of clouds or as flickering as lightning.
Know that the entire course of worldly existence is momentary. 121.
And it has been said:
"A refuge is no refuge, and a kinsman is the root of bondage;
even that which is a refuge is, from another perspective, the gateway to the graspings of calamity."
O sons of impaired intellect, you enemies, abandon all this and take refuge in the stainless Dharma that severs the noose of karma. 122.
For those wandering in saṃsāra, dharma alone is their refuge;
and thus it has been said: "Dharma, when protected, protects; indeed, when destroyed, it surely slays living beings."
Therefore, that very [self] which is to be slain is in every way the refuge for those wandering in saṃsāra;
for Dharma brings about prosperity in this world, and thus yogins meditate upon it.
There is no friend other than Dharma, nor are there any who are happy or wise apart from the righteous Dharma. (123)
And so,
Dharma is capable of ordaining the essence of the city of the serpent-dwelling Śarmā;
furthermore, Dharma always bestows eternal joy even upon mortal beings.
Dharma is the abode for the arising of the experience of uninterrupted happiness on the mountain of heaven;

what does Dharma not accomplish—does it not produce a body fit for the enjoyment of the maiden that is liberation? (124) Therefore, a wise person should give wealth acquired for the sake of gathering merit to a worthy recipient.
When given to such a person, that gift becomes manifold in its merit. As it has been said:
"In this world, wealth bestowed upon a distinguished recipient acquires a different quality for the donor;
just as water poured into a pearl-oyster shell produces a pearl from the cloud. (125)
Moreover,
just as a tiny seed of the nyagrodha tree, when sown in fertile soil,
attains great expansion, so too does a gift bestowed upon a worthy recipient.

Having reflected thus in many ways, he summoned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and Brahmins; from them, he heard the descriptions of the gifts of cows, maidens, knowledge, land, and water as set forth in the *Dānakhaṇḍa* of Hemādri. Having bestowed those gifts upon worthy recipients and possessing a purified inner heart, he reflected again: "This practice of giving, vows, and so forth performed by me will bear fruit only when I go to Dvāravatī and behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having thus resolved, he departed toward the city of Śrīnivāsa.

Then, having gone to the seashore and summoned a boatman, he gave him abundant wealth; and having embarked the mendicants, yogis, foreigners, the destitute, and others, as he traveled with them while engaging in pleasant conversation and religious discourse, a certain small mountain was seen in the midst of the ocean. Upon that mountain stood a great temple.

Then, having gone to that temple and worshipped the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and having offered his salutations, as soon as he cast his gaze toward her left side, he saw a headless couple—a man and a woman—and beheld inscribed upon the surface of the wall standing before him these words: "If anyone who is benevolent toward others and endowed with great fortitude worships Bhuvaneśvarī with the blood from his own throat, then this couple shall become alive."

"It shall be so. Having thus read what was written, Dhanada, filled with wonder, again boarded the ship and went to Dvārāvatī. There, upon seeing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he realized that even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of ten horse-sacrifices.
One who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but one who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return for the sake of rebirth. || 127 ||

Thus, reflecting upon how bowing to Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the means for attaining the fruit of liberation, he prostrated before Him with all eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga-praṇāma), worshipped Him with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and returned to his own city. Then, after greeting all his kinsmen by bestowing the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon them, he took some unprecedented object and went to have an audience with the King. For it is said:
"One should not see a king, a deity, or a guru with empty hands;
especially on special occasions, one should present a fruit as a gift. (128)
Likewise, one should not see a beloved wife, a dear friend, or a very young son with empty hands; nor should one see an astrologer or the king with empty hands. 129
Then, having placed the gift from Kṛṣṇa’s grace and the offering into the king’s hand, he sat down.
Thereupon, the king, having inquired after his safe journey, asked that Dhanada about some unprecedented account.
He, too, related the story of the temple of the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī situated in the midst of the ocean.

Hearing that, the king, filled with wonder, went to that place together with the giver of wealth (Kubera) and beheld a pair of headless trunks situated on the left side of the deity in the temple. Thereafter, having fixed his mind upon the deity, just as he was about to strike his own neck with a sword, the two trunks suddenly became possessed of heads and restored to life.
The deity also, drawing the sword from the king's hand, said: "O King, I am pleased; choose a boon."
The king said, "O Queen! If you are pleased, then grant the kingdom to this couple.

Thereupon, the queen granted the kingdom to that couple, and the king, together with Dhanada, returned to his own city. Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja, "O King! If such power to perform altruistic deeds exists in you, then sit upon this throne."
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the seventh episode, titled "The Resuscitation of the Dead," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja, in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the service of the throne. 7.

Now begins the eighth narrative, titled "The Filling of the Lake. Then, seated as before near the throne, the lord of the earth—overcome by the impetuous force of his curiosity and delight—was addressed by one of the mechanical dolls: "Listen, O King! King Vikrama is renowned throughout the world; he is filled with various diversions and wonders, and likewise, he learns of the curiosities and events of others through the mouths of his spies. As it has been said:
'Cows see by scent, and the twice-born by the Vedas.'"
Kings see through their spies, while other people see with their eyes. ||130||

Listen, O King! That one who is a king must understand the entire order of the world, he must comprehend the minds of all, his subjects must be protected properly, the wicked must be punished, wealth must be acquired through justice, and impartiality must be maintained toward petitioners; these indeed are the five great sacrificial duties (*pañcamahāyajña*) of a king. And it has been said: "Punishment of the wicked, honor for the virtuous, and the just increase of the treasury."
Impartiality toward supplicants and the protection of the kingdom—
these alone are declared to be the five sacrifices of kings.
Moreover,
what is the business of fate for kings, or what is their conflict with adversaries?
That is the work of the gods— recitation, sacrifice, and oblation—
when tears do not fall upon the kingdom.

While Vikrama was thus ruling the kingdom, once some spies, having traversed the earth, returned to the presence of the king. When questioned by the king, they said: "O Lord, there dwells in the land of Kashmir a certain merchant possessed of great wealth. That merchant has excavated a lake five *krośas* in extent; in the midst of it, he has caused a bed for Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa reclining upon the water to be constructed within a newly built, divine palace, yet the water does not reach it."

Furthermore, that merchant had the Brahmins perform recitations, worship, fire-offerings, consecrations, and other rites dedicated to Cakrin for the purpose of making water rise; nevertheless, the water did not emerge. Consequently, becoming deeply distressed, the merchant sat upon the embankment of the pond and sighed every day, saying: "Alas! By no means does the water appear; our labor has become in vain."

Once, while the merchant sat upon the embankment of that pond with his mind absorbed in thoughts regarding the arrival of water, a superhuman voice suddenly arose in the sky: "O merchant's son, why do you sigh? When this pond is sprinkled with the blood from the throat of a man endowed with the thirty-two marks, then pure water will emerge here; not otherwise."

Having heard that, the merchant established a great almshouse for food on the shore of the lake. All people living in foreign lands came to that almshouse to eat. While they were staying there, the officials spoke thus in the presence of those foreigners: "Whoever shall sprinkle this tank with the blood from his own neck, marked by the thirty-two auspicious signs, to him a hundred bhāras of gold shall be given.
Everyone heard these words, yet it was seen as a great marvel that no one immediately accepted them.

Having heard their words, King Vikramārka went there himself; seeing the most enchanting and vast great temple of Viṣṇu situated by the reservoir, as well as the lake itself, he was filled with wonder and reflected in his mind: "If I sprinkle this lake with the blood from my own throat, it will undoubtedly become full of water, and thereby it will bring benefit to all the world."

This body of mine, even if it were to remain for a full hundred years, will ultimately meet with destruction; therefore, a great person endowed with the knowledge of what is real and what is unreal should not harbor a sense of "mine-ness" toward the body. For the sake of benefiting others, even the body must be given away. As it has been said:
"Even after sustaining life for a hundred years, one who lies upon his bed meets with total destruction."
Those who do not harbor a sense of "mine" toward a body that is easily subject to calamity—an object of universal reproach—are indeed transcendent beings. 133.
The cage-like body of embodied beings is always assailed by disease, is always a dwelling place of sorrow, and is always on the verge of falling apart. (134)
By those very meritorious deeds, this fruit has been secured by them who, having become detached from birth for their own sake, did not subject the body to hardship. (135)

Having reflected thus, he performed worship to Viṣṇu, who was reclining upon the waters in the palace situated before him, and after bowing down, he said: "O Goddess of Water! If you desire the blood from the throat of a man endowed with the thirty-two marks, then, being satisfied by this blood of mine offered with joy, fill this pond completely with water. Having said this, just as he raised his sword to strike his own throat, that goddess—
Holding his sword, he said, "O Hero! I am pleased with this magnanimity of yours; choose a boon.

The king replied, "O Queen! If you have become pleased with me, then fill this pond with water. Again the goddess said, "O King! Depart quickly from this place; as soon as you see it while departing, it will be filled with water."

Hearing that, the king went quickly to the embankment of the tank, and the tank became filled with water. Beholding such a marvel, King Vikrama, filled with joy, returned to his own city. Having thus told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "O King! If such magnanimity, as well as virtues such as the essence of altruism and courage, exist in you, then sit upon that throne."
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the eighth episode, titled "The Filling of the Lake," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 8.

Now begins the ninth narrative, titled "The Slaying of the Rākṣasa. Then Bhoja, his heart filled with longing, was about to ascend the throne when he was stopped by another puppet, which addressed him, saying: "O King, this throne must be occupied only by one who possesses valor, generosity, and other such qualities equal to those of Vikrama. Bhoja replied, "O puppet, tell me the account of his valor and generosity!"

She said: "O Lord of the world of men! While Vikrama was ruling the kingdom, Bhaṭṭi was the minister, Govinda the vice-minister, Candraśekhara the commander-in-chief, and Trivikrama the family priest. There, Trivikrama’s son was Kamalākara; by his father's favor, having eaten rice with ghee and being well-nourished in body through garments, ornaments, betel, and other luxuries, he remained there enjoying the pleasures of the senses."

Once his father said, "O son! Having attained birth as a Brāhmaṇa, how is it that you live in this manner according to your own whims? This self undergoes various births for hundreds of lifetimes. Birth in a Brāhmaṇa family is obtained through great merit; having obtained it, why have you become so ill-behaved? You always dwell outside and only come home at mealtime; this which you do is improper. This is your time for the study of knowledge."
If you do not engage in the study of knowledge at this time, there will be great mental anguish later on; for:
"Those who do not study knowledge during childhood, being afflicted by desire and having their minds lost in youth..."
In their old age, being treated with contempt,
they burn with cold even when naked in winter. Furthermore,
those who possess neither knowledge, nor austerity, nor charity—
Possessing neither virtue, nor excellence, nor righteousness, they are indeed a burden upon the world of mortals;
in human form, they roam like wild beasts. 137.
In this worldly existence, there is no ornament for a man superior to knowledge. And it has been said: Knowledge is a man’s supreme beauty; it is hidden and protected wealth;
knowledge provides enjoyment, fame, and happiness; and knowledge is the teacher of teachers.
Knowledge is one's kinsman when traveling abroad; knowledge is the supreme deity;
knowledge is honored among kings, for wealth is not—indeed, one devoid of knowledge is but a beast. 138.
Moreover, what is the use of a vast lineage for an embodied being devoid of learning?
Even one of low birth who is wise is honored by all. (139)
O son! As long as I live, you must devote yourself solely to the study of knowledge. For:

as long as this body is healthy and free from disease, as long as old age is far off, as long as the power of the senses is unimpaired, and as long as there is no exhaustion of one's lifespan—so long should one strive for learning.
A wise person should exert great effort toward their own welfare only so long as [the danger] has not yet arrived;
for when the house is already ablaze, what kind of endeavor is it to dig a well? || 140 ||
Moreover, knowledge that has been mastered will perform every function of a kinsman for you. As it is said:
"Like a mother, it protects; like a father, it enjoins one to what is beneficial; and like a beloved wife, it brings delight by removing all weariness."
What does knowledge not accomplish, like a wish-fulfilling creeper? It spreads prosperity and extends fame in all directions. || 141 ||

Having heard those words of his father, Kamalākara was filled with remorse and said, "When I have become omniscient, only then shall I show my face to my father. Having said this, he departed for the land of Kaśmīra. Arriving there in the presence of the teacher Candramauli Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, he prostrated himself like a staff and said, "O venerable master, I am a fool; having heard your name and the weight of your virtues, I have come here for the purpose of studying the sciences."

"Having shown compassion toward me, may you, O illustrious ones, act in such a way that knowledge may be attained by me," he said, and again prostrated himself like a staff. When they had consented, he performed service for them day and night. For it is said:
"Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, or by abundant wealth;
or else, knowledge is acquired through knowledge—a fourth means does not exist. (142)

As he was thus performing his service, a great deal of time passed. Once, the preceptor, having conceived compassion for him, bestowed upon him the instruction of the Siddhasārasvata mantra. By means of that instruction, Kamalākara became omniscient; then, taking leave of his preceptor, as he was returning to his own city, he reached the city of Kāñcī by way of the road. There, King Narasena reigned.
In that city there was a certain courtesan named Naramohinī; she was peerless in beauty, and whoever beheld her became afflicted by the fever of passion and fell into a state of madness.

Furthermore, having heard the rumor that "whosoever sleeps with her after their enjoyment, a certain Rākṣasa dwelling on the Vindhya mountain comes there and drinks his blood, whereby he becomes lifeless," Kamalākara remained there; and having witnessed this marvel with his own eyes, he returned to his own city. Upon seeing him returned home after a very long time, adorned with the virtues of learning, humility, and other qualities, great joy arose in the hearts of his parents. And so it is said:
even many sons devoid of learning [are better than one who is not].

What is the use of these [worldly pleasures] for a father whose life lasts for an eon? Even if they were to exist, his delight would be like that of the ocean at the sight of the moon— transient and merely partial.

On the second day, having gone to the royal palace with his father, he offered blessings to the king and displayed his own cleverness in the assembly. Then, after Vikramārka had honored him with garments and other gifts, he asked: "O Kamalākara! What wonder did you see in the land where you went?
He replied, "O King! Nothing at all was seen in that land; however, on the occasion of my return, I saw one unprecedented marvel in the city of Kāñcī."

The king said, "Tell me, what was seen? Kamalākara replied, "In the city of Kāñcī, ruled by King Narasena, there is a certain beautiful courtesan named Naramohinī. Whoever beholds her falls into a state of madness; furthermore, whoever sleeps with her at night, a certain Rākṣasa dwelling on the Vindhya mountains comes there and drinks his blood, whereupon he becomes lifeless. This marvel was witnessed by me."
Having heard that, the king said, "If it is so, then you come; let us go there.
Then, having arrived at the city of Kāñcī with him, the king, filled with curiosity, went to Naramohinī's house. Upon seeing her beauty, he was struck with wonder.

She honored him with the washing of his feet, anointing, fragrant flowers, and other offerings; and she said, "O King! Today I have become blessed, and my home has become praiseworthy through the grace of your presence. Thereupon, she gave him a betel-roll (*vīṭikā*).

The king, having taken her, spent some time with her in sweet and blameless conversation. Then she spoke to the king with humility: "O King, this place is not empty of danger; whoever other than myself sleeps here at night is found lifeless at dawn. This has been reported to you so that you may take precautions; let whatever is appropriate in this matter be carried out," and she ceased speaking.

Then the king, who had already learned the circumstances, spoke with the granting of safety as his preface: "Now, you may rest in peaceful sleep; I shall strive for what is appropriate to provide a remedy for that."

Thus, when the first watch of the night had passed, Naramohinī fell asleep; at the end of the second watch, a Rākṣasa of terrifying appearance, with hideous fangs and a craving for human blood, arrived there with a fierce roar. But the king, remaining awake and undaunted in heart, gave him no opportunity for battle and struck him down instantly with his sharp sword.

Awakened from her sleep by the sound of his falling, that woman who infatuates men saw the Rākṣasa slain and spoke with humility to the king: "O King! That you, such as you are, should show such perfect compassion toward a person like me, who possesses nothing, is solely due to the impartiality of the great toward both high and low, like the rays of the moon. By your grace, I have become fearless; from this day forward, my affliction by the Rākṣasa has ceased.
How can I ever repay the favor bestowed by you?"

"Having slain that night-stalker of wicked conduct who was destroying the lives of many creatures, I have protected my own dharma; by that very act, great satisfaction has arisen within me. There is nothing further for you to do here," said Kamalākara, and he set out toward Ujjayinī together with him.
Having told this story, the statuette addressed King Bhoja: "O King! If such fortitude, heroism, magnanimity, and other virtues exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the ninth episode, titled "The Slaying of the Rākṣasa," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 9.
Now begins the tenth narrative, titled "The Bestowal of the Fruits of Sacrificial Attainments.

Again, another statuette spoke to Bhoja, who was desirous of ascending that very throne: "Listen, O King! While Vikramārka was ruling the kingdom, a certain yogi arrived at Ujjayinī. He was an expert in all the arts, including the Vedas, the Shastras, medicine, astrology, and the Bharata-śāstra; what more need be said? There was no one else like him; he was truly omniscient."

Once, King Vikrama, having heard of his fame, dispatched his domestic priest to summon him. The priest went to him, paid his respects, and said, "O Master, the king summons you; you must come there. The yogi replied, "In that case, I shall go. Then, having gone there, he said to the king, "O King, if you perform the practice of this mantra, you will thereby become free from old age and death. The king said, "Teach me the mantra; I shall perform its practice."

Then the yogin, having instructed him in the mantra, said: "O King! Having recited this mantra for one year while observing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), you shall perform an oblation (*havana*) in the fire with *dūrvā* sprouts numbering one-tenth of the recitation. Then, at the time of the final offering (*pūrṇāhuti*), a certain person will emerge from the sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*) holding a fruit in his hand and will give one fruit to you. By eating that fruit, you shall become free from old age and death and possess a body of diamond (*vajrakāya*). Having thus instructed the king in the mantra, the yogin departed for his own abode.

The king also, having recited the mantra with celibacy for one year outside the village, performed a fire-oblation (homa) in the fire ten times the required portion using *dūrvā* grass blades; while he was performing the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), a certain person emerged from the sacrificial pit and gave a divine fruit to the king.

When the king, having taken that fruit, entered the city and was proceeding along the royal road, a certain Brahmin whose limbs were withered by the disease of leprosy offered a blessing to the king and said: "O King! A king is appointed to the position of a mother, father, and so forth for the world. And it is said:
'The king is the kinsman of the friendless; the king is the eye of the sightless.
The king is indeed the mother and the father; he is the teacher who removes the suffering of all. (144)

Since you dispel the suffering of the entire world, therefore, destroy my suffering as well. By this disease, my body is perishing; with the destruction of the body, even religious practice is destroyed, because the body alone is the instrument for every righteous deed. Therefore, you must act so that this body of mine becomes free from disease and fit for enjoyment.

Having heard those words of the Brahmin, the king gave him that fruit. Then the Brahmin, having attained great satisfaction, went to his own place, and the king also returned to his palace. Having said this, the statuette addressed King Bhoja: "O King! If such generosity and fortitude exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
Hearing that, the king remained silent.

Thus ends the tenth episode, titled "The Bestowal of the Fruits Attained through Sacrifice," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 10.

Now begins the eleventh narrative, titled "The Warding Off of Fear from Rākṣasas. Then, as Bhoja was wandering about, another statuette addressed him: "O King, listen! While Vikrama ruled the kingdom, there was no slanderer, thief, or person devoted to evil deeds upon the face of the earth. Furthermore, that king who is constantly burdened by the anxieties of state affairs and the concerns of conquering powerful enemies does not even find sleep at night. As it is said:
'For those tormented by worldly cares, there is neither father nor kinsman.'"

For those afflicted by lust, there is neither fear nor shame; for those afflicted by anxiety, there is neither happiness nor sleep; for those afflicted by hunger, there is neither strength nor vigor. (145)

This King Vikramāditya is not like that; having brought all the kings who seek his favor under the shelter of his lotus-feet, he governs the kingdom by the mere granting of his commands. And it is said:
"The fruit of sovereignty is command alone; the fruit of asceticism is celibacy;
the fruit of knowledge is understanding alone; and the fruit of wealth is giving and enjoying. (146)

Once, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his ministers, he himself departed for another land in the guise of a yogi. He would stay for a few days wherever his mind found peace, and he would spend his time even in places where he beheld wonders. Wandering in this manner, one day when he entered the midst of a great forest, the sun had set. Seeing this, the king took refuge at the foot of a tree and stayed there for the night.

In that tree there lived a certain aged king of birds named Cirañjīvin. His sons and grandsons, having gone to other lands and satisfied their own hunger, would each bring back a single fruit every evening and present it daily to that aged Cirañjīvin. And thus: "The aged parents, the virtuous wife, and the infant son—even after committing a hundred wrongs, these must be supported," so said Manu (147).

Then, at night, Cirañjīvī sat comfortably and questioned those birds. The king, standing at the foot of the tree, heard their words: "O sons! While you were wandering through various lands, what wonder did you see?
Thereupon, one bird said, "I have seen no marvel whatsoever; however, today a great sorrow arises in my heart."

Cirañjīvin said, "Tell me then, what is the cause of your sorrow? He replied, "What is the use of merely speaking about it? The elder said, "O son! He who is suffering becomes relieved of that suffering by disclosing it to a friend."

Having heard his words, he explained the cause of his sorrow: "O father, listen! In the northern region there is a mountain named Śaivālaghoṣa. Near that mountain lies the city of Palāśa. A certain Rākṣasa dwelling on that mountain comes to the city every day and, having seized any man, woman, child, or anyone else who happens to come before him, carries them off to the mountain and devours them."

Once, he was addressed by the city-dwellers: "O Bakāsura! Do not devour just anyone who happens to come before you at your whim; we shall give you one human being every day for the sake of your food. He accepted those words.

Thereafter, the people of that place gave one human being each day to him in turn according to the order of their households. In this way, a great deal of time passed. Today, it was the turn of a certain Brahmin, a friend of mine with whom I had formed a bond of affection in a previous birth; he had only one son. If he were to give his son, there would be an end to his lineage; if he were to give himself, his wife would become a widow.
“Widowhood is a great misery; if he gives me to his wife, there will be a fall from my ascetic stage. Because of their suffering, I am greatly distressed. This was the cause of my great sorrow.

Upon hearing his words, the birds dwelling there said: “Aha! He alone is a true friend who becomes sorrowful himself at the sorrow of his friends. This indeed is the essence of friendship. And it is said:
‘He who rejoices when a friend is happy, and grieves when a friend is in pain—he is a kinsman.’”
The ocean is joyful when the moon has risen, and utterly diminished when the moon sets.
Moreover,
when the milk had previously lost all its qualities to the water that had entered it,
and having perceived the heat within that milk, the milk itself was cast into the fire.

Upon seeing the calamity that had befallen his friend, his mind became eager to go toward the fire; for the friendship of the virtuous is such that it is extinguished by water, yet it is likewise kindled by fire.

Having heard these words of the birds, the king, who understood the meaning of the birds' cries, went to that city near the execution stone. There, having looked upon the Brahmin and granted him safety, and having sent him back to his own home, he bathed in a nearby lake and sat down upon the execution stone.

At that time, a rākṣasa arrived and, seeing the man with a smiling face, was astonished and said to him: "O Great Being! Whoever sits upon this rock every day dies before my arrival. Yet you appear endowed with great fortitude and a smiling countenance. The senses of one whose time of death has arrived fall into decay; you, however, have attained even greater radiance and are laughing.
Therefore, tell me, who are you?"

The king said, "I am giving this body for the sake of others of my own free will; therefore, I feel no distress whatsoever. Let it be as it may—what does this deliberation matter to you? Do what you yourself desire.

Then the rākṣasa reflected within his mind: "Oh! How noble is this man, who, having abandoned the desire for his own pleasure and enjoyment, comes here having become pained by the suffering of another! And it is said: "Having abandoned the desire for one's own pleasure and pain, he seeks the welfare of all beings."
The virtuous become exceedingly pained by the suffering of others. || 150 ||
Those who are devoted to helping others and are free from desire for their own welfare or pleasure—such virtuous ones as these are born upon this earth for the benefit of the world. (151)

Having reflected thus, he said to the king: "O Great Being! You are the teacher who removes the suffering of all, for you dispel the affliction of the entire world. This body is indeed praiseworthy only for one like you who offers his body for the sake of others. Why?
For even beasts live, merely filling their own bellies;
only the life of him is praiseworthy who lives for the sake of others. (152)
For those like you who are intent on helping others, this is not surprising. As it has been said:
"What is there to marvel at here? That the virtuous are devoted to the welfare of others; for sandalwood trees do not grow merely to cool their own bodies. (154)

O Great Being! By this very act of benefiting others, you shall attain all perfections. As it is said: "The man who is born with the activity of benefiting others attains prosperity in this world and the supreme state in the next. (154)

Having spoken thus, he addressed the king again: "O Great Being! I am pleased with you; choose a boon. The king said, "O Rākṣasa! If you are well-disposed toward me, then from this day forward, renounce the eating of human flesh. Furthermore, listen to another instruction being offered by me: 'As one's own life is dear to oneself, so too are the lives of all living beings dear to them.
Therefore, wise men should protect those living beings from the fear of death. (155)
Moreover, in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, living beings are constantly tormented by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age; mortals tremble before death. (156)
The suffering that arises for a person at the thought "I shall die" cannot be described by anyone anywhere through inference. (157)
And likewise:
just as one's own life is dear to oneself,
so too is the life of others dear to them.
Just as you regard your own life, so too should you protect the lives of others. 158.
Having been thus instructed by the king, Rākṣasa abandoned the killing of living beings from that time forward. The king, for his part, returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "If such qualities as altruism, compassion, and the like exist within you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the eleventh episode, titled "The Warding Off of Fear from Rākṣasas," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 11.
Now begins the twelfth episode, titled "The Liberation from the Brahmin’s Curse.

Then, as the festivities were proceeding in the same manner, another statuette said: "O King, listen! While Vikramāditya was ruling the kingdom, there lived in his city a certain merchant named Bhadrasena. There was no limit to his wealth; however, he was not inclined toward even the slightest expenditure. As time passed, Bhadrasena died."
His son, Purandara, having obtained his father’s entire fortune, began to spend it according to his own whims.

Then, one day, his dear friend Dhanada said to him: "O Purandara! Although you are the son of a merchant, you spend wealth like a great prince; this is not the characteristic of one born into a merchant family. A merchant's son must accumulate by whatever means possible, and he should be hesitant even to spend a single cowrie."
Wealth that has been acquired may sometimes prove useful to a man in some particular calamity; therefore, a wise person should accumulate wealth for the sake of emergencies. As it is said:
"One should save wealth for times of distress, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth.
One should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (159)

Having heard these words, Purandara said: "O Dhanada! He who says that wealth acquired may perhaps be of use in some future calamity appears to be devoid of discernment. When calamities arrive, even the wealth that has been acquired will perish. Therefore, a wise man should not grieve for what is past, nor should he worry about what is yet to come; rather, only the present should be considered. And it is said: 'One should not grieve for what is gone, nor should one worry about what is yet to come.'"
The wise reflect upon the tasks that are currently present.
Whatever is destined to happen will come to pass even without effort; whatever is destined to be reached will surely be reached. As it has been said:
"What is destined to be must indeed come to be, like the water inside a coconut fruit.
What is destined to be traversed is said to have been traversed, like the kapittha fruit already eaten by an elephant. (161)
Thus, by the word of Purandara, Dhanada became destitute.

Thereupon, Purandara squandered his entire paternal wealth. Consequently, his kinsmen, friends, and others no longer honored the impoverished Purandara; what need is there to say more? They would not even engage in conversation with him. Then, Purandara thought to himself: "As long as I possessed wealth in my hands, these friends and others were like my servants; now they do not even exchange a word with me."
Alternatively, only he who possesses wealth has friends and the like; and it is said:
"He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth is a scholar. (162)
Moreover,

when a man's wealth is exhausted, his circle of kinsmen no longer behaves as they did before; even dependents who were supported solely for the sake of their maintenance abandon their subservience and act according to their own will.
Friends become fickle, and what is the use of further words?
For even with one's own wife, there will certainly be constant and intense quarreling once wealth has departed. 163.
Moreover, he who possesses wealth is a man of noble birth,
he is a scholar, he is learned, and he is a knower of virtues.
He alone is the speaker and he is the one worthy of being seen;
all virtues take refuge in gold.

And so, the wind becomes a friend to the fire as it burns the forests; yet that very same wind serves to extinguish it once the fire is spent. When one's power has waned, who possesses any affection? || 16.5 ||
Therefore, death is better than this poverty. And it is said:
"Arise for a single moment, my friend! Bear the burden of my poverty;
I am weary and shall thus enjoy your happiness for a long time until I attain the bliss of death."
Having heard these words spoken by one destitute of wealth, the corpse in the cremation ground remained silent, realizing that for one in poverty, death is indeed better than life. || 166 ||

A poor man is as good as dead; sexual union that results in no offspring is dead; a gift given by one who lacks Vedic learning is dead; and a sacrifice without a priestly fee is dead. (167) Moreover: the mother censures him, the father does not rejoice in him, the brother does not converse with him, the servant grows angry at him, the son does not follow him, and the wife does not embrace him.
Fearing that it might be a request for wealth, even a friend does not so much as engage in conversation;
therefore, my friend, acquire wealth, for all things are under the sway of wealth.

Having reflected thus, he departed for another land. Then, wandering through various countries, he arrived at a certain city situated near the Himalayas. Not far from that city was a forest of bamboos. Having entered the interior of the village, he slept at night upon a platform in someone's house.

In the meantime, at the hour of midnight, while in the middle of the Bamboo Grove, he was awakened by the cry of "Alas! Alas! from a certain weeping woman; he heard that sound of lamentation: "O great people! Save me, save me! Some rākṣasa is killing me!
Then, at the time of dawn, he asked the people living in the village: "O noble ones! What is this? Why does a certain woman weep here in the middle of the Bamboo Grove at night?"
They said, "In the midst of this bamboo forest, the sound of weeping is heard every night; however, out of fear, no one goes there, nor does anyone investigate.
Then, after some time, Purandara returned to his own city and saw the king. Thereupon, the king asked him, "O Purandara! While traveling through foreign lands, did you see anything extraordinary?
Then Purandara related the account of the bamboo forest to the king.

Having heard of that marvel, the king went to that city with him. At night, hearing the sound of a woman weeping in the middle of a bamboo grove, as he entered the heart of the forest, he saw a *rākṣasa* of most terrifying form killing a helpless, weeping woman. He said, "O most wicked one! Why do you beat this helpless woman? The *rākṣasa* replied, "What is the use of this deliberation of yours? Go by your own way; otherwise, you shall die at my hands for nothing."

Hearing that, the king became enraged and struck him with his sword; thereupon a battle ensued between the two, and the king killed that rākṣasa. Then that woman approached, fell at the king's feet, and said: "O King! By your grace, the end of my curse has come. I have been rescued by you from the great ocean of suffering.
The king asked, "Who are you?"

She said, "In this very city there was a certain Brāhmaṇa endowed with great wealth; I was his wife. Although I had become unfaithful, he no longer felt even the slightest affection for me, yet he maintained a great passion for me. Full of pride in my beauty and other qualities, I did not go to him even when summoned for sexual union."

Therefore, tormented by desire throughout his life, my husband cursed me at the moment of his death, saying: "O you of wicked conduct! Just as you have caused me unbearable mental anguish for as long as you lived, so shall some terrifyingly shaped Rākṣasa dwelling in the bamboo forest beat you every night for the sake of sexual union, even though you are unwilling.
When I had been thus cursed, I again requested the end of the curse, saying: "O Lord, please grant an end to this curse!"

He said, "When some man, devoted to the service of others and endowed with great fortitude, arrives and slays that Rākṣasa, then you shall be released from the curse by bowing at his feet. Give this wealth of mine to him. Having spoken thus to me, he gave up his life.

"Until that time, I was seized by the hand of a Rākṣasa every night; now, by your grace, the end of my curse has come. Therefore, take this," she said, and gave him a jar full of wealth. The king, having respectfully accepted that jar full of wealth, gave it to the merchant Purandara and went to Ujjayinī with him; the Brāhmaṇa’s wife also returned to her own home.
Having told this story, Puttantikā said to Bhoja: "O King! If such fortitude and magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the twelfth episode, titled "The Liberation from the Brahmin Woman’s Curse," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.

Now begins the thirteenth narrative, titled "The Deliverance of the Brahmarākṣasa. Then, once again, as Bhoja was about to ascend toward the throne out of a desire for further advancement, another statuette restrained him and said: "Listen, O King! Once upon a time, King Vikrama, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his circle of ministers, set out to wander about himself in the guise of a yogi. He would spend one night in a village and five nights in a city. Wandering in this manner, he once arrived at a certain city."

On the bank of a river situated near that city, there was a temple. In that temple, all the great men and citizens were listening to the Purāṇa from a reciter of the Purāṇas. The king also, having bathed in the river, gone to the temple, and paid obeisance to the deity, sat down near the great men. At that time, the reciter of the Purāṇas was chanting the words of the Purāṇa, as follows: "Bodies are impermanent; wealth is not eternal."
Death is ever-present; therefore, one should practice the accumulation of dharma.
Listen to the essence of all dharma as it has been declared in tens of millions of texts:
helping others leads to merit; causing pain to others leads to sin. (170)
He who becomes sorrowful upon seeing beings in distress, and likewise happy when they are happy, knows the ultimate Dharma. (171)
I know that there is no other dharma greater than this for an embodied being:
that which bestows fearlessness upon living creatures who are terrified by fear. (172)
The fruit of giving life to a single frightened person is superior;
the fruit of giving a thousand cows to a thousand Brahmins would not equal it.
For one who, devoted to compassion, grants fearlessness to all beings, there is no exhaustion of that merit even at the end of a kalpa. || 174 ||
Givers of golden cows, land, and other such gifts are easily found on earth;
however, a person in this world who is devoted to compassion for all living beings is rare.
The fruit of even great sacrifices perishes with time;
it does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of granting fearlessness.
He who gives this earth bounded by the four oceans, and he who grants fearlessness to all beings—of these two, the giver of fearlessness is superior. (177)
He who does not acquire the eternal Dharma with this transient body that perishes at every moment is a person of deluded mind and is to be pitied. || 178 ||
If this body is not of use for the benefit of living beings, then why is it nourished by men day after day? || 179 ||

Thus, at the time of narrating this ancient tale, a certain elderly Brahmin, while crossing a river with his wife, was being carried away by a great flood. Crying out "Alas! Alas!", he spoke to the people in the midst of the river: "O noble ones! Run, run! I am an elderly Brahmin with my wife, being forcibly swept away by the current of the river. Let some virtuous person of superior strength grant the gift of life to me and my wife!"

Hearing such a piteous cry from one being carried away by the water, all the people watched with curiosity; yet, not a single person entered into the middle of the river to rescue him from the current or grant him safety.

Then King Vikrama, giving him the assurance of safety by saying, "Do not fear," entered into the middle of the river and, together with his wife, pulled that Brahmin out of the great flood and brought him to the bank.

The Brahmin, having recovered his composure, said to the king: "O Great Being! This body of mine was first produced by my parents; now, however, I have obtained a second birth from you. Therefore, if I do not offer some recompense to you, who have been so greatly beneficial by granting me life, then my own life would be in vain."

"Therefore, my merit from twelve years of mantra-recitation performed in the midst of the waters of the Godāvarī is given to you. Furthermore, whatever spiritual merit I have acquired through penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, take all of that. Having said this, he offered his own merit to the king, gave him his blessing, and went to his own abode along with his wife.
At that moment, a certain Brahmarākṣasa of most terrifying form approached the king.

The king, having seen him, said, "O Great Being! Who are you? He replied, "I am a certain Brāhmaṇa living in this city who was always a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa's property, lived by accepting improper gifts, and officiated at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice. Furthermore, I reviled my gurus, the elderly, holy men, and great beings. Due to the power of that sin, I remain here as a Brahmarākṣasa in this Aśvattha tree, enduring extreme suffering for ten thousand years."
"You are a benefactor of others and one of virtuous conduct; through your favor, I shall be liberated from my sin. Trusting this, I take refuge in you as my protector.

Hearing these words, the king immediately gave that merit he had acquired from the Brahmin to him. By means of that merit, the man was also liberated from that birth; assuming a divine form, he praised the king and departed for heaven, while the king returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja: "If such altruism, fortitude, and magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king, however, cast his face downwards.
Thus ends the thirteenth narrative, titled "The Deliverance of the Brahmin-Rākṣasa," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*. 13.

Now begins the fourteenth tale, titled "The Gift of the Kāśmīra Liṅga. Again, when the king was proceeding to sit upon the throne, another statuette stopped him and said: "Once, King Vikramāditya, wandering about in the guise of a yogin himself to observe what wonders existed on the surface of the earth, who were the virtuous, what sacred fords, or what deities there might be, arrived at a certain city. Near that city, there was a grove of ascetics."

In that penance grove there was a great temple of the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā), and near it a certain river flowed. After bathing in the river and bowing to the deity, the king sat down in that temple; while he was looking about, a certain yogi named Avadhūtasāra arrived there. Saying, "Are you well?", the king sat with him in the temple. The yogi asked, "From where have you come?
The king replied, "I am a certain pilgrim on the way."
The yogin said, "Are you not King Vikramāditya? I saw you once in Ujjayinī, therefore I know you. For what purpose have you come?
The king replied, "O King of Yogins! There is a desire in my mind that, by traveling across the earth, some wonder should be beheld, and likewise, there shall be the sight of the virtuous."
Avadhūtāsara said, "O King! Though you are such a wise man, you have come to another land as if distracted. If some upheaval should occur within your kingdom, what will you do?
The king replied, "I have come having entrusted the entire burden of the kingdom into the hands of my minister.
The yogin said, "O King! Even so, you have acted in contradiction to the treatises on statecraft (nītiśāstra). For it is said:"

Those lords of the earth who remain with their burden of sovereignty entrusted to the hands of ministers, finding their essence only in sporting upon the mountains—those fools sleep while a pack of cats has already drained the jars of their milk. 180.
Furthermore, because the kingdom has descended through one's own lineage, it must not be neglected; rather, it must be made very firm. And it is said:
"Agriculture, learning, trade, a wife, one's own wealth, and the riches of a kingdom—these must be made as secure as the mouth of a black cobra. (181)

Having heard that, the king said: "O Yogin! All this is useless; here, the power of destiny alone is powerful. Even when a kingdom is made very firm and provided with all necessary resources, and even if a man is endowed with human effort (*pauruṣa*), he meets with defeat due to the hostility of destiny. As it has been said:
'He whose leader is Bṛhaspati, whose weapon is the thunderbolt, whose soldiers are the gods, whose fortress is heaven, whose favor belongs to Hari, and whose mount is Airāvata—'"
Even though he was endowed with such sovereignty, the slayer of Bala was defeated by his enemies in battle; surely, therefore, destiny alone is the refuge—fie, fie upon useless human effort! 182.
And so it is:
neither physical form bears fruit, nor lineage, nor character, nor even learning; nor does service rendered with effort bring success.
Indeed, fortunes accumulated through past austerities bear fruit for a person in due time, just like trees. || 183 ||
Moreover,
there where the maces of Indra’s elephant-teeth remained unbroken in battle,
and where the edge of the axe of the wielder of the Pināka attained bluntness;
Even that chest of his was torn by the dust from the claws of the Man-Lion;
for when fate has turned weak, even a blade of grass generally acts like a thunderbolt.
Have you not heard this verse of King Rājaśekhara, which is rooted in unprecedented confidence?
"The yakṣas dwelling in the banyan tree give and take away here.
Cast the dice, O auspicious lady; whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass. (18.5)
The yogin asked, "How was this?

The king replied, "In the northern region, there is a city named Nadīparvatavardhana. There, a king named Rājaśekhara bore the burden of sovereignty. He was exceedingly righteous and devoted to the gods and the twice-born."

Once, all his heirs gathered together, entered into conflict with him, and having seized the kingdom by force, they banished him from the city along with his wife. Then that king, wandering through various lands with his wife and son, arrived at a grove near a certain city. At that time, the sun had also set; accompanied by his wife and son, he went to the foot of a banyan tree and sat down.

In that tree there were five yakṣas who were conversing with one another. There, one said, "The king in this city has died, and he has no offspring; who shall become the king? The second said, "What concern is that? Let him who sits here at the foot of this banyan tree be consecrated to this kingdom. The others said, "So be it. The king, along with his retinue, also heard those words of the yakṣas.

Then sunrise occurred, and all the people set about their respective duties. When the king, having performed his morning prayers and other rites, went out toward the royal highway, a female elephant—having been released by the ministers for the purpose of electing a king for that kingdom—beheld the king, placed a garland around his neck, mounted him upon her back, and led him to the royal palace.
Thereupon, all the ministers assembled and, having performed the consecration, installed Rājaśekhara as king over the realm.
Once, all the rival kings, having heard that Rājaśekhara had once again regained his kingdom, formed an alliance and besieged his city in order to uproot him from that realm.

While that king was engaged in a game of dice with his queen, he suddenly heard news of this situation from the mouth of a spy. Observing that his master remained completely indifferent there, the queen said with astonishment: "O Lord! Why do you remain silent even now? This city of yours has been besieged by rival kings; tomorrow morning they will seize not only the city, but us as well."

The king said, "O foolish woman! What is the use of effort? When destiny is favorable, then every task is accomplished of its own accord; when destiny is adverse, then everything perishes of its own accord. Have you not experienced that in growth and decay, destiny alone is the supreme cause? The yakṣas dwelling in the banyan tree give and take away here."

"Cast the dice, O auspicious lady! Whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass. Surely, even the anxiety of him who gave me the kingdom while I sat at the foot of a tree has now descended upon him.

As he was speaking thus, the Yakṣa who had granted him the kingdom, perceiving through his inner witness the words of that man who placed supreme trust in the divine, thought to himself: "It was I alone who, relying upon him, entrusted this burden of sovereignty to him; if I do not now exert effort in his protection, then great infamy will befall me. Having reflected thus, he assumed a terrifying form and struck fear into all his enemies.

Upon seeing that most terrifying form, all those rivals fled. Thereafter, King Rājaśekhara ruled his kingdom free from all thorns. Therefore, I say: "The banyan tree... and so forth. This story was told by Vikrama to the Lord of Yogins (Yogīndra). Then, having heard this tale, the Lord of Yogins was exceedingly pleased; he gave the king a single Kāśmīra-liṅga and said: "O King, this Kāśmīra-liṅga grants whatever is desired, like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi). Therefore, worship it properly."

The king, having said "So be it," and having bowed to him, was proceeding along the road to the city when a certain Brahmin approached. Seeing that linga in the king's hand, he addressed the king with a blessing: "O King, I have a vow to worship the Shiva-linga every day; without worshipping it, I never drink even water. However, my Shiva-linga has been lost, and for that reason I have fasted for three days.
Therefore, you must give this Shiva-linga to me today for the purpose of worship."

The king, too, having given that Kāśmīra liṅga to the Brāhmaṇa, returned to his own city. Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "If such virtues as magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the fourteenth episode, titled "The Gift of the Kāśmīra Liṅga," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, in the section concerning the Throne. 14.

Now begins the fifteenth narrative, titled "The Story of Manmathasañjīvinī. Then, having restrained King Bhoja—who, though his mind was distressed by the constant failure of his attempts to ascend the throne, remained subject to his own desires—another statuette spoke once more: "Listen, O King! While Vikramārka was ruling the kingdom, he had a domestic priest named Vasumitra. He was exceedingly handsome, proficient in all the arts, the king’s most beloved, a supreme benefactor to all people, and possessed of great wealth."
Once he reflected: "Indeed, for the sins already accumulated, there is no means of destruction other than bathing in the Gaṅgā. And it has been said:
'By austerity, by celibacy, by sacrifices, or again by charity—without attaining that goal, a living being shall go there only after serving the Gaṅgā. (186)
The purity that comes to self-restrained men who have bathed in the pure waters of the Ganges cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Just as the sun rises after dispelling the intense darkness,
so too does one who has bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā shine forth, having cast off all sins.
Just as a heap of cotton is instantly destroyed upon reaching fire, so too is every sin destroyed by the current of the Gaṅgā. || 189 ||
But he who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā heated by the rays of the sun shall indeed obtain a fruit greater than that from drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 190 ||
He who would perform purification of the body through a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances,
and he who would drink the water of the Gaṅgā— both of these would be equal.
For all living beings whose minds are struck by suffering and who are searching for a refuge, there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā—
especially for those whose hearts have been destroyed by many great sins. (192)
The Ganges protects one from falling into a terrible hell through her service.
A man who has immersed himself in the waters of the Gaṅgā certainly and eternally delivers seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors.
Through seeing, touching, meditating upon, and likewise chanting the name of the Gaṅgā,
she purifies meritorious persons by the hundreds and thousands.
For those who are unable to see the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of sins, are not equal to those born blind, nor indeed to birds or beasts. (196)

Having reflected thus, he went to Vārāṇasī and beheld Viśveśvara. Then, having performed the Māgha ablution at Prayāga, he set out toward his own city. On his way back, there was a certain city. In that city, a certain celestial nymph, fallen due to a curse, was ruling as queen. She had no husband. There stood a great temple of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and near it, a wedding pavilion had been prepared.

At the gate of the temple of the deity, oil was being heated in a large iron vessel. The men stationed there said to those arriving from other lands: "If any person of superior merit should fall into this boiling oil, the Apsaras named Manmathasañjīvanī will place a garland around his neck. Vasumitra, seeing and hearing all this, went to his own city. There he met with all his kinsmen.

Everyone was filled with joy, thinking, "He has returned safely. Then, on the following morning, he went to the royal palace; having seen the king, he gave him water from the Ganges and a gift from Viśveśvara, and sat down.
Thereupon the king asked, "O Vasumitra, have you completed your pilgrimage in safety?
He replied, "O Lord, by your grace, I have performed the pilgrimage and have returned in safety."
The king asked, "What unprecedented thing did you see while traveling in that foreign land?

When thus questioned by the king, Vasumitra related the account of the celestial nymph and the boiling oil. Thereupon, the king went to that place with him; having bathed there and bowed to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, he threw himself into the midst of the boiling oil. Seeing this, the people present there raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! At that moment, the king's body took on the appearance of a mere lump of flesh. Hearing of this, Manmathasañjīvanī brought nectar and performed an aspersion over the lump of flesh.

Then, by the power of destiny, that king was transformed into a man possessing a divine form. Thereupon, as she, with a very joyful heart, was about to place the garland around the king's neck, the king said to her: "O Mammathasañjīvanī! If you are mine, then listen to my words.
She replied, "O Lord! Having considered it, I shall certainly fulfill your command in every way."
The king said, "If you will do as I say, then choose my domestic priest.
She replied, "So be it," and having placed a garland around the neck of the priest, she performed the marriage ceremony.
Then the king departed for his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja, "If you possess such fortitude, then sit upon that throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the fifteenth narrative, titled "The Story of Manmathasañjīvanī," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.

Now begins the sixteenth narrative, titled "The Gift of Gold Equal to a Virgin. "Since this throne is our right, why should it not be ascended because of the prohibition by a woman?"—having thus reflected, as the king was about to mount the throne, another statuette stopped him and spoke again: "Listen, O King! King Vikramārka, having set out for the conquest of the quarters, wandered through the east, south, west, north, and the intermediate directions; having caused the kings residing there to bow down before his feet, he took from them all manner of articles never tasted by others, which were offered to him."
Having established them once more in their own positions, he returned toward his own city.
Then, at the time of entering the city, a certain astrologer said, "O King! For four days there is no auspicious moment (muhūrta) for entering the city.

Upon hearing those words, the king had clothed pavilions (paṭamaṇḍapa) constructed in a grove outside the village and began to spend those four days right there. At that time, the king of seasons, Spring, arrived.

Then, having observed the splendor of spring, the minister Sumantra approached the king and said: "O King! Vasanta, the king of seasons, has arrived; today the worship of Vasanta must be performed. When he is worshipped, all the gods will be pleased with you, the entire world will become happy, and there will be the pacification of every misfortune.
Having heard those words of the minister, the king accepted them, saying, "So be it," and commanded him specifically to carry out the performance of the Vasanta-pūjā.

Thereafter, that minister had a most beautiful assembly hall constructed and summoned Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas and Śāstras, Bharatas skilled in song and instrumental music, and female dancers proficient in other arts; as for the poor, the blind, the deaf, the lame, and the hunchbacked, they arrived of their own accord. Having installed a throne inlaid with the nine gems in that assembly hall, he consecrated there two images of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

For the purpose of worship, fragrant substances such as saffron, camphor, musk, sandalwood, and agallochum, as well as flowers such as jasmine, yūthikā, mallikā, kunda, śatapatra, madana, campaka, and ketakī, have been gathered.

Thus, according to the prescribed ritual, the king himself worshipped Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with the sixteen modes of service, beginning with the ceremonial bath; he then honored the Brāhmaṇas and other artisans skilled in the arts with garments and other gifts. Immediately thereafter, the singers performed a musical composition in the Vasantarāga and sang of the spring season. Then the king gave them betel rolls.
At that moment, a certain Brāhmaṇa arrived accompanied by his daughter and said:
"May there be auspiciousness for you, who hold the Pināka bow, as you take her hand—she who is adorned with the serpent-bracelet."
The face of Ambikā, with a startled gaze, suddenly uttered "Namas Shivaya," its mouth bowed in shame at having spoken only half the word.
Having offered these benedictions, he said, "O King, I have a request. The king said, "Speak.

The Brāhmaṇa replied, "I am a Brāhmaṇa residing in the city of Nandivardhana. Eight sons were born to me, but not even a single daughter was born. Therefore, being deeply distressed along with my wife, I made this vow before the Mother of the World: 'O Mother Ambikā! If a daughter shall be born to me, then I shall give her your name.'"

Furthermore, I shall give you the gold weighed out by that maiden, and I shall bestow the maiden upon some worthy bridegroom learned in the Vedas. In time, by the grace of the Mother of the World, this daughter of mine, endowed with auspicious marks, was born. Now the time for her marriage has arrived; moreover, since Jupiter currently occupies the eleventh house in her horoscope, this moment must not be neglected by any means. Therefore, I am prepared to give her in marriage right now.

Therefore, I wish to give to Your Majesty the gold weighed against my daughter, as previously promised. There is no other king on the face of the earth who, lacking valor, is capable of giving this gold weighed against my daughter; it is for this reason that I have come into your presence.

The king said, "O Brahmin! You have performed well; take whatever amount of wealth you require. Thereupon, the king summoned the treasurer and said, "O treasurer! Give this gold, weighed against the maiden, to this Brahmin; furthermore, let another half of the eight divisions—eighty million pieces of gold—be given separately."

Then, commanded by him, the treasurer gave that much gold to the brahmin. The brahmin, being exceedingly satisfied, went to his own home along with his daughter. The king also entered the city at an auspicious moment. Then the statuette said, "O King, if such generosity exists in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king, however, remained silent.
Thus ends the sixteenth episode, titled "The Gift of Gold Equal to a Maiden," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. ||16||

Now begins the seventeenth narrative, titled "The Offering of One’s Own Body as an Oblation for the Benefit of Others. Then, as the King was about to ascend that very throne, another statuette spoke again: "Listen, O King! There has never been another equal to Vikrama in magnanimity; his fame has spread throughout the three worlds by virtue of his stainless quality of generosity. All supplicants praise only that king. Such words of blessing always serve to delight those who give. As it is said:
'Words of blessing from those seeking wealth serve only to please the givers.'"
For the roar of the battle-drum is indeed for the striking of heroes. || 198 ||
Virtues such as vigor, fortitude, knowledge, and practice may belong to everyone, but the virtue of renunciation does not. As it has been said:
"All animals are capable of harming, and parrots and other birds can recite;
he who gives a gift is alone a hero and a wise man. (199)
For some are indeed heroes by nature, while others are heroes through compassion;
yet all of them do not equal even a sixteenth part of the heroism of generosity.
Generosity alone is a praiseworthy virtue; what is the use of other multitudes of virtues?
For it is through generosity alone that even animals, stones, and trees are honored. 201.
In my view, the quality of renunciation is superior to a hundred other virtues;
if even learning adorns it, what more need I say?
And as for that which is called heroism—if it exists therein, then let there be salutation to him!
And yet, even in such great prowess, those three [qualities] were not present, nor was there any pride.

These four qualities were always present in that Vikramārka. Once, before a certain king residing in another realm, a panegyrist recited a series of Vikramārka’s virtues. Having heard this, that king conceived a sense of rivalry in his mind and said to the panegyrist: "O bard! For what reason do all these panegyrists praise only King Vikrama? Is there no other king in the three worlds?"

The bard said, "O King! In renunciation, in beneficence, in daring, in valor, and in fortitude, there is no king equal to him even in the three worlds. In performing service for others, he had no sense of ownership even toward his own body.

Having heard those words of his, the king reflected in his mind, "I too shall perform service for others," and having summoned a certain yogi, he said to him, "O yogi! Is there some means by which new and fresh wealth may be obtained every day for the sake of performing service for others?"
The yogin said, "O King, why is it that it does not exist?
The king replied, "If it exists, then reveal that means before me; I shall accomplish it.

The yogin said, "On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the circle of the sixty-four yoginīs must be worshipped. Having performed the preliminary mantra-repetition (puraścaraṇa) before them, a fire-offering (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number must be made; at the conclusion of the homa, for the sake of the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one's own body must be offered into the fire."

Then, when the king had acted accordingly, the circle of Yoginīs, having consumed his flesh, became exceedingly pleased; they consecrated him with nectar (*amṛta*), bestowed upon the king a new body, and said: "O King! Choose a boon.
The king replied: "O Mothers! If you are pleased, then let those seven great jars that are in my house be filled with gold every day."

When they had spoken thus, [the king said], "If you will offer your own bodies into the fire in this manner every day for three months, then we shall do so. The king also said, "So be it," and began offering his own body into the fire every day; the circle of Yoginīs likewise did the same every day. One day, King Vikramārka, having heard this news during the course of conversation, arrived at that place. Before the arrival of the local king, he performed the worship and other rites, and at the moment of the final oblation, he cast his own body into the sacrificial fire.

Then, at the time of eating, the yoginīs said to one another, "Today there is meat of an extraordinary kind that is exceedingly delicious; his heart is of great essence. Since he is the essence of uncommon courage, he must not be eaten. Having said this, they restored him to life again and spoke: "O Great Being! Who are you? What was the purpose of your sacrifice of your body?
He replied, "I have offered my body into the fire for the sake of helping others. The yoginīs said, "In that case, we are pleased; choose a boon."

The king said, "If you ladies are pleased with me, then this king experiences great suffering every day on account of death; that must be prevented. Without his body even falling [into the water], seven large jars should be filled daily with gold. The yoginīs replied, "So be it; we shall do so," and having agreed, they prevented the king's death and filled the jars with gold every day.
Then the king returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja: "O King! If such altruism, fortitude, and compassion exist within you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.

Thus ends the seventeenth tale, titled "The Offering of One’s Own Body for the Sake of Altruism," in the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja within the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.

Now begins the eighteenth narrative, titled "The Journey to the World of the Sun. Again, as Bhoja was about to ascend the throne, another statuette stopped him and said: "O King! King Vikrama, skilled in statecraft, while protecting his subjects with wise policy, became the most desirable among all people due to his virtues such as magnanimity. This is his throne; if you possess the corresponding skill in statecraft and virtues such as magnanimity, then this throne should be occupied by you."

The king said, "Tell me, what is the path of political ethics (nītimārga) like? The statuette replied, "O King, listen! In Maṇipur there was a Brahmin named Govindaśarman, who was a knower of all the treatises on ethics. He used to expound the science of ethics to his son, and at that time I too heard that science of ethics; I shall relate it to you.
The king said, "Describe it."
The statuette said: "Listen, O King! A wise man should not form an association with wicked people, for such an association is the very cause of a succession of misfortunes. As it is said:
'Association with the ill-behaved is the cause of a succession of misfortunes; this applies even to the virtuous—what need is there to say more in this regard?'"
The Lord of Laṅkā carries off the wife of the son of Daśaratha,
while the King of the Southern Ocean incurs captivity.
Moreover,
in this world, association with the wicked deprives one of discipline and propriety, destroys one's reputation, and swiftly leads men to hell. (204)

One should cultivate association with the virtuous. In this world, there is no gain superior to the company of the good, for from it arise qualities such as great bliss and the like. And it has been said:
"The company of the virtuous causes joy to blossom, holds in contempt the gentle breeze, the moon, and sandalwood;
