it subdues dullness and brings together even all forms of prosperity. (2.05) Furthermore:

One should not harbor enmity toward anyone, nor should one cause distress to others. Servants must not be punished for no fault; a wife must not be abandoned except for a grave offense, for by doing so, one becomes a partaker of hell. As it is said: "He who abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, beautiful, and adorned with virtue—provided she is free from fault—shall go to an eternal hell. (206)
One should not think that fortune (*lakṣmī*) is stable; rather, it is as fickle as water resting upon a lotus leaf. And it has been said:
"Experience wealth with caution, honor those worthy of respect, and serve the virtuous;
for fortune is as flickering as the flame of a lamp tossed by a violently harsh wind. (207)

One should not disclose secret words to a woman. One should not worry about the future. One should speak only what is beneficial even to one's enemies. One should never let the day pass without giving gifts, studying, and so forth. Service to one’s parents must be performed. One should not converse with thieves. One should never utter a harsh reply. One should not do much for the sake of a small cause. As it is said: "A wise man should not destroy a great deal for the sake of a little. This indeed is true wisdom: that one protects the greater from the smaller. (208)

One should give gifts to the distressed; one should perform service for others through knowledge of the Dharma, through thought, through action, and through speech. This is the code of conduct taught for ordinary men. King Vikrama was, by his very nature, a knower of this science of ethics.
As time passed in this manner, once a certain foreigner arrived, and having seen the king, sat down. Then the king said, "O noble soul! Where is your residence?"

He said, "O King! I am a foreigner; I have no fixed residence and wander constantly. The king asked, "What extraordinary things have you seen while wandering the earth? He replied, "O King! I have seen one great marvel."
The king asked, "What of it?

He replied, "On the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayācala), there is a great palace of the Sun; there the Gaṅgā flows. On the bank of the Gaṅgā, there is a temple of Śiva named Pāpavināśana. From the current of the Gaṅgā, a certain golden pillar emerges, upon which is a throne inlaid with the nine gems. That golden pillar, having attained full growth after sunrise, reaches the solar disc at midday."

Then, as soon as the sun went down, he would himself turn back and immerse himself in the current of the Gaṅgā. This occurred there every single day. I witnessed this great marvel. King Vikrama, having heard of it, went to that place with him and fell asleep at night. At the time of dawn, just as the sun was rising, a golden pillar equipped with a jeweled lion-throne emerged from the current of the Gaṅgā. At that moment, the king himself sat upon the pillar.

The pillar also set out to go toward the solar disc; as it approached the vicinity of the sun, the king’s body was reduced to the form of a lump of flesh by the sun’s rays, which resembled sparks of fire. Then, having reached the solar disc in the form of that mass, [he offered:
"Homage to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe."
To Him who consists of the three Vedas, who assumes the nature of the three qualities (guṇas), and whose essence is Viriñci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara; || 209 ||
Thus he paid homage. Sūrya sprinkled the pillar with nectar; by that, the king became possessed of a divine body.
Sūrya said, "O King, you are preeminent in great courage, for you have reached this orb which is inaccessible even to others. Therefore, I am pleased; choose a boon.
The king replied, "Is there anyone superior to me? Since I have reached your abode, which is inaccessible even to the sages, every object of my desire has been attained through your grace."

Highly pleased by those words, Sūrya gave him his own earrings encrusted with nine gems and said, "O King! These two earrings yield one *bhāra* of gold every day. Then the king, having taken the two earrings and having again paid obeisance to Sūrya, descended from that pillar and set out toward Ujjayinī; meanwhile, a certain Brāhmaṇa met him on the road and recited:
"In the Vedāntas, they speak of Him as the One Person who stands pervading the two worlds (heaven and earth)..."

May that Sthāṇu— who is sought by those seeking liberation through the restraint of the vital breaths and other faculties, and in whom the word "Lord" (Īśvara) is used as its primary referent with its syllables corresponding exactly to reality— be for your ultimate well-being, being easily attained through the yoga of steadfast devotion. 2.10.
Having uttered this blessing, he said, "O patron! I am a householder, a Brahmin, but extremely poor; I wander for alms everywhere, yet even so, my belly is not filled.

Hearing this, the king gave him a pair of earrings and said, "O Brahmin! This pair of earrings will yield one *bhāra* of gold for you every day. Hearing this, the Brahmin was exceedingly delighted; having honored the king with special respect, he went to his own place, and the king also returned to Ujjayinī.
Having told this story, the statuette said, "O King! If such generosity and fortitude exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the eighteenth narrative, titled "The Departure for the World of the Sun," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*. 18.

Now begins the nineteenth narrative, titled "The Demonstration of Bali. Again, just as the king was about to ascend the throne, another statuette stopped him and said, "O King! If you possess virtues such as magnanimity equal to those of Vikrama, then sit upon this throne. The king replied, "O statuette! Tell me the account of the virtues and deeds of that Vikrama's magnanimity."

She said, "Listen, O King! While Vikrama ruled over this vast circle of the earth, the hearts of all people were filled with joy. The Brahmins were devoted to the six duties; women were faithful to their husbands; men lived for a hundred years; trees always bore fruit; the rain-cloud poured down according to desire; the earth was always adorned with abundant crops; there was fear of sin among all people; guests were honored; compassion was shown toward living beings; service was rendered to teachers; and gifts were constantly given to the poor—such was the conduct of the subjects."

Now, once upon a time, Vikrama was seated upon his throne. There in the assembly sat princes from various lands who were vassals of the king. Among them, some were having bards recite genealogies of praise; some, being arrogant, themselves extolled the strength of their own arms; some bearded youths, skilled in the employment of the sixfold army and weapons, mocked one another; some were intent on protecting those who had come for refuge; and others... [were] elsewhere.

Some were engaged in their respective spheres with the necessary means, while others were occupied with the collection of religious duties. At that moment, a certain hunter, who lived by the slaughter of wild animals, arrived there; having prostrated before the king, he said, "O Lord! A great boar, resembling Mount Añjana in appearance, has appeared in the middle of the forest; may Your Majesty come and behold it."

Having heard his words, the king went to the forest with those very princes and beheld a boar within a bower situated on the bank of a river. Then that boar, hearing the clamor of the heroes, emerged from that bower. Immediately thereafter, twenty-six weapons fell upon it from the hand of Vikrama, who displayed great skill of his own hands along with all the princes.

Varāha, disregarding those weapons, entered a certain cave situated within the mountain. The king also followed closely behind him and reached the mountain. There, seeing a golden entrance to a subterranean passage, he entered it himself and traveled some distance through the great darkness; further on, there was a vast light.

Then, after traveling some distance, he saw a city with golden walls, distinguished by white palaces that scraped the clouds. There, in a place adorned with temples and groves, beautified by marketplaces filled with every kind of commodity, crowded with wealthy people, and frequented by various pleasure-seekers, he beheld an exceedingly enchanting assembly of beautiful women. Having entered it, as he proceeded into the midst of the marketplace, he saw a royal palace provided with most captivating pavilions.
There, Bali, the son of Virocana, was ruling the kingdom.
As soon as the king had entered the royal palace, Bali approached him suddenly and embraced him; he was seated upon an exceedingly beautiful throne and asked, "O Lord, from where have you come here?
Vikrama replied, "I have come here for the purpose of beholding you.
Hearing this, Bali said to the king, "Today my lineage has been purified and rendered fruitful. By a great upsurge of merit, your arrival at our home has come to pass."

Vikrama said, "O King! Your inner being has been purified; your very birth is praiseworthy, since Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha himself, always resides in your palace. Then Bali said, "My lord! What is the purpose of your visit, other than this?
Vikrama replied, "O Lord of the Dānavas! I have come solely for the sake of beholding you; there is no other reason here whatsoever."

Then Bāli said, "If my lord has come to me considering me a dear friend, then, overcome by compassion for me, you should ask for some object from me. Thereupon Vikrama replied, "By your grace, I lack nothing; I am complete in every respect. Bāli said, "O Lord, I do not say that you lack anything; however, out of friendship, I wish to give something. And it is said:"
Affection never arises in anyone without some benefit;
behold, it is by means of fulfilling their requests that the gods indeed grant what is desired.
Moreover, I consider that gift to be dearer even than a son to that beast who is devoid of discernment—
by which [gift] all the milk was indeed given to the wicked man.
See how the queen, together with her son, gives [this] constantly.
Having spoken thus, he gave the elixir and the mercury to King Vikrama.

Then, having obtained permission from him, the king emerged from the cave and mounted his horse; as he was proceeding along the royal highway, an old Brahmin arrived, accompanied by his son and overcome with great misery and affliction, whose body bore the marks of being bound by extremely tight leather straps.
May that Viṣṇu Dāmodara protect you, in whom the portions of the sacrificial offerings shine forth. || 213 ||

Having thus uttered a blessing, he said to the king: "O sacrificer! I am an extremely poor and afflicted Brāhmaṇa with a large family. Give me today some wealth sufficient for the food of my family; we are tormented by great hunger."

Having heard that, the king said, "O Brahmin! At present I have no wealth in my hand, but I possess two things: a mercury-elixir (*rasa*) and an elixir of longevity (*rasāyana*). Through contact with this mercury, the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) turn into gold; likewise, whoever consumes this elixir of longevity becomes free from old age and death. Choose one of these two.
Then the father said, "Give me that elixir by the consumption of which I shall become free from old age and death."

Having thus heard his father’s request, which was contrary to his own wishes, the son said, "What is the use of this elixir? Even though one is freed from old age and death by it, one must still experience poverty. Only that substance should be taken through contact with which silver and other metals turn into gold. Thus, a dispute arose between the two.

Then Raji, having heard the dispute between the two, gave both the elixir and the rejuvenator to them. Thereupon, the Brahmin, together with his son, departed for his own abode, praising the king with joy. The king also returned to his own palace. Having told this story, the statuette spoke again: "O King! If such fortitude and generosity exist in you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.
Thus ends the nineteenth episode, titled "The Vision of Bali," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 19.
Now begins the twentieth narrative, titled "The Vision of the Yogin.
Again, as soon as the king attempted to sit upon the throne, another statuette said, "O King! If you possess virtues such as magnanimity and the like, just as Vikrama did, then sit upon this throne.
The king replied, "O statuette! Tell me of those virtues of Vikrama, such as his magnanimity."

The statuette said: "Listen, O King! King Vikrama rules for six months and wanders through foreign lands for six months. Once, while traveling abroad and wandering through various countries, he arrived at a city named Padmālaya. There, having seen a certain lake of exceedingly pure water in a most enchanting grove, he drank its water and sat down."

Then, several other foreigners arrived from elsewhere; having drunk water, they sat down there and held a conversation among themselves, saying: "Oh! We have seen many countries and traveled to numerous sacred pilgrimage sites; we have even climbed mountains that are extremely difficult to access and unreachable by most, yet nowhere did we obtain a vision of a Great Being."

Thereupon, one of them said: "How will the vision of the Great Being come about? It is not possible to go where the great Siddha resides, because the path there is extremely difficult to traverse, many obstacles arise along the way, and the destruction of the body is likely. Who would wish to experience the fruit of an endeavor that first gives rise to the fear of one's own ruin? For a wise person must, by all means, protect themselves first.
As it has been said:
A wife can be obtained again, wealth again, and likewise a field;
good and evil karma can be acquired again, but the body cannot be obtained again and again. (214)
Therefore, a discerning person should not perform actions that are harmful to oneself. As it has been said:
"A wise man should not undertake undertakings that lead to endless calamities, those whose results are ruinous, or those that are impossible to accomplish. (215)
And likewise:
A wise person should never, under any circumstances, ascend a mountain that is rugged, formidable, and infested with many predatory beasts, for it is fraught with danger. (216)
Then the king, having heard their words, said: "O stranger! Why is this being said? When a man exerts manly effort and courage, then no task whatsoever becomes difficult for him. And it is said:
'Even things that are difficult to attain and desired objects are obtained by men who have embarked upon doubt; never by those who are indolent. (217)
And so it is:
sometimes water falls from the sky, and at other times it comes even from the netherworld (pātāla).
Fate is inconceivable and powerful; indeed, he who is reckless is truly powerful. (218)
Without employing the limbs of affliction, no pleasures whatsoever can be obtained here;
one embraces Lakṣmī with arms that have been exerted in churning honey.
How could the arrow of Viṣṇu, even in his form as Nṛsiṃha, not be unsteady against him, who constantly stays within the water and subjects me—the four-faced one—to sleep? 220.
The higher state is difficult to attain as long as a person has not exerted human effort;
even so, the sun, having ascended the scale, triumphs over the masses of clouds.

Having heard these words of the king, they said, "O Mahāsattva, tell us what must be done. The king replied, "If one travels twelve *yojanas* from this place, there is a certain rugged mountain in the midst of a great forest. Upon it dwells a lord of yogins named Trikālanātha. If he is seen, he will grant every desired object; I am going there.
They said, "We too shall come.
The king said, "Come with ease."

Then, having set out with the king, they saw a most treacherous path in the great forest and said to the king: "O Great Being, how far away is the mountain? The king replied: "It is located eight yojanas from here."

They said, "Even though this is a great distance and the path is exceedingly treacherous, we shall nevertheless go. As they were saying this and proceeded forward for six *yojanas*, they saw a certain serpent with a face like that of Mahākāla, emitting the fire of poison and standing most terrifyingly across the path; seeing this, they fled in fear.

Nevertheless, the king proceeded on his way. Then a serpent approached, coiled around the king, and bit him. Thereupon, having bound the bitten spot with a piece of cloth as if it were poisoned, he—though accompanied by the serpent which was ablaze with venom—ascended a difficult mountain. Having seen the yogin Trikālanātha, he paid homage to him. By the mere sight of the yogin, the serpent abandoned him and departed; the king also quickly became free from poison.
Then the yogin said, "O Mahāsattva! For what purpose have you come with such great hardship to this superhuman place, which is so full of great negligence?
The king replied, "O Master! I have come for the sake of seeing you."

The yogi said, "Indeed, you have experienced great hardship. The king replied, "There is no hardship at all; by the mere sight of you, every sin has vanished. By accepting such suffering, I am blessed today, for the great are exceedingly rare to behold. Even a single association with them produces self-elevation; indeed, even when faced with a cause for great transformation, their innate nature does not change. As it is said:
'Though rubbed again and again, sandalwood remains fragrant.'"
Though cut again and again, the sugarcane stalk remains sweet;
though burnt again and again, gold retains its lovely color.
Even at the end of life, when seized by adversity, no transformation occurs among the noble.

Then, being pleased, the yogin gave him a stylus, a staff of yoga, and a patched garment (kaṇṭhā). He said, "O King! As many lines as are drawn upon the ground with this stylus, for that many *yojanas* one can travel in a single day. If this staff of yoga is touched with the right hand, then a dead army is revived and rises up; if it is touched with the left hand, then the destruction of the entire opposing army occurs."
This rag-robe (*kanthā*) also bestows whatever desired object exists within its reach.

Having taken those three items and paid homage to the yogin, the king departed; as he was proceeding along the royal road, he saw a certain prince standing before him, having established a fire and piling up wood. Then the king asked him: "O gentle one, why is this being done?"

He said, "I am a certain prince whose kingdom has been seized by his kinsmen. Being poor and unable to sustain my life, I am gathering wood to enter the fire. Then the king granted him freedom from fear and gave him that stylus, the staff of yoga, and the patched garment, and he also explained their virtues to him. Thereafter, the prince, being exceedingly gratified, bowed to the king and departed for his own country; Vikrama also returned to Ujjayinī.
Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "O King! If such virtues as magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.
Thus ends the twentieth narrative, titled "The Vision of the Yogī," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.
Now begins the twenty-first narrative, titled "The Attainment of the Eight Great Siddhis.
Again, just as the king was about to sit upon the throne, another statuette stopped him and said: "One may sit upon this throne only if one possesses a magnanimity like that of Vikrama.
The king replied, "Tell me that account of Vikrama’s magnanimity."

She said, "Listen, O King! When Vikrama was ruling the kingdom, there was a certain minister named Buddhisindhu. He had a son named Anargala. Having eaten rice with ghee, he lived in the manner of a prince; he did not engage in any study of the sciences."

Once his father said, "O Anargala! Although you were born from my own breast, you are exceedingly perverse; you do not practice learning, but remain empty-hearted and a fool! For he who is empty-hearted is indeed a fool. And it is said: 'The home of one without a son is empty; a land without kinsmen is empty;
the heart of a fool is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all. (223)
I have no need whatsoever for you. For instance: what is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous?
What is the use of that cow which neither calves nor gives milk? (224)
Furthermore, between one who is unborn and one who is dead, and two children who are foolish, it is better to have the latter two;
for they cause only slight grief, whereas a fool would burn [his parents] for as long as he lives. (225)
Furthermore,
what is the use of that which is born, merely robbing its mother of youth,
if it does not rise like a banner at the forefront of its own lineage? (226)

Having heard these words of his father, Anargala was filled with remorse; embracing a life of renunciation, he departed for another land. There, in a certain city, having studied the entire science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*) under a teacher, he set out to return to his own city. On the way, in the middle of a forest, he saw a temple. Near that temple was a lake of extremely clear water, adorned with clusters of lotuses and frequented by pairs of *cakravāka* birds.

In one part of that lake, the water was extremely hot. Having seen all this, while Anargala was seated there, the sun set. Subsequently, at the hour of midnight, eight divine women emerged from the midst of that heated water; having gone to the temple and performed the sixteen modes of worship, such as the ritual ablution for the deity, they gratified the Lord with arts such as dance and song. Then the Lord, being pleased, bestowed his grace upon those who had worshipped him. Anargala witnessed all of this.

Then, at the time of departure at dawn, Anargala was seen by them. Thereupon, one celestial woman among them said, "O gentle sir! Come with us toward our city. Having been thus addressed, she entered the midst of the boiling water together with her companions. He also desired to go with her, but once she had entered there, Anargala was unable to enter out of fear.

Then, having returned to his own city, he saw all his kinsmen, including his father; because of this, a great festival arose among them. Then, on the second day, he went to the royal assembly hall for an audience with the king, and having saluted the king, he sat down.
The king, having inquired after his welfare, said, "O Anargala, where have you been staying for all these days?
He replied, "I went to another country to practice my learning."
The king asked, "What unprecedented thing was seen there in that foreign land?
And Anargala related to the king the account of the heated water.

Having heard that, when the king went to that place with him, the sun had already set. At the time of midnight, those celestial women returned again, performed the sixteen services as before, and after attending upon the deity with dance and other offerings, they departed at dawn. Then, one among them, seeing the king, said: "O gentle sir! Come with us toward our city."

Having heard this, the king went out with her. Then all the women entered into the midst of the boiling water and went to their own city in Pātāla. The king also, having submerged himself in the midst of the boiling water, went along with them. Then all the women performed for him the rites of lustration and other services, and said: "O Great Being! There is no one at all equal to you, endowed as you are with qualities such as heroism; therefore, you alone shall be the sovereign of this kingdom. We, all of us women, shall perform service for you."
The king said, "O queens! I have no need for this kingdom; I have come solely to witness this marvel. I too possess a kingdom.
They replied, "O Great Being! We are pleased; choose a boon.
The king asked, "Who are you?"
They said, "We are the eight great siddhis. The king said, "In that case, the eight great siddhis must be given to me. Having heard this, those women gave eight jewels to the king;
these were indeed endowed with the eight qualities beginning with *aṇiman*.
Then, as the king was returning after taking those jewels, a certain elderly brahmin approached him on the road and said:
"May he who dwells in the navel-lotus of Hari, who possesses four faces, and who is the original reciter of the Vedas, protect you always. (227)
Thus he offered this blessing.
Then the king asked, "O Brāhmaṇa, from where have you come?

That Brāhmaṇa replied, "I am a Brāhmaṇa residing in the city of Campā; I have a large family, yet I am extremely poor. Reprimanded by my wife, I have come to another land. O King, this is a well-known saying in popular proverb and in political science: even wives and others abandon a man who is destitute. And it is said:
Even when well-served, the master suddenly shows hatred; kinsmen abandon one along with all their kin;
virtues do not shine and sons desert; calamities expand;
and even a wife born of a noble lineage does not remain faithful, nor do friends stay.
For those men whose wealth does not exist, even when they have displayed valor through just means, [what is the use of such valor]? 228.
And likewise:
the Guru should be handsome, fortunate, eloquent, and the best among the learned in both the scriptures and the weapons.
For in the world of mortals, a human being indeed does not attain the full range of arts without wealth. (229)
Moreover,
those very faculties are unimpaired, that same intellect is indeed unimpeded, and his speech is likewise.
It is truly strange that a man, when deprived of the warmth of wealth, becomes someone else entirely in a single moment. || 230 ||
Moreover,
the desires of the poor, upon arising, dissolve back into the heart,
just as the breasts of noble women consumed by early widowhood shrink away. 231.
Having heard these words of his, the king was exceedingly pleased and gave him eight jewels. Having praised the king, he departed for his own city, and the king likewise returned toward Ujjayinī.
Having told this story, the statuette said to the king, "O King, if you possess such fortitude, heroism, and other virtues, then sit upon this throne.
Hearing that, the king remained silent.

Thus ends the twenty-first episode, titled "The Attainment of the Eight Great Siddhis," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the story of the throne. 21.

Now begins the twenty-second narrative, titled "The Attainment of Kāmākṣī’s Favor. Again, when the king went to sit upon the throne, another statuette stopped him and said, "O King, one should sit upon this throne only if he possesses valor as well as virtues such as magnanimity. The king replied, "O statuette, do I not possess all that you have mentioned, such as magnanimity? Is anything lacking? Have I not also given to all supplicants what was appropriate for the time?"
Having heard that, the statuette said: "O King! Are you proclaiming yourself once again with your own mouth? Have you not heard:
'Neither happiness nor good fortune comes from describing one's own virtues, just as it is for women to massage their own breasts with their own hands. (2)
Having heard what was said by the puppet, King Bhoja, feeling ashamed, replied: "Truly, you have spoken well; now tell me the account of that Vikrama’s magnanimity.

She said: "O King, listen! Once, while King Vikramāditya was governing his kingdom, he set out to travel across the earth. Having visited various holy places (*tīrthas*), temples, cities, mountains, and so forth, he eventually beheld a certain city surrounded by walls of great jewels, adorned with palaces that scraped the clouds, and containing many shrines and temples dedicated to Śiva.
Having gone there to the temple of Viṣṇu situated outside the city, and having bathed in the lake located there and paid obeisance to Viṣṇu, [I said]:
"O Lord, what is known by me of Your supreme majesty?
Even Brahmā does not know You, for You are beyond the reach of words. (233)
I worship none other, I speak of none other, nor do I take refuge in another; I hear of none other, I read of none other, nor do I contemplate any other—
with devotion and reverence for your lotus feet.
O Śrī Śrīnivāsa! O Puruṣottama! Grant me servitude. || 234 ||
Having offered praise with these and other such words, the king spoke to the Brahmin seated in the theater hall: "O Brahmin, from where have you come?
The Brahmin replied, "I am a pilgrim; I am traveling across the earth. From where have you come?"

The king said, "I too am some pilgrim like yourself. The Brahmin, having observed him thoroughly, replied, "O sir! It is not so; you appear exceedingly majestic, and all the marks of royalty are visible upon you. You are worthy of the lion-throne of a sovereign of kings; for what purpose do you wander the earth? Or rather, who can transgress what is written upon the forehead? For it is said:
Even by Hari, by Hara, by Brahmā, or even by the thirty gods, The line inscribed on the forehead cannot be erased. (235)
The king accepted his words and said, "O Brahmin, why do you appear as if you have lost all hope?
He replied, "What cause for despair shall I tell you?
The king said, "Tell us the reason for the suffering you have personally experienced."

The Brahmin said, "Listen, sirs! Nearby there is a mountain named Nīla, where a deity named Kāmākṣī resides. Near her, the door to the opening of a subterranean cavern remains closed; it is opened by the recitation of the mantra of Kāmākṣī. Within it there is a single pool of mercury; by means of that mercury, the eight metals are transformed into gold.
I have performed the recitation of the Kāmākṣī mantra for twelve years, yet I have not been able to open the door of the cavern."

Upon hearing those words, the king went there at that very moment, worshipped the goddess with the sixteen-fold offerings, and bowed down. Just as he was about to place his sword upon his own neck, the deity said, "I am pleased with you; choose a boon.
The king replied, "O Goddess, if you are pleased, then grant this nectar to this Brahmin."

The deity, saying "So be it," opened the entrance to the cave and gave the nectar to the Brahmin. That Brahmin, having praised the king, departed for his own city, and the king likewise returned to his capital.
Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "O King! If such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the twenty-second episode, titled "The Attainment of Kāmākṣī’s Grace," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja, in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 22.
Now begins the twenty-third narrative, titled "The Vision of a Bad Dream.

Again, as soon as the king attempted to sit upon the throne, another statuette stopped him and said, "O King! Only he is worthy to ascend this throne who possesses a generosity equal to the generosity of Vikrama.
The king asked, "O statuette! Tell me the account of that Vikrama’s generous conduct."

The statuette said: "Listen, O King! Once, after wandering over the earth, King Vikramārka returned to his own city. A great joy arose among all the inhabitants of that city. Having entered his palace, the king performed his midday ablutions, including an oil massage and a bath; then, adorned with sandalwood paste, fine garments, and other ornaments, he entered the temple of the deity. Having offered the sixteen-fold worship (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) to the deity, he recited this hymn of praise:
'Thou alone art my mother, and thou alone art my father; thou alone art my kinsman and thou alone art my friend.'"
You alone are knowledge, you alone are wealth; you alone are everything to me, O God of gods. || 236 ||

Having thus praised and bowed to the Lord, and having given gifts of Kapila cows, land, sesame seeds, and so forth to the Brahmins, he subsequently gave abundant alms to the poor, the blind, the deaf, the hunchbacked, the lame, the destitute, and others. Then, having entered the dining hall and fed the children, newly married women, the elderly, and others, he himself ate together with his other kinsmen. And so it is said:
"Children, newly married women, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, and young maidens, as well as guests and servants—having first fed these, the husband and wife may eat what remains. (237)
One who desires his own success should not eat alone;
a man should take his meal together with two, three, or many others. (238)
The attainment of desired fruits, contentment, fulfillment of wishes, and excellent prosperity arise when eating together with two, three, or many people. (239)
Then, after finishing his meal, he sat down and rested for a short while. And so it is said: "For one who sits after eating, and likewise for one who lies down after eating, there is ease;
but for one who walks on, life is long, whereas for one who runs, death pursues. (240)
Furthermore:
"From excessive drinking of water, from irregular eating, from sleeping during the day and staying awake at night, and from the suppression of urine and feces—diseases arise in these six ways. (24.1)

Thereafter, having performed his duties for the time at the hour of twilight and having eaten, he went to his place of rest. There, he lay down upon a couch spread with a coverlet as white as the mass of moonbeams and strewn with flowers such as the kunda, mallikā, and śatapatra. He fell asleep.

Then, at the time of dawn, the king saw himself in a dream mounted upon a buffalo and traveling toward the southern direction; waking up suddenly, he sat upon his couch while recollecting Viṣṇu. Thereafter, having performed his morning duties and observed the twilight rituals, he sat upon the throne and related the account of his dream before the Brahmins. Upon hearing that, a certain omniscient person said, "O King!"

Dreams are of two kinds: some are auspicious and bestow auspicious results, while others are inauspicious and indicate misfortune (*ariṣṭa*). Among these, auspicious dreams include mounting an elephant, ascending a palace, weeping, death, approaching a woman who should not be approached, and the sight of a parasol, chowries, the ocean, a Brāhmaṇa, the Gaṅgā, a devoted wife (*pativratā*), a conch, gold, and so forth.
And it has been said:
"Ascending cows, bulls, and elephants..."
In a dream, climbing a palace, a mountain peak, or a great tree; being smeared with excrement; weeping; death; and approaching a woman who should not be approached—these are indeed auspicious.
Inauspicious dreams include mounting a buffalo, mounting a donkey, climbing a thorny tree, and seeing ash, cotton, smoke, tigers, snakes, boars, monkeys, and the like. As it has been said:
"He who mounts a donkey, a camel, a buffalo, or a tiger in a dream will certainly meet his death within six months. (243)
Furthermore: in dreams occurring during the first watch of the night, the fruition occurs within a year;
in the second, within eight months; and in the third, within three months.
At the time of releasing the cows, however, the fruit is said to be immediate. || 244 ||
"What more need be said? O King! This dream is an omen of misfortune for you.
The king asked, "O Brahmin! What must be done to pacify the ill fortune resulting from this bad dream?"

Sarvajñabhaṭṭa said: "Having performed your ablutions and supervised the sacrificial rites, give all your ornaments along with garments and other items to a Brāhmaṇa. Then, having put on another set of clothes and caused the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the deity to be performed, conduct worship with the nine gems (navaratna). Give cows and the ten kinds of grain to the Brāhmaṇas, and honor the blind, the deaf, the lame, the hunchbacked, the destitute, and others with abundant gifts.
By this performance and the benedictions of the Brāhmaṇas, there shall be well-being for you through the destruction of the evil results arising from the bad dream."

Having heard all these words of the Bhaṭṭa and having carried out exactly what was instructed, the king summoned the treasurer for the purpose of making abundant gifts for three days and gave him his orders. Then, whoever was satisfied with whatever amount of wealth, he took that much wealth away. Having told this story, the statuette said to the king, "O King! If such generosity and fortitude exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the twenty-third episode, titled "The Vision of a Bad Dream," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. ||23||

The Twenty-Fourth Narrative: The Description of the Battle with Śālivāhana Again, as soon as the king attempted to ascend the throne, another statuette stopped him and said, "O King, only one who possesses virtues such as magnanimity like those of Vikrama is worthy to sit upon this throne.
The King of Bhoja asked, "O statuette, tell me the account of Vikrama's deeds and his qualities, such as magnanimity."
She said, "Listen, O King! In the realm of Vikramāditya, there was a city named Purandarapurī. A certain very wealthy merchant lived there, and he had four sons."

Then, on one occasion, he called them together and said, "O sons! If it should not be possible for all four of you to remain together after I have died, then quarreling will ensue later; therefore, while I am still alive, I have divided your inheritance among you four according to the order of seniority. These four portions have been deposited beneath my bed; take them according to the sequence of eldest to youngest," and they agreed to this.

Then, after he had departed for the next world, the four brothers remained together for one month. Subsequently, a dispute arose among their wives. Thereupon, they deliberated: "Why do we quarrel? While our father was still alive, he already made a division of the inheritance for us four; let us take that division plan lying beneath the couch and, having divided [the estate], let us live in peace. Having said this, they began digging beneath the couch.

Beneath those four feet, four hollow cavities were seen. In the midst of them, in one cavity there was earth; in another there were embers; in another bones were situated; and in the fourth, a heap of straw was situated.

Having seen these four caskets in this manner, those four brothers were filled with wonder and said to one another, "Aha! By what means can the order of the division of wealth be known from this sequence of the father's correct division? Having spoken thus, they went to the royal court and reported the entire account before the assembly. Even the members of the assembly could not understand the sequence of the division.
Furthermore, the four brothers went wherever there were kinsmen and reported this matter before them, yet no one was able to reach a decision.

Then, on one occasion, having arrived at Ujjayinī, they went before the royal court and recounted the details of the partition from beginning to end. Neither the king nor the assembly could determine the sequence of the division. Subsequently, on another occasion, they went to another city named Pratiṣṭhāna and began to relate that account before the local merchants and citizens; they too were unable to reach a decision.

In that city, a certain man named Śālivāhana, staying in the house of a potter, heard this news and spoke to the great crowd who had gathered there: "O worthy ones! What is difficult to understand here? And what is the wonder? Tell me! Hearing this, one among them said: "These four are the sons of a single wealthy man. While their father was still alive, he made this division of inheritance according to the order of seniority."
For example, there was clay in one casket, charcoal in another, bones in yet another, and a heap of straw in another; no one was able to determine the distinction between them.

Having heard that, Śālivāhana said: "To the first, earth was given; by him, whatever land he had acquired, all of that was given to him. To the second, charcoal was given; by him, all his gold was given to him. To the third, bones were given; by him, all his livestock was given to him. To the fourth, a heap of straw was given; by him, all kinds of grain and other crops were given to him."

Thus Śālivāhana explained the underlying intent of their father’s distribution of the inheritance. Having heard this, those sons of the wealthy man also felt fulfilled and happy, and returned to their own city.
Then King Vikrama, having heard this account of the resolution regarding the division from them, was filled with wonder and dispatched a certain letter to the city of Pratiṣṭhāna.

"Thus, King Vikrama, having first inquired after the welfare of the great men residing in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna—who are devoted to the six duties consisting of sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts, and who are endowed with virtues such as restraint and observance—announces: 'He who is the one deciding the partition among those four sons of wealthy men in your village must be sent into my presence.'"

The local people there, having read that letter sent by the king, summoned Śālivāhana and said to him: "O Śālivāhana! King Vikrama—overlord of kings, supreme lord, sovereign of the earth as far as the oceans, ruler of Ujjayinī, and a wish-fulfilling tree for all arts, wealth, and poetry—summons you; therefore, go there."

He said, "Who is this king named Vikrama? I will not go when summoned by him. If he has some business with me, let him come to me himself; I have no need for him. Having heard those words of his, the people sent another letter to the king, saying that he would not go, but desired the arrival of the illustrious one right there.

Then the king, having heard the contents written on that letter, his body blazing with the fire of wrath, set out with an army of eighteen akṣauhiṇīs. Having arrived at the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, he dispatched a messenger to Śālivāhana. The messenger sent by him went there and said to Śālivāhana: "O Śālivāhana! King Vikrama, the sovereign lord, summons you; therefore, come to have an audience with him."
Śālivāhana said, "O messenger! Being alone, I shall not see the king; rather, endowed with my sixfold army, I shall show my prowess on the field of battle. Therefore, go and report this to the king."

Having heard those words, the messenger reported everything exactly as it was to the king. Upon hearing this, King Vikrama arrived at the battlefield with his army. Śālivāhana, for his part, having brought to life by means of a mantra the forces of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry fashioned from clay in the potter’s house, emerged from the city with that sixfold army and advanced toward the field of battle. At that moment, when both divisions had set out—
The circle of the quarters trembled, and the ocean became violently agitated; the lord of serpents in the netherworld was struck with fear, and the mountain ranges shook.

The earth quaked, and the serpent-king, bearing the poison, thrust his formidable chest forward. Thus, when the commander of the army set forth, every event occurred in manifold ways. The splendor of the host shone forth with infinite herds of horses equal to the speed of the wind and with throngs of rutting elephants.
The entire sky was covered with banners, chowries, and excellent weapons, while the three worlds resounded with the sounds of drums, kettledrums, clay drums, and war-drums.
Then the two wings met together. At that moment, the entire sky was pervaded by the abundant dust from the hooves of horses and other animals;
the space between them was covered with umbrellas, and it was incessantly filled with the roar of kettledrums.
With the rattling sounds produced by chariots, the cries of elephants and horses, the tinkling of small bells,
and the roars of heroes that inspired great terror, the opposing armies appeared magnificent.

With skull-topped staffs, bhalla-weapons, wicked hooves, maces, clubs, crescent-shaped arrows, iron shafts, slings, excellent ploughs, pestles, spears, lances, swords, battle-axes, javelins, thunderbolts, and other such divine weapons of extreme sharpness, the noble warriors engage in combat with one another as the two assembled divisions clash. 248.
In that battle on the field of combat, some excellent warriors, being struck down, fall deprived of life;
others fall into a swoon, yet even they rise again by their own strength.

Laughing with loud, boisterous laughter, they display their own supreme pride and primordial arrogance; having filled themselves with confidence and cast off the fear of death, they run forward, manifesting boldness in their very limbs.
Indeed, some among the enemies instill terror by bringing about a state of panic through the power of the battle.
Some, their bodies struck by full-scale blows, may become dear to the celestial nymphs;
others, the foremost of heroes, even when their bellies are struck by enemies, being pierced by weapons and their bodies split apart by missiles, proceed to battle free from fear.
There, heaps of weapons such as polished daggers shine like fish;
a mass of hair, sinews, veins, and a network of entrails appears like aquatic moss. Such fallen bodies of elephants and lords of men are not seen in the battle of Śambhu.
Those bones shine forth in the blood like conch shells on a sandy shore.

Then Vikramārka struck down the entire army of Śālivāhana. Seeing this, Śālivāhana remembered his father, the lord of serpents named Śeṣa. Śeṣa sent forth serpents; bitten by those snakes, the host of Vikramāditya’s army fell unconscious from the poison upon the field of battle.

Thereafter, King Vikramārka went alone to his own city and, standing in shallow water for nine years, recited the mantra of Vāsuki in order to restore his army to life. Then Vāsuki, being pleased with him, said: "O King, choose a boon! Vikrama replied: "O King of Serpents, if you are pleased with me, then give me a jar of nectar to revive my army which has been rendered unconscious by the force of the serpents' venom."
Then, having accepted that jar of nectar given by Vāsuki with the words "So be it," as King Vikrama was proceeding along the road, a certain Brāhmaṇa approached and said:
"May that staff-like tusk of Hari in his Līlā-Varāha incarnation protect you—upon which the Earth, like a golden mountain-pitcher, bore the splendor of an umbrella. (252)
Thus he uttered this blessing.
Then the king said, "O Brahmin, from where have you come?
The Brahmin replied, "I have come from the city of Pratiṣṭhāna."
The king asked, "What do you say?

The brahmin replied, "Your Majesty is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) for those who seek wealth, since you are capable of granting whatever is desired. I have affection for one particular object; if it is granted, then I shall speak.
The king said, "O brahmin! Whatever you request, that I shall give."
The Brahmin said, "This jar of nectar must be given to me.
The King asked, "By whom have you been sent? The Brahmin replied, "I have been sent by Śālivāhana.

Upon hearing this, the King reflected: "Previously, I spoke without any deliberation, saying that I would give it to him. Now, if it is not given, there will be not only ill repute but also unrighteousness. Therefore, I must certainly give this to him under all circumstances."
Then, seeing that the king was left without an answer, the brahmin said: "O King! Why do you deliberate? You are exceedingly virtuous.
The speech of a virtuous person never turns out otherwise. As it is said:
'Even if the sun were to rise in the western quarter...'"
If Mount Meru should move, if fire should turn cold,
if a lotus should bloom upon a rock at the mountain peak— even then,
the speech of the virtuous would never change.

Hearing this, the king said, "What you have said is true. It shall be done exactly so; please accept this jar of nectar. Having spoken thus, he gave the jar to him. That Brahmin, praising the king, departed for his own place, and the king also returned to Ujjayinī. Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja, "O King! If such generosity and fortitude exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth episode, titled "The Description of the Battle with Śālivāhana," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, in the section concerning the Throne. 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth tale, titled "The Description of the Means for Warding off Drought.

Then, as the king again attempted to ascend the throne, another statuette stopped him and said, "O King, only he who possesses virtues such as magnanimity like those of Vikrama may sit upon this throne.
Bhoja replied, "O statuette, tell me the account of Vikrama’s magnanimity and other virtues."

She said: "Listen, O King! While Vikramāditya was ruling the kingdom, once a certain astrologer approached and, addressing the king, said: 'The Sun [bestows] valor; the Moon, the station of Indra; Mars, auspiciousness; Mercury, good intellect; Jupiter, greatness; Venus, a son; and Saturn, peace.'"
May Rāhu exert his strength of arms, may Ketu ensure the constant elevation of the family, and may all the planets be favorable and bring you perpetual joy. (254)

Having spoken this blessing, he explained the five limbs [of the year]. Then the king asked the astrologer: "O divine sage! What kind of auspicious or inauspicious events will occur in this year? The astrologer replied: "In this year, the Sun is the king, Mars is the minister, and Mars alone is the lord of the clouds. Saturn, moreover, will pass through piercing the cart of Rohiṇī; therefore, there will certainly be a drought. And it is said in the Saṃhitā:
For when the son of the Sun (Saturn) indeed consumes the cart of Rohiṇī, having pierced it, the cloud does not rain for twelve years. || 255 ||
And likewise:
if the son of the Sun pierces the cart of Rohiṇī, the earth becomes drenched in streams of blood.
What can I say? For the water in the ocean does not undergo depletion by all the worlds. || 256 ||
And according to another opinion:
"When this dull-witted one [Rāhu] pierces the cart of Rohiṇī, then for twelve years the bringer of rain does not pour here. (257)

Having heard these words of the astrologer, the king asked, "Is there any remedial measure for this drought, or not? The astrologer replied, "How could there not be? If certain rites such as planetary oblations (*graha-homa*) and others are performed, rain will surely fall."

Then King Vikrama summoned learned Brahmins and, having related before them the previous events as heard from the mouth of the astrologer, began to have the fire-oblation (homa) performed by them. Thereupon, they completed the entire ritual of the oblation. The king satisfied the Brahmins with wealth, food, clothing, and other gifts, and bestowed the ten types of charity (daśadāna). Following that, he also gratified the poor, the blind, the deaf, the lame, the helpless, and others with abundant alms.

However, no rain fell. Due to its absence, all the people, afflicted by famine and hungry, underwent extreme suffering. The king also, being himself deeply distressed by their misery, was once seated in the sacrificial hall when he began to reflect; at that moment, an incorporeal voice arose: "O King! The goddess residing in the temple standing before you will fulfill your hope.
If a human being endowed with the thirty-two marks has his head severed and offered as a sacrifice before this deity, there will be rain."

Having heard this, the king perceived himself as a man endowed with the thirty-two marks; he went to the temple, prostrated before the goddess, and just as he was about to take up his sword to cut off his own head, the deity seized the sword and said, "O King, I am pleased by your magnanimity; choose a boon.
The king replied, "O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, then put an end to this drought. The deity said, "So shall it be," and vanished.

Then, as the king emerged from the temple and set out toward his own city, the expanse of the sky was suddenly shrouded by thick clouds. These clouds, producing the thunderous roar of lightning that repeatedly struck the ears with terror—thus inspiring joy in the peacocks, causing the *cātaka* birds, parched for divine water, to look upward, illuminating the quarters of the horizon with flashes of lightning, and filling the lakes, ponds, and other reservoirs with heavy downpours of water resembling the trunks of elephants—removed the distress of all living beings. Seeing this, the king, filled with exceeding joy, returned to his own assembly hall.
Having told this story, the statuette said: "O King, if such fortitude and a desire to benefit others exist within you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth tale, titled "The Description of the Means for Warding off Drought," in the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja, within the *Siṃhāsanopākhyāna* of the *Vikramārka-carita*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth narrative, titled "The Dialogue with the Wish-Fulfilling Cow.

Again, just as the king was about to sit upon the throne, he was stopped by another statuette, who said: "O King, only one who possesses virtues such as magnanimity like those of Vikrama is worthy to sit upon this throne.
Hearing this, Bhoja said: "O statuette, tell the story of that Vikrama's virtues, such as his magnanimity."

Thus questioned by the king, she replied: "O King, listen! On this earth there is no other king equal to Vikrama in qualities such as magnanimity, compassion, discernment, and fortitude. Furthermore, whatever he says is never done otherwise; what remains in his heart, that he speaks with his voice; and what he reveals in his speech, that he performs accordingly. Therefore, he is exceedingly virtuous. As it is said: 'As is the mind, so is the word; as is the word, so is the deed.
In thought, in speech, and in action, the virtuous possess a single uniform nature. (258)

Once, in the city of the gods, Indra was seated upon his throne. In his assembly hall, there were eighty-eight thousand sages; thirty-three crores of deities were seated there, as well as the eight world-protectors (*lokapālas*), the forty-nine Maruts, the twelve Ādityas, Nārada, Tumburu, and divine women such as Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā, Miśrakeśī, Ghṛtācī, Mañjughoṣā, and Priyadarśanā. They all sat together.

The entire host of Gandharvas sat down. At that moment, Nārada spoke there: "In the circle of lands beginning with Abhra, there is no king equal to Vikramārka in fame, benevolence toward others, or possession of great courage. Hearing those words of his, all those present in the assembly of the gods were struck with great wonder. Then Surabhi said: "What doubt is there in this? Or what cause for wonder? And it is said:
In generosity, in austerity, in heroism, in knowledge, in modesty, and in statesmanship—"
One should not feel astonishment, for the earth abounds in many jewels. || 259 ||
And so it is said:
"Between horses, elephants, and iron; between wood, stone, and cloth; and between women, men, and water—there is a vast difference. (260)
Having heard that, Indra spoke to the daughter of Surabhi, Kāmadhenu: "Go to the world of mortals to ascertain the virtues of Vikrama, such as his valor, compassion, and benevolence."

Then Kāmadhenu, assuming the form of an extremely weak cow and traveling toward the mortal world, showed herself to be in great distress through her own illusory power: just as Vikramārka arrived on the path, she appeared submerged in a very difficult-to-cross mire and was being greedily eyed by a tiger standing nearby. Upon seeing the king, she let out a piteous cry.

Thus, while the king—his heart nearly shattered by hearing those words of despair—was making an effort to raise that cow from the mud, the sun set. Then, in due course, the night consisting of darkness arrived. He remained right there, protecting that helpless cow. In this manner, the end of the night came.

Then, when sunrise had occurred, that cow, having observed the king's virtues such as compassion and fortitude, rose up of her own accord and said to the king: "O King! I am the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu). I have come from heaven to test your virtues, such as compassion. Having come here myself, my proof has been witnessed. There is no king on earth more devoted to compassion than you. I am pleased with this quality of yours; choose a boon. The king replied, "By your grace, there is no deficiency in me whatsoever; so what should I request?"
She said, "My word can never be in vain; therefore, I shall remain right by your side," and having spoken thus, she went out with the king.

Then, as the king was traveling along the road with her, a certain Brahmin approached and joyfully recited: "When the lord of serpents enters the aperture of his nostrils—terrifying the peacock of Kumāra, who is summoned by the sound of the drum struck by Nandin's hand—he contracts his coils."

May the long, whirling movements of the faces of Ganesha protect you—faces that resound with swarms of bees flying up from his temples during the dance of the Trident-Bearer, and which are filled with his own trumpeting cries. 261.

Having offered this blessing, he said: "O King! By the power of fate, I am poor; for the sake of obtaining food for my belly, I wander here and there day and night. I see everyone constantly with a timid gaze, yet due to my misfortune, no one sees me. And it is said:
'Homage to you, O Poverty! By your grace I have achieved my goal:
I see the entire world, yet no one sees me. (262)

But for one who is sealed by poverty, there is always nothing but birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) in his house. As it has been said: "O fortunate woman, give a morsel of food to the traveler! 'No, no,' you say—why are your words fruitless? Speak, O Makha! Is this a state of birth-impurity? Is there no end to its duration?"
As long as I live, this ill fortune arising from the birth of a son does not depart;
for what child has been born to me, who am destitute of all wealth? A son named "Poverty" has been born. (26.3)
The king said, "O Brahmin, what do you ask for?
The Brahmin replied, "O King, you are like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) to those who depend upon you; please act in such a way that my poverty may be eliminated for as long as I live.

The king said, "In that case, this wish-granting cow (*kāmadhenu*) will grant you whatever you desire; take her. Having said this, he gave the wish-granting cow to him. The Brahmin, as if having attained the bliss of heaven, took the wish-granting cow and went to his own place; the king also returned to his own city.

Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja: "O King, this is the twenty-seventh tale, called 'The Conversation with the Gambler. O King, if such magnanimity exists in you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth tale, called 'The Conversation with the Wish-Fulfilling Cow,' within the section on the Apsaras and the Conversation with Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, in the cycle of tales concerning the throne. 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh tale, titled "The Conversation with the Gambler.

Again, as soon as the king endeavored to sit upon the throne, another statuette stopped him and said: "O King, only one who possesses virtues such as compassion, courtesy, and magnanimity, like those of Vikrama, is worthy to sit upon this throne.
The king replied, "O statuette, tell me the account of the virtues of that Vikrama—his compassion, courtesy, magnanimity, and the rest."

She said, "Listen, O King! Once, while wandering the earth, King Vikrama arrived at a certain city. The king of that place was exceedingly righteous, devoted to the performance of duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, and he properly protected the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who resided there. Every person in that land was devoted to virtuous conduct, hospitable toward guests, and compassionate."
King Vikrama, having resolved that he would stay there for three or five days, went to a certain most enchanting temple, bowed to the deity therein, and sat down in the performance hall.

In the meantime, someone of exceedingly charming appearance, like a prince, wearing fine silk garments, his body adorned with various ornaments, and his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste mixed with saffron, camphor, and musk, arrived there with his companions. After spending some time diverting himself with various conversations and topics concerning the objects of desire, he departed from that place along with them. The king, having seen him, remained there reflecting in his mind, "Who is this?"

Then, on the second day, he alone, stripped of clothes and possessions, with nothing remaining but his loincloth, arrived and collapsed in the performance hall of the temple. Seeing him, the king said, "O noble-minded one! Yesterday you came here adorned in body like a prince, attended by your companions; how is it that today you have fallen into such a miserable state? He replied, "O Lord, what can be said? I was exactly as I was yesterday; now, through the turn of fate, I have become thus. For instance:
Those bees, who were nourished by the ichor from the temples of elephants and whose bodies were made fragrant by the pollen of full-blown lotuses,
now spend their time day after day [in this state].
And by the turn of fate, among the nimba trees and the arka flowers. ||264||
And so,
the bee, once solely devoted to the playful fragrance of rows of juicy mango trees,
now wanders through a forest of *arka* plants teeming with *śarabha* beasts, by the power of a cruel fate. (265)
And likewise,
those who were nurtured in the midst of the pollen of golden lotuses amidst the undulating waves of the pure waters of the Mandākinī;
Now, by the power of fate, those very same young swans have taken refuge in water thick with masses of moss. || 266 ||
Moreover,
he who formerly shone with a body anointed by the mass of pollen fallen from lotuses shaken by the wind, and felt joy upon hearing the warbling of honey-bees;
This very same swan, who was once incapable of even seizing a grain of rice situated at the tip of his beloved’s beak, now, by the power of fate, searches for a snail.
Furthermore, what hardship does a person not encounter when constrained by their past actions? As it has been said:
Having offered the entire web of karma accumulated over a long time to the Divine, dwell at ease and in comfort; what is the use of further supplications?
For even as the sun circumambulates Mount Meru, [it does so without seeking anything].
He had those seven horses; never eight.
Moreover,
by whom Brahmā was constrained like a potter within the vessel of the cosmic egg, and by whom Viṣṇu was cast into the great peril of the thicket of his ten incarnations;
Salutation to that karma by which Rudra was made to wander for alms with a skull held in the hollow of his hands, and by which the sun revolves eternally in the sky. ||269||
Alternatively,
whatever wealth— be it small or great— that has been inscribed by the Creator upon his own forehead, he certainly obtains that even in a desert; yet on Mount Meru, he receives no more than that.
Therefore, be steadfast among the wealthy; do not adopt this piteous way of life in vain.
Look! A jar draws an equal amount of water from both a well and the ocean. ||270||
The king asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a gambler named Devadatta.
The king said, "Do you know how to play at dice?"
He said, "I am skilled in the art of gambling. Furthermore, I know the games of chess and *caturaṅga*, yet all of that is useless; fate alone is powerful. And it is said:
"The eclipsing of the moon and sun by planets, and even the binding of elephants and serpents—"
And having observed the poverty of even those possessed of intelligence, it is my conviction that "Alas! Fate is all-powerful. || 271 ||

The king said, "O Devadatta! Though you are so exceedingly wise, how is it that you are addicted to the most sinful practice of gambling? He replied, "What is there that even a wise man will not do when impelled by his karma? The king remarked, "O Devadatta! Gambling is the root of great calamity; gambling alone is the refuge of all vices."
And it has been said:
"This world is the abode of infamy, the generous lord of calamities for thieves and courtesans, and the repository of those who partake in evil."
For who indeed, possessing pure and clear intelligence through wisdom, would resort to gambling on this path to the uneven hells? || 272 ||
For that reason, the seven great sins and vices must be abandoned. And it is said:
"Gambling, meat, liquor, prostitutes, hunting, theft, and another's wife—these seven great sins and vices a wise man should renounce. (273)
Furthermore:
"If a man who is addicted to even a single vice does not see his way out, how much less so a person overwhelmed by being joined with all seven vices? (274)
For instance:

here, Dharmasuta perished through gambling; Baka through liquor; the joy of the Yadus through theft; King Brahmadatta through the power of lust; and Śivabhūti through his habit of thievery. Furthermore, the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa) fell due to his forceful attachment to another's wife. When men are struck down by even a single vice, who among all of them does not perish? || 275 ||
"Therefore, you must renounce these.
The gambler said, "O Master! That alone is my livelihood; how can it be abandoned? If, out of compassion for me, you will tell me some means of acquiring wealth, then I shall give up gambling.

At this moment, two Brahmins living abroad arrived and, sitting down in a corner of the temple, began to consult with one another. One of them said, "I have examined the entire ritual manual of the Piśāca script."

In that very place, it was written thus: "In the northeast corner of this temple, at a distance of five bows, three jars filled with dīnāras have been placed; near them is an image of Bhairava. Whoever shall consecrate Bhairava with his own blood, by him those [treasures] are to be taken.
Having heard these words, the king went there and began to consecrate Bhairava with the blood from his own body. Just then, the gratified Bhairava said: "O King, choose a boon!"
The king said, "Give this gambler three jars filled with dīnāras.
Then, at his command, Bhairava gave that wealth to the gambler. Having obtained it, the gambler praised the king and departed for his own city; the king also returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to the king: "O King, if such qualities as fortitude, magnanimity, and altruism exist in you, then sit upon this throne."
The king remained silent.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh episode, titled "The Conversation with the Gambler," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 277.
Now begins the twenty-eighth narrative, titled "The Warding Off of Narabali.

Again, just as the king was about to sit upon the throne, another statuette suddenly stopped him and said, "O King! Only Vikrama, endowed with qualities such as magnanimity and fortitude, is worthy to sit upon this throne, and no other.
Hearing this, Bhoja said, "O statuette! A powerful curiosity has arisen in me; therefore, relate the account of Vikrama’s virtues, such as his magnanimity."

He said: "Listen, O King! Once, while traveling across the earth, King Vikramāditya arrived at a certain city. Near that city flowed a river of pure water, and on its bank stood a forest adorned with various kinds of trees, flowers, and fruits. In the midst of it was a most enchanting temple.
Having bathed in the clear waters of that river, the king entered the temple, paid homage to the deity enshrined there, and sat down."

In the meantime, four foreigners arrived there and sat down near the king. Then the king asked them, "O good sirs, from where have you come? One of them replied, "We have come from an unprecedented land.
The king said, "What unprecedented things did you see in that country?"

He said, "In that region there exists a city named Vetālapurī. There dwells a certain deity who is fond of blood. Every year, the local populace and the king offer a human sacrifice to that deity for the fulfillment of their own desires and for the warding off of misfortune. On that day, if any foreigner happens to arrive, they surrender him to the deity like an animal."

"On that very day, we too arrived at that city by the course of our journey. Then, the local people came there to rescue us. Hearing that, we fled out of fear for our lives and arrived here. This great marvel was witnessed by us.
Hearing this, King Vikrama, overcome with curiosity, went there. Beholding that terrifying goddess and bowing down, he praised her:
"Brahmāṇī, whose face is as serene as the lotus and the moon; Māheśvarī, who by her mere play—"

May the Mothers protect me: Kaumārī, who destroys the pride of enemies; Vaiṣṇavī, whose weapon is the discus; Vārāhī; the stainless Śakti of Narasiṃha; Śākrī, whose weapon is the thunderbolt; Cāmuṇḍā; and she who is honored by Gaṇanātha and Rudra. ||276||
Having thus offered praise, he sat down in the performance arena.

At that moment, a certain person with a distressed countenance arrived, accompanied by a great multitude and preceded by musical instruments. Upon seeing him, the king reflected in his mind: "This very person has been brought here by these people for the sake of an offering to the deity; therefore, he appears as if utterly exhausted. Thinking, "At this very moment, I shall offer my own body and liberate him," [he remained seated].

This body, having endured for a hundred years, will ultimately meet with destruction; therefore, even by means of the sacrifice of one's own body, embodied beings must acquire merit (*dharma*) and fame (*kīrti*). As it has been said:
"Fortune is fleeting, life is fleeting, the body is fleeting, and youth is fleeting;
the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is both moving and unmoving, but fame and merit are immovable. (277)
Furthermore:
Bodies are impermanent, and worldly power is certainly not eternal;
death is ever-present, so one must practice the accumulation of dharma. (278)
And thus:
Wealth is like the dust of the feet; youth is like the current of a mountain river;
human existence is as fickle and unstable as a drop of water; and life is like foam.
He who, with a steady mind, does not practice the Dharma that unlocks the bolt of heaven, is later struck by remorse and, aged by old age, is consumed by the fire of grief. ||279||
Having reflected thus, the king said to those great people: "O great people! Where is this man with the dejected face being led?
They replied, "We shall give him as an offering to the deity.
The king asked, "For what reason?"

They said, "The deity, being pleased by this human offering, will fulfill our desire. The king said, "O great people! This man is extremely small of stature and, moreover, terrified; what satisfaction will the deity derive from the offering of his body? Therefore, release him. I myself shall give my own body for that purpose. I am well-built in limb, and through the offering of my flesh, there will be great satisfaction for the deity."

Saying, "Therefore, kill me," he released him. The king himself went before the deity and, just as he was about to strike his own throat with the sword, the deity seized the sword and said, "O Great Being, I am exceedingly pleased by your fortitude and your act of altruism; choose a boon. The king replied, "O Goddess, if you are pleased with me, then from this day forward, abandon the offering of human flesh.
Hearing this, the deity said, "So be it."
Having observed all this, those great people said to the king: "O King! Being one who has no desire for your own happiness, you surely bear suffering like a tree for the sake of others. For indeed:
'Either you suffer day after day against the injuries of the world while having no desire for your own happiness, or else your very nature is of such a kind.'"
For the tree indeed endures the intense heat with its crown, yet it allays the fever of those who take refuge in its shade.

"Never before, anywhere, have we seen anyone like you who is so devoted to the welfare of others. Therefore, we are greatly alarmed by this conduct and pray for your well-being," they said, and then all of them departed. Then the king, having taken leave of them, returned to his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said to Bhoja: "O King! If such qualities as fortitude, magnanimity, and altruism exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth episode, titled "The Prevention of Human Sacrifice," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the legend of the throne. 28.
Now begins the twenty-ninth tale, titled "The Liberation from Poverty.
Again, as soon as the king sat upon the throne, another statuette said, "O King! Only one who possesses virtues such as magnanimity like those of Vikrama is worthy to sit upon this throne.
Bhoja replied, "Statuette, tell the story of that Vikrama’s virtue of magnanimity."
She said, "Listen, O King! Once, while King Vikramārka was seated in the assembly hall being attended by the princes, a certain bard approached and recited:
'As long as the holy Ganges, the river of the gods, carries its waves;
and as long as the Sun, the protector of the world, shines upon the earth from the path of the sky...'"
O King, as long as the diamond, sapphire, and crystal gemstones exist upon the peak of Mount Meru, so long may you enjoy the kingdom, surrounded by your sons, grandsons, and kinsmen! ||281||

Having uttered this benediction, he praises the king: "O King, just as the cātaka bird, tormented by the summer heat and parched with thirst, longs for and begs water from a rain-cloud, so do I [long] for the sight of you. (282)
For I am a dweller in a distant land; having heard of your fame, I have come from afar.

Your fame adorns the circle of the earth bounded by the seven oceans—more than camphor, more than the night-lotus, more than the blossoming jasmine, more than the surging waves of the celestial river, and even more than the glancing sidelong glance of a moving, beautiful woman.
And how [is it] without remainder? Just as the earth with its seven oceans has been whitened by your white glories, even more so than by a fragment of the moon free from blemish. ||283||

"O King! Having come to you, who are a wish-fulfilling tree for seekers, I am today liberated from the disease of poverty. Moreover, seeing you here in this land—a wish-fulfilling tree for all supplicants—the name of a certain king named Dhaneśvara arises in our memory. In the northern direction, in the region of Īśāna, in the city of Jambīra, there was a king named Dhaneśvara who bestowed wealth upon those in need in order to dispel their suffering of poverty."

Once, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when Dhaneśvara had performed the Vasantapūjā, many beggars arrived from even great distances. At that time, the king gave eighteen crores of gold for the purpose of charity. Just like him, who was preeminent in such supreme magnanimity, you alone have been seen in this land.

Having heard his words, Vikramāditya summoned the treasurer and said, "O treasurer! Take this reciter of praises to the treasury and show him the most precious jewels. Then, let him take as many jewels and other articles as he desires to acquire."

Immediately thereafter, the treasurer led him to the treasury and showed him many divine objects. The panegyrist also took the treasures and jewels he desired, and with his wishes fully satisfied, approached the king and said: "O King! By your grace, I have become a lord of wealth; your hidden treasures have come into my hands. Now your character has surpassed all comparison;
even Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the other gods do not possess a likeness to yours. For instance:"
By whom can you be compared—you who are the Creator entered into the Vedas, Govinda the wielder of the mace, and Śambhu the bearer of the trident who consumes poison? || 284 ||

Having thus offered praise, the panegyrist Brahmāyu and Bhava pronounced their blessings and departed for their own abodes. Having related this story, the statuette said to Bhoja: "O King! If such magnanimity exists within you, then sit upon this throne.
The king remained silent.
Thus ends the nineteenth episode, titled "Liberation from Poverty," in the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja within the *Vikramārka-carita*, in the section concerning the Throne. 29.
Now begins the thirtieth narrative, titled "The Demonstration of Magic.

Again, as soon as the king sat upon the throne, another statuette spoke: "O King, he alone who is endowed with virtues such as magnanimity like those of Vikrama is worthy to sit upon this throne; no other.
The king said, "O statuette, tell me the account of that Vikrama's magnanimity."

She said, "Listen, O King! Once, while the king was seated upon his throne, being attended by all the vassal princes and others, a certain magician arrived at that time. Having offered the blessing, 'May you live as long as Brahmā,' he said, 'O Lord, you are an expert in all arts; many great magicians have come before you and displayed their feats of dexterity. Today, with a gracious glance, one feat must also be observed from me.'"
The king said, "This is not the time for us now; it is the hour for bathing and eating. We shall see you tomorrow morning.

Then, at dawn, a certain man of massive body, his form radiant with a great beard, with broad shoulders and wielding a gleaming sword, arrived accompanied by an exceedingly beautiful woman. He bowed before the king as he sat in the assembly hall. Thereupon, the officials present, seeing this improper conduct, spoke with astonishment: "O Leader! From where have you come?"

He said, "I am a servant of Mahendra. Once cursed by my master, I now dwell upon the earth. This is my wife. Today, a great battle between the gods and the demons has begun; therefore, I shall go there. Considering that this Vikramāditya has conquered his senses, I will entrust my wife to him and depart for the war. Upon hearing this, the king was filled with great wonder.

Then, having entrusted his wife to the king and informed the king, just as he was leaping into the sky with his sword, a great and terrifying roar arose in the air: "Ho! Ho! Kill! Kill! Strike! Strike! All the people seated in the assembly hall looked upward with curiosity.

Immediately thereafter, after a moment had passed, a sword smeared with blood and a single arm fell from the sky into the midst of the royal assembly. Seeing this, everyone exclaimed, "Aha! This woman's heroic husband has been slain by his enemies in battle; one of his arms and his sword have fallen.
