While the members of the assembly were speaking thus, his head fell, and then his headless torso (kabandha) also fell.

Having seen all this, the wife of the hero said: "O Lord! My husband, having engaged in battle on the field of war, has been slain by his enemies. This is his head, this is his arm still clutching a sword, and even his headless trunk (kabandha) has fallen. Therefore, my beloved husband is being chosen by celestial maidens. He for whose sake this body exists—my lord, who was struck down by opposing warriors on the battlefield—is now gone; for whose sake shall I preserve this body now? It is known even to the senseless that women follow the path of their husbands. For instance:"
The moonlight departs with the moon, and the lightning dissolves along with the cloud; indeed, even those devoid of consciousness have realized that women follow after their lovers. 285.
Moreover,
that night which is full, beautiful with the moon, and free from clouds is truly a night;
she who is endowed with the quality of beauty and devoted to her husband is truly a loving woman.

That sweetness which is as sweet as the delight in the nectar of Govinda is true sweetness; and that cleverness which accomplishes the welfare of both worlds for embodied beings is true cleverness. 286.
And so says the Smṛti:
"A woman who, upon the death of her husband, ascends the funeral fire, shall be as worthy of honor as Arundhatī, dwelling eternally in the heavenly world. (287)
As long as a woman does not cause herself to be cremated when her husband has died in the fire, she is by no means released from hell. (288)
She who follows her husband indeed delivers three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and likewise that of her father-in-law. (289)
And likewise:
"A woman who follows her husband shall dwell in heaven for as long a time as there are hairs on three and a half crores of human beings. (290)
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoices together with him alone. || 291 ||
Whether her husband is ill-behaved or well-behaved, or even if he is devoted to every kind of sin, this wife, being firmly established in dharma, delivers him. 292.
Furthermore, the life of a woman deprived of her husband will certainly be fruitless;
what benefit is there in the life of a wretched woman who has lost her husband? (293)

For a father gives but a limited amount, a brother gives a limited amount, and a son gives a limited amount; who would not honor her husband, the giver of the unlimited? Furthermore, even if a woman is surrounded by hundreds of kinsmen and many sons—
That woman who is deprived of her husband becomes an object of pity, perspiring [with distress]. And likewise:
"What will a widow do with perfumes, garlands, various incenses, ornaments, garments, and even beds? (296)
And so it is:
there is no lute without strings, no chariot rolls without wheels;
a woman does not attain happiness even with hundreds of kinsmen if she has no husband. (297)
Whether he be poor, unfortunate, old, diseased, or even disabled; whether fallen or wretched—such a man is the supreme refuge for women. (298)
There is no kinsman equal to a husband; there is no refuge equal to a husband.
For women, no other sorrow exists like widowhood. Blessed among all women is she who dies before her husband. (299)

Having spoken thus, she fell at the king's feet in order to enter the fire. Hearing her words, the king, his ears drenched with the sap of compassion, prepared a funeral pyre with sandalwood and other materials and granted her permission. Having obtained permission from the king, she entered the fire together with her husband’s body. Then the sun set.

At dawn, after the king had performed his morning rituals such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and was seated upon the throne being attended by all the feudatories, princes, and others, that very same leader appeared as before, sword in hand, with an exceedingly tall stature and a radiant body. Having approached, he placed around the king’s neck a garland woven from *kalpavṛkṣa* lotuses—which was densely swarming with a multitude of charming bees greedy for its fragrance—and then began to speak of various martial discourses for him.
He set out. Seeing him arrive, the entire assembly was filled with wonder.

He spoke again: "O King! When I departed from this place for heaven, a great battle took place there between Mahendra and the Daityas. At that time, many Rākṣasas and Daityas were struck down, while some fled. At the conclusion of the battle, the Lord of the Gods spoke to me graciously: 'O Leader! From this day forward, you must not go toward the world of mortals; the end of your curse has arrived.'"

"I am pleased with you; take this bracelet," he said, and placed a pearl bracelet set with jewels from his own hand into my hand. I replied again, "O Lord! At the time of coming here, I deposited my wife in the presence of Vikramārka. Having taken her back, I shall return immediately. Having spoken thus to Purandara, I have come here. You are the crest-jewel of the righteous; that wife of mine must be returned to me, for with her I shall go once more to the heavenly realm.

Having heard those words, the king, together with everyone in the assembly, became indifferent; overcome with great astonishment, he remained silent. Again he said, "O King, why do you sit in silence? Those standing near the king replied, "Your wife has entered the fire. He asked, "For what reason? But they were left without an answer.
Then he said, "O crest-jewel of kings! O brother of another's wife! O wish-fulfilling tree for the world! O King Vikrama! Why is this improper act being performed? Give me back my wife!

Thereupon the king replied, "O leader! Having seen your head fallen by the sword from your arms and your body, and considering you slain in battle, your wife entered the fire along with your remains, having obtained the consent of the members of the assembly and myself."

The leader said, "O King! Even though she was another man's wife, a beautiful young woman, you yourself concealed her within your house after looking upon her with lustful eyes; for there was a rule that since I had died, she must go to heaven in that very body without entering the fire.
Then all the members of the assembly said, "O sir, it is indeed true; she entered the fire in our very presence."

Then, saying "No, no," the hero rose quickly, took that very heroine by the hand from within the chamber behind the throne, brought her into the midst of the royal assembly, removed the veil from her face, and revealed her; thereupon, everyone, with faces bowed in shame, was filled with supreme astonishment.

Then, with a smile, he said to the king: "O Great King, sole vessel for the multitude of all virtues! May you live as long as Brahmā! I am that great master of illusion, and before you I have displayed the dexterity of the art of *indrajāla*.

The king, filled with wonder, became pleased. At that moment, the treasurer approached and said, "O Great King, the tribute has been sent by the King of Pāṇḍya to our lord. The king asked, "What was sent? He replied, "My Lord, listen attentively:"
Eight crores of gold, ninety-three *tulās* of pearls,
fifty elephants adorned by bees greedy for the scent of honey,
three hundred very swift horses, and a hundred courtesans.
O illustrious King Vikrama! This has been sent to you by the glorious Pāṇḍya king. || 300 ||
Then the king said, "Give all of this to the magician.
Thereupon, the treasurer gave everything to him.
Having told this story, the statuette said to King Bhoja, "O King! If such generosity exists in you, then sit upon this throne. The king hung his head in shame.
Thus ends the thirtieth episode, titled "The Demonstration of Sorcery," within the dialogue between the Apsaras and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, concerning the story of the throne. 30.
Now begins the thirty-first tale, titled "The Attainment of the Vetalasiddhi.

Now, as soon as the king sat down upon the throne once more, another statuette spoke: "O King, only he is worthy to sit upon this throne who possesses virtues such as magnanimity, just like those of Vikrama. The king said, "O statuette, tell me the account of that Vikrama’s magnanimity."

She said, "O King! Listen: once, while Vikramārka was ruling the kingdom, a certain naked ascetic (digambara) arrived, gave a fruit into the king's hand, and after pronouncing a blessing, said, 'O King! On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, I shall perform a fire-sacrifice (havana) in the great cremation ground. It is known to me that you are a benefactor of others and preeminent in courage; therefore, you must serve as my assistant (uttarasādhaka) there.'"
"Not far from that great cremation ground stands a śamī tree, where a certain vetāla dwells; he must be carried by you in silence, otherwise my purpose will not be accomplished.
The king promised, "I shall do so."

Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the mendicant arrived at the great cremation ground and remained there having taken the materials for the fire-oblation. When the king saw the Vetāla whom he had been shown standing at the base of a Śamī tree, he took him upon his shoulder; as they were proceeding along the road, the Vetāla said, "O King, tell me some story to dispel the fatigue of the journey.
Out of fear of breaking his vow of silence, the king remained silent.

The Vetāla spoke again: "Out of fear of breaking your vow of silence, you do not tell the story; however, I shall tell it myself. If, at the conclusion of the story, you do not speak out of fear of breaking your silence, your head shall shatter into a thousand pieces. Having said this, he began the tale.

"O King, listen! On the southern slope of the Himalayas, there was once a city named Vindhyavatī. There lived a king named Suvicāraka, and his son was Mayasena. Once, having gone to the forest for the sake of hunting, he saw a deer in the woods; pursuing it, he entered a great wilderness. Then, having reached the path to a certain city and proceeding alone, he saw a river in the midst of his way."
There, on the bank of a river, a certain Brahmin was performing his religious rites. The prince went up to him and said, "O Brahmin, hold my horse for as long as I drink water.
The Brahmin replied, "Am I your servant that I should hold your horse?"

Then, struck by him with a whip, the Brahmin approached the king weeping and reported the incident. Upon hearing this, the king’s eyes reddened with anger, and he commanded that his son be banished from his own country. At that moment, the minister said, "This prince is indeed worthy of enjoying the kingdom; he must not be banished from his own land. This is not appropriate."

The king said, "O Minister! This is indeed appropriate, for this [man] struck the body of a Brāhmaṇa with a whip; therefore, this is a fitting punishment, and the cutting off of his hand must be carried out. A wise person should not harbor hatred toward Brāhmaṇas. O Minister! Have you not heard the Purāṇas? In ancient times, by the curse of a Brāhmaṇa, the fall of Śiva’s *liṅga* occurred, as did a deer’s transformation into a chameleon, Indra’s connection with poverty, and Nahuṣa’s state as a great serpent. Even if one is personally prosperous, one should not insult those worthy of worship. And it is said:"
One who has attained a very exalted position must never insult those worthy of honor;
Nahuṣa fell from his state and became a serpent because he insulted Agastya.
Therefore, all these Brāhmaṇas are to be honored at all times. || 301 ||
And so it is said:
"Who would not perish by provoking those by whom fire was made all-consuming, the great ocean was rendered undrinkable, and the moon was seized by consumption? Furthermore:
Since the denizens of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings (havya) from below, and the ancestors likewise consume the ancestral offerings (kavya), who could be superior to him? || 303 ||
And likewise,
O Bhārata, one should honor those brahmins who are worshipped by all the gods and by men alike, and who observe vows and ascetic penances. (304)
And likewise, it was said by Kṛṣṇa himself in Dvārāvatī: "I do not honor that Brāhmaṇa who does not honor one who curses him a hundred times or speaks harshly to him."
That evildoer is always our own, to be slain and punished in the midst of the fire of Brahma's wrath.
Furthermore, whoever desires to worship me with supreme devotion must always honor the Brahmins; in this way, I become truly pleased. (306)

"O Minister! The hand by which the Brahmin was struck must be cut off," he said; and as he was about to have that hand amputated, the Brahmin approached and said, "O King! At that time, I acted thus under the influence of ignorance. From this day forward, he shall not commit such an improper act again. Out of consideration for me, the prince should be spared; I have become well-pleased.
Having heard his words, the king released his son, and the Brahmin also returned to his own home.
Having told this story, the Vetāla said, "O King, between these two, which one is superior in merit? King Vikrama replied, "The king himself is superior in merit.

Hearing that, because his silence had been broken, the Vetāla returned to the śamī tree. The king also went back there, placed him upon his shoulder, and as he was returning, the Vetāla told him another story. In this manner, twenty-five stories were told by the Vetāla, and the king gave the appropriate answer to each of them.
The Vetāla was pleased by his subtle intellectual acuity and said to Vikrama: "O King! This naked mendicant is making an effort to kill you."

The king asked, "How so? Vetāla replied, "When I have been placed there by you, he will say, 'You are weary; now, having circumambulated the fire-pit and prostrated like a staff, go to your own place. Upon hearing these words of the naked ascetic (Digambara), when you have prostrated yourself like a staff, he will strike you with his sword and perform a sacrifice (homa) with your flesh. If this is done, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā), will come under his control.
Vikrama said, "What should be done now?"

When the Vetāla said, "Do exactly this: bow down like a staff before the naked mendicant and go to your own place," you must say: "I am a sovereign emperor; all kings bow down to me alone, and I have never bowed down to anyone. Therefore, I do not know how to bow. You show me first by bowing down yourself; having seen that, I shall then prostrate."

"Therefore, when he bows down to offer salutation, you must cut off his head; by that, the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) shall come into the palm of your hand. When the Vetāla had thus instructed him, King Vikrama did exactly so. The king attained the eight great *siddhis*.
Then the Vetāla said, "O King! I am pleased with you; choose a boon."
The king said, "If you are pleased with me, then whenever I remember you, you must come to my presence. Having promised, "So be it," he went to his own place, and the king also entered his own city.
Having told this story, the statuette said, "O King, if such virtues as magnanimity exist in you, then sit upon this throne. The king remained silent.

Thus ends the thirty-first episode, titled "The Attainment of Success by the Vetāla," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-carita*, in the section concerning the Throne.
Now begins the thirty-second narrative, titled "The Liberation from the Curse."

Again, as soon as the king sat upon the throne, another statuette spoke: "O King! Only Vikramārka is worthy to sit upon this throne, and no other; there is no king on the face of the earth equal to that Vikrama. He, wandering through the middle of the earth with a sword made of wood, conquered all the rulers of the world and ruled with a single umbrella; he who, having dispelled the fears of others, brought fear upon himself."

"The mantra for subjugating all the kings who exist upon the circle of the earth has been employed. Having expelled all wicked people and liberated the beggars from poverty, and having warded off the sufferings of famine and other calamities, was the earth protected through valor? Therefore, there is no king equal to Vikrama. If such qualities as magnanimity and the like exist in you, then sit upon this throne.
Upon hearing this, King Bhoja remained silent.

Once again, the thirty-two statues spoke to King Bhoja: "O King Bhoja! King Vikramāditya was indeed such a man; you too are no ordinary person. You two are both incarnations of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, in this present age, there is no king whose conduct is more pure than yours, who is more proficient in all the arts, or who is distinguished by the quality of magnanimity. By your grace, the destruction of our sins has occurred for us, the thirty-two statues, and we have also been liberated from the curse.
Bhoja asked, "How so? Tell me the account of that curse."
The statuette said, "Listen, O King! Pārvatī had thirty-two celestial nymphs as her dancers, who were the objects of her supreme affection. Listen to each of their names:"

Miśrakeśī (1), Prabhāvatī (2), Suprabhā (3), Indrasenā (4), Sudatī (5), Anaṅganayanā (6), Kuraṅganayanā (7), Lāvaṇyavatī (8), Kāmakalikā (9), Caṇḍikā (10), Vidyādharī (11), Prajñāvatī (12), Janamohinī (13), Vidyāvatī (14), Nirupamā (15), Harimadhyā (16), Madanasundarī (17), Vilāsarasikā (18), Śṛṅgārakalikā (19), Manmathasañjīvanī (20), Ratilīlā (21), and Madanavatī (22), Citrarekhā (23).
Suratagahvarā (24), Priyadarśanā (25), Kāmonmādinī (26), Sukhasāgarā (27), Śaśikalā (28), Candrarekhā (29), Haṃsagāminī (30), Kāmarasikā (31), and Unmādinī (32).

Once, while the two Śaṅkaras were staying in the pleasure-pavilion, gazing at one another with supreme love and playfulness, they were observed by us—under the influence of poor judgment and driven by the curiosity natural to women.
Then the goddess Pārvatī, being firm, cursed us angrily: "Become lifeless dolls and cling to Indra's throne! Thereupon, we entreated her with prostrations for the end of the curse.

Then the goddess said: "When that throne is occupied by Vikrama, and subsequently comes into the hands of Bhoja, and when King Bhoja hears the *Vikramacarita* from you, at that very moment the end of the curse shall occur."

"After a very long time, today by your grace we shall behold the feet of the Lord of Pārvatī and rejoice. You too, having caused a temple to be built upon this throne and having installed the image of Umā-Maheśvara there on an eight-petaled lotus, should perform worship daily with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Protecting the people who are devoted to the duties of their respective castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), rule the earth; thereby, those two [deities], becoming pleased with you, will fulfill all your desires."

Thus ends the thirty-second episode, titled "The Liberation from the Doll’s Curse," within the dialogue between the Apsarā and Bhoja in the *Vikramārka-caritra*, concerning the story of the throne. || 32 ||
Conclusion: When this story of the puppets has thus concluded, those dancing girls of yours, having obtained permission from the king, are coming right here; look, look!
When the Supreme Lord had thus spoken to Pārvatī and ceased speaking, those thirty-two [goddesses] approached the peak of Kailāsa and prostrated at the feet of Umā and Maheśvara.

The Goddess, too, having seen them, joyfully honored them with blessings and said to the Supreme Lord: "O Lord! That curse which was given by me to these women when I was unable to restrain the force of my anger—may this story of Vikrama, which has issued from your own mouth, which is the very root of that curse, which fascinates the minds of all people, and which instigates activity toward virtues such as compassion and altruism, exist for the welfare of the world, becoming a source of increasing celebration for all living beings in their acts of helping others."
"By your grace, may these [arts] also be victorious in all respects regarding the arts of dance, song, and so forth.
The Lord also said with a smile, "So be it."
